text: What is the right bootstrap flow when Portal finds no tmux server running, and does the idea's proposed sequence (detect no server, check resurrect data, start a _boot session, poll for restore, kill _boot, proceed) hold up?

Portal is plugin-agnostic: it has no knowledge of tmux-continuum, tmux-resurrect or any other tmux plugin, never checks for resurrect data (~/.local/share/tmux/resurrect/last), holds no conditional logic on plugin presence, and has no awareness of how sessions get restored. Its only job is to ensure a server is running.
why: Whether the user has resurrect/continuum, another plugin or nothing is tmux's business; dropping the resurrect check removes a second code path and simplifies the design.
rules_out: Option A: check resurrect data first and wait conditionally, two code paths
alternatives: Option A (original proposal): check resurrect data at ~/.local/share/tmux/resurrect/last first, conditionally wait
Option B: always start the server, always poll briefly, proceed regardless

text: Portal's source code held zero references to resurrect or continuum: it was already decoupled from them, every reference sitting in idea docs and old workflow discussions.
how: Searched the codebase during the discussion.

text: Option C: Portal starts the server and drops into the TUI at once with a loading interstitial; sessions appear as tmux and its plugins restore them, through the TUI's refresh cycle, with no blocking poll before entry.
why: Keeps x responsive, keeps Portal plugin-agnostic, and gives the user visual feedback that something is happening.
rules_out: A blocking poll loop before the TUI opens
alternatives: Option B: always start the server, always poll briefly, proceed regardless

text: Bootstrap first checks whether the tmux server is running (for example tmux list-sessions or tmux info succeeding); if it is, bootstrap is skipped entirely and Portal proceeds normally, the fast path; if not, the bootstrap flow runs.
why: Only a missing server needs bootstrapping.

text: Bootstrap has two phases with different owners: the server start runs in PersistentPreRunE, shared by all commands, calls tmux start-server and returns immediately; the session wait is owned by the Bubble Tea model on the TUI path (the interstitial its initial state, its existing refresh cycle detecting sessions, transitioning to the normal view once the min/max bounds are satisfied) and by the command on the CLI path (print the stderr message, poll for sessions within the same bounds, then proceed to normal output).
why: Cleanly separates ensuring the server exists (shared, fast) from waiting for sessions (context-specific presentation).

text: How should the _boot session's lifecycle be handled, and is a throwaway session needed at all to keep the server alive?
tmux start-server (alias start) explicitly starts the tmux server without creating any sessions.
how: Checked man tmux.

text: Bootstrap starts the server with tmux start-server; no throwaway _boot session is created, named, hidden or cleaned up.
why: start-server runs the server without any session, so a throwaway session is unnecessary.
rules_out: tmux new-session -d -s _boot

text: tmux's server exits by default when it has no sessions.
how: tmux docs, as the discussion notes.

text: That continuum, where present, hooks into the started server quickly enough to create sessions before the empty server exits is an assumption, not verified.
how: Stated as an assumption in the discussion and the spec; nothing measured it.

text: No keepalive session is added upfront; one may be added later only if the server is actually found to exit before continuum creates sessions.
why: Treated as an edge case to handle if it actually occurs.

why: They do not need tmux.

text: What happens when things go wrong: timeouts, no resurrect data, partial restores, and the risk of a loop where the server starts, has no sessions, exits and is started again?

text: Bootstrap is a one-shot attempt: tmux start-server is tried once with no retry if it fails, then Portal waits briefly and proceeds regardless; the session wait that follows polls for sessions to appear, not for the server start to succeed.
why: Portal does not need the server running to show its UI; it needs tmux only when the user creates or attaches a session, and those commands handle the server's lifecycle natively, so no loop is needed.
rules_out: A retry loop restarting the server

cites.section: Q4: Error Handling and Edge Cases > Decision

text: Every scenario converges to a sensible state: with continuum and saved sessions, the server starts and the TUI shows the restored sessions; with continuum and no saved data, or no continuum at all, the server starts, nothing restores, the server may exit and the TUI shows the empty state; with tmux already running, bootstrap is skipped. A session the user later creates through Portal starts the server implicitly through tmux new-session, with no Portal intervention.
why: Portal only needs tmux when the user acts, and tmux new-session starts a server itself.

text: How long should the loading interstitial and the CLI wait last, balancing responsiveness against a jarring flash when sessions appear almost at once?
The loading state ends as soon as sessions are detected, within a minimum and a maximum bound, the same timing logic on the TUI and CLI paths with different presentation.
why: Balances responsiveness with avoiding a flash.

text: The minimum wait is 1 second.
why: Prevents a jarring flash of the loading state when sessions appear very quickly.

text: The maximum wait is 6 seconds, after which Portal proceeds regardless, even if no sessions have appeared.
why: Bounds the wait when nothing restores.

text: The bounds are not user-configurable, and both are defined as named constants in the code for easy adjustment.
why: Sensible defaults cover the common case without adding user-facing complexity.

text: The CLI path detects sessions by polling tmux list-sessions every 500ms; the TUI path uses its existing refresh cycle, which already polls session state, rather than a separate poll loop.
why: Reuses the TUI's own polling and gives the CLI a direct check.

text: Is removing the com.leeovery.tmux-boot LaunchAgent workaround part of this feature?

This feature eliminates the need for the com.leeovery.tmux-boot LaunchAgent, making Portal self-contained for tmux server lifecycle; removing the LaunchAgent file itself, which lives in dotfiles, is a separate manual cleanup, not a Portal code change.

text: On macOS, Portal silently writes its config files (projects.json, aliases, hooks.json) to ~/Library/Application Support/portal/ instead of the documented ~/.config/portal/; every command works at the wrong path, no error shows, and users or tooling checking ~/.config/portal/ find nothing. It reproduces always on macOS, and affects all macOS users; Linux is unaffected.
how: Read in the investigation's symptoms, reproduced by checking both directories after running Portal on macOS, and restated in the spec's problem statement.

text: Severity is medium: the documentation and tooling disagree with where the files are, and real user data already sits at the wrong path, so a fix needs a migration.
how: Read in the investigation's impact assessment.

text: The root cause is cmd/config.go's configFilePath(envVar, filename), which checks the per-file env var first, then falls back to Go's os.UserConfigDir() and joins portal/<filename>; on macOS os.UserConfigDir() returns ~/Library/Application Support, the Apple-native path, not the XDG ~/.config the project documents on every platform.
how: Read by tracing the code path through cmd/config.go.

text: configFilePath is the single entry point, with three callers, all in the cmd package: cmd/alias.go (PORTAL_ALIASES_FILE, aliases), cmd/clean.go (PORTAL_PROJECTS_FILE, projects.json) and cmd/hooks.go (PORTAL_HOOKS_FILE, hooks.json).
how: Read in the code trace.

text: The per-file env var overrides (PORTAL_PROJECTS_FILE, PORTAL_ALIASES_FILE, PORTAL_HOOKS_FILE) are user-facing features documented in the README, not test-only; they bypass configFilePath's directory logic entirely, so the bug and the fix leave them unaffected.
how: Read in the code trace and the README, as the investigation's notes correct the trace's first reading of them as test-only.

text: No XDG_CONFIG_HOME handling existed anywhere in the codebase; the project chose XDG conventions cross-platform but used a platform-aware stdlib function, and on Linux os.UserConfigDir() already respects XDG_CONFIG_HOME.
how: Read in the investigation's contributing factors and notes.

text: It wasn't caught because cmd/config_test.go compares against os.UserConfigDir() itself, verifying consistency with the stdlib rather than the intended path; the bug is silent; and development and testing happen on macOS, where the wrong path became normal.
how: Read in the investigation and the spec's problem statement.

text: The blast radius is cmd/config.go and cmd/config_test.go, and all three config files; CLAUDE.md, the README and the v1 specification already document ~/.config/portal/ correctly, and existing macOS users hold real data at ~/Library/Application Support/portal/ that the fix must migrate.
how: Read in the investigation's blast radius.

text: How should configFilePath resolve the config directory so macOS uses ~/.config/portal/ as documented?
configFilePath replaces os.UserConfigDir() with XDG resolution: XDG_CONFIG_HOME when set and non-empty, else ~/.config (os.UserHomeDir() + /.config), then portal/<filename> appended as before.
why: It fixes macOS while preserving Linux users' custom XDG_CONFIG_HOME, which os.UserConfigDir() already respected there; the project has chosen XDG conventions and users and tooling expect ~/.config/portal/.
rules_out: Hardcoding ~/.config via os.UserHomeDir(), which would regress Linux users with a custom XDG_CONFIG_HOME
Keeping os.UserConfigDir() on macOS and changing the docs to Apple-native paths
alternatives: Option A: hardcode ~/.config via os.UserHomeDir() + /.config
Option C: keep os.UserConfigDir() on macOS, update docs

text: XDG_CONFIG_HOME gets no special handling for trailing slashes or relative paths.
why: filepath.Join normalises trailing slashes, and matching os.UserConfigDir(), which validates neither, is sufficient.

text: The per-file env var check (PORTAL_PROJECTS_FILE and the others) stays first in the resolution order, unchanged.
why: The overrides are user-facing and bypass the directory logic, so the fix leaves them as they are.

text: How should existing macOS users' files at ~/Library/Application Support/portal/ reach the new path?
A one-shot migration moves projects.json, aliases and hooks.json from ~/Library/Application Support/portal/ to the new config path.
why: Real user data exists at the old path.

text: The migration runs inside configFilePath() before it returns the resolved path, and migrates only the one file it was called with; no sentinel is kept, since it acts only when the file exists at the old path and not at the new, so once moved every later call is a no-op.
why: It is idempotent by construction.

text: The migration does not check runtime.GOOS; it checks only whether the old path exists.
why: That path won't exist on Linux, so it is implicitly macOS-only and the logic stays platform-agnostic.

text: A file that already exists at the new path is never overwritten: that file is skipped, so partial state (some files at the old path, some at the new) is handled file by file.
why: Migration must preserve existing data.

text: The move uses os.Rename.
why: Both paths are under $HOME, so always on the same volume.

text: After migrating, the old ~/Library/Application Support/portal/ directory is removed if empty.
why: The spec's migration behaviour leaves no empty old directory behind.

text: The migration is best-effort and silent on success: a move that fails (e.g. permission denied) logs a warning to stderr and the rest carries on; a partial migration is acceptable, the next run retrying any file still at the old path.
why: Retry comes free from the per-call idempotent check.

text: configFilePath() still only returns a path and creates no directory for its callers, whose stores already call os.MkdirAll before writing; the migration itself calls os.MkdirAll on the target directory before moving files.
why: A rename needs its target directory to exist.

text: What tests should cover the fix?

cmd/config_test.go tests that configFilePath returns ~/.config/portal/<file> with no env var or XDG_CONFIG_HOME set (not os.UserConfigDir()), respects XDG_CONFIG_HOME when set, and that the per-file env var overrides still take precedence over both the XDG and fallback paths.
why: The old tests compared against os.UserConfigDir() itself, which is how the bug went uncaught.

text: Migration tests cover moving files from ~/Library/Application Support/portal/ to ~/.config/portal/, a no-op when files are already at the correct path, never overwriting an existing target file, partial state, and removing the empty old directory after moving.
why: Each tests one rule of the migration's behaviour.

text: Fix complexity and regression risk are both low (one function change plus migration logic; the migration preserves existing data and the env var overrides bypass the changed code), and a regular release was recommended.
how: Read in the investigation's risk assessment.

text: The daemon's structural index merge re-introduces sessions killed in tmux: mergeSkippedPanes -> mergePane -> findOrAppendSession (internal/state/capture.go:154) appends sessions from prev.Sessions into the freshly built index without checking that they still exist in tmux, so any paneKey in the @portal-skeleton-<paneKey> marker set whose session was killed re-commits the dead session to sessions.json, and the next bootstrap's restore reconstructs it: to the user, killed sessions reappear after a Portal restart.
how: Read in the code during the investigation; restated in the approved spec's bug summary.

text: The skeleton marker is meant only to preserve pre-hydrate state for panes skeleton-restored but not yet hydrated; it must not override the live tmux session list.
how: Read in the investigation's statement of expected behaviour.

text: Root cause: mergeSkippedPanes treats the @portal-skeleton-<paneKey> marker set as authoritative evidence that a session is in flight and does not validate against the live tmux session list, which the same CaptureStructure call already knows as keep / idx.Sessions; a stale marker makes findOrAppendSession append a dead session, which is committed to sessions.json and persists into prev indefinitely, self-reinforcing through captureAndCommit's deps.PrevIndex = &idx. The merge was designed under the implicit assumption that markers cannot be stale.
how: Read in the code during the investigation.

text: The bug's code path: tick (cmd/state_daemon.go:77, every 1s in _portal-saver) -> captureAndCommit reads the full marker set with state.ListSkeletonMarkers (line 115) -> state.CaptureStructure (line 121) lists live session names (capture.go line 66), strips internal ones into keep (line 71), builds the fresh sessions from keep (lines 85-96, killed sessions correctly absent), then calls mergeSkippedPanes when skipSet is non-empty and prev non-nil (line 100) -> mergeSkippedPanes (117-130) merges each prev pane whose SanitizePaneKey is in skipSet with no reference to keep or idx.Sessions -> mergePane / findOrAppendSession (137-148, 154) re-create the dead session -> captureAndCommit commits it via state.Commit (line 152) and sets deps.PrevIndex = &idx (line 156) -> the next bootstrap's Restore step reconstructs it.
how: Read in the code during the investigation.

text: Key files: internal/state/capture.go (mergeSkippedPanes, mergePane, findOrAppendSession) is the defective layer; cmd/state_daemon.go (captureAndCommit, tick) is the caller that sets PrevIndex to the committed index every tick; internal/state/markers.go (ListSkeletonMarkers) reads markers faithfully and is not at fault; cmd/bootstrap/ and internal/bootstrapadapter/ are where the cleanup step goes.
how: Read in the code during the investigation.

text: Marker lifecycle: set by internal/restore/session.go:380-384 (setSkeletonMarker -> state.SetSkeletonMarker) during bootstrap's skeleton restore; unset by the hydrate helper at cmd/state_hydrate.go:312 (UnsetSkeletonMarkerForFIFO) after scrollback replay; server-scoped (set-option -s), so it persists across hydrate failures, daemon restarts and manual tmux operations, indefinitely if no cleanup runs.
how: Read in the code during the investigation.

text: Markers leak through any of: a hydrate timeout, a daemon crash mid-hydrate, a tmux kill-session against a not-yet-hydrated pane, a version upgrade of _portal-saver mid-hydrate, or a manual tmux set-option -s @portal-skeleton-<key>. No cleanup path exists: bootstrap's CleanStale prunes only hook entries and SweepOrphanFIFOs only orphan FIFO files, so a leaked marker persists for the tmux server's lifetime.
how: Read in the code during the investigation.

text: The bug self-sustains: prev in captureAndCommit is replaced with the just-committed index every successful tick (cmd/state_daemon.go:156), so a dead session committed once lives in prev indefinitely, even if the marker were later cleared; and keep, the live-tmux truth, is not threaded into mergeSkippedPanes.
how: Read in the code during the investigation.

text: Impact: severity high (silent corruption of persisted state, user-visible zombie sessions, a trust regression on the promise that the user controls their session list); scope all users running portal state daemon, triggering under any path that produces a stale @portal-skeleton-* marker.
how: Read in the investigation's impact assessment.

text: A killed session reappears in ~/.config/portal/state/sessions.json within one daemon tick, about 1s under normal load since the daemon's TickerPeriod is 1s (the 30s figure is MaxGap, the forced-save fallback for idle systems, not the tick interval), with no error or warning surfacing.

text: Every consumer reading sessions.json sees the ghost session: internal/restore reconstructs it on bootstrap, and the CLI list commands and the TUI session picker show it after a restart.
how: Read in the code during the investigation.

text: Synthetic reproduction, needing no hydrate cascade: with portal state daemon running and a session it has already captured and committed at least once (so it is in prev.Sessions), set tmux set-option -s @portal-skeleton-<paneKey> 1 for one of its panes, kill the session, wait one tick (about 1s, up to 30s on an idle system where MaxGap bounds it), and sessions.json holds the killed session. Reproducible always given the marker set and the session killed.
how: Read in the investigation and the approved spec's reproduction steps.

text: Observed in the wild on 2026-05-08: three sessions resurrected after kill (agentic-workflows-XXrJ3J, leeovery-Gi5NLG, leeovery-feqhpg), and tmux show-options -s held exactly three matching stale markers (each <session>__1.1); killing an unmarked session (game-ideas) did not resurrect it. Marker presence is necessary and sufficient, given a daemon tick, for the symptom.
how: Observed by the person on their live tmux server and read with tmux show-options -s.
result: Exactly three stale @portal-skeleton-* markers, agentic-workflows-XXrJ3J__1.1, leeovery-Gi5NLG__1.1 and leeovery-feqhpg__1.1, matching the three resurrecting sessions; the unmarked game-ideas did not resurrect.

text: Why it wasn't caught: the unit test TestCaptureStructureMergeSkippedPanes/merges a skipped pane's session and window from prev when missing from fresh (internal/state/capture_test.go:570-617) asserts the buggy behaviour as correct; the built-in-session-resurrection spec framed the merge around hydrate-in-progress without modelling stale markers; that feature's integration tests cover only the happy skeleton -> hydrate flow, not the killed-mid-flight path; and reproducing it needs a hydrate failure or a manual marker injection, hard to engineer in CI.
how: Read in the code and the earlier feature's work during the investigation.

text: While a marker is live for a paneKey, the daemon's capture loop skips the scrollback save for that pane (cmd/state_daemon.go:131-133), so panes whose markers leaked but whose sessions are still alive, or were re-created with the same key, silently have no scrollback saved; the merge fix alone does not close this.
how: Read in the code during the investigation.

text: Every consumer of sessions.json and the daemon's prev was traced: none depends on the merge introducing arbitrary prev sessions, and hydrate-in-progress, the merge's intended use, survives because restore's phase A creates the session in tmux before the marker is set.
how: Read in the code during the investigation.

text: How should the daemon's merge stop re-introducing sessions killed in tmux?

mergeSkippedPanes builds a structural map from the fresh index (session names, then each session's window indices, then each window's pane indices) and merges a prev pane only when all three levels exist in the fresh index; a skeleton marker is no longer authoritative and protects only panes whose whole path tmux still acknowledges.
why: The person asked for a proper fix hardening both layers; the same flaw exists at window and pane level, where kill-window or kill-pane on a live session leaves an analogous resurrection path.
rules_out: Session-level filtering only: leaves the window- and pane-level resurrection paths open.
Pre-filtering skipSet in captureAndCommit: costs an extra ListSessionNames tmux call per tick that CaptureStructure already makes, and staleness is a merge-layer concern.
Dropping the merge's introduce-missing-session behaviour entirely: may break the hydrate phase-A race where a skeleton-restored session is briefly invisible to list-sessions; higher behavioural risk.

cites.section: Fix Component A: Live-Set Filtering in `mergeSkippedPanes`

text: Session level: a prev session whose name is not in the fresh index is not merged, even when its paneKey is in skipSet.
why: The killed session's resurrection is the symptom.

text: Window level: a prev window in skipSet whose window index is not present in the otherwise-live fresh session is dropped from the merge result.
why: kill-window against a still-live session would otherwise leave an analogous resurrection path.

text: Pane level: a prev pane in skipSet whose pane index is not present in the otherwise-live fresh window is dropped from the merge result.
why: kill-pane against a still-live session would otherwise leave an analogous resurrection path.

text: The structural map is built locally inside mergeSkippedPanes from idx.Sessions, already in scope at its call site (capture.go:100), rather than threading keep or another live-truth value through its signature; it may grow a small private helper (such as buildLiveStructure(idx)) but its public surface stays the same.
why: idx.Sessions already holds the live tmux truth there, built from keep just above; it keeps the change inside mergeSkippedPanes with no signature or caller updates, and leaves mergePane and findOrAppendSession's surface alone.

text: mergePane and findOrAppendSession keep their behaviour and contracts unchanged, and get no belt-and-braces defensive checks: the filter at the merge's entry point is the single point of enforcement.
why: They are helpers of the merge, listed among the files touched only because the merge logic in the same file changes.

text: Once mergeSkippedPanes no longer reintroduces dead sessions, sessions.json self-heals on the next daemon tick: the polluted prev's dead session no longer survives the merge, captureAndCommit commits the clean index, and deps.PrevIndex = &idx carries clean state forward.
how: Read in the code during the investigation.

text: The merge's intended use, hydrate-in-progress panes briefly invisible to list-sessions, stays correct: phase-A skeleton-restored panes, marker set and session, window and pane present in tmux, are still merged from prev.
why: Restore's phase A creates the session in tmux before the marker is set, so legitimate hydrate-in-progress panes always have their path in the fresh enumeration and the filter is structurally distinct from this case.

text: The merge does not assume marker validity: markers can go stale through process crashes, a version-upgrade restart or manual tmux operations even with a perfect hydrate FIFO handshake, so the merge holds regardless of how the companion hydrate-cascade bug is resolved.
why: This bug is wrong independently of the companion bug.

text: Should stale skeleton markers be cleaned up, and how?

This work unit adds a new bootstrap step that unsets stale @portal-skeleton-* markers, those whose paneKey has no live pane, closing the skipped-scrollback gap and stopping markers accumulating over the tmux server's lifetime.
why: The merge fix alone resolves the resurrection symptom, but the scrollback save stays skipped for panes with leaked markers, a harm real for the user now; the person moved from a tight surgical fix to fixing it properly once that surfaced.
rules_out: Deferring marker cleanup to a separate work unit: rejected per the person's direction, since the scrollback-save side effect is real now and both changes are local to layers already in scope.

text: The cleanup step goes into the bootstrap orchestrator (cmd/bootstrap/) between the existing step 6, clearing @portal-restoring, and step 7, SweepOrphanFIFOs, becoming the new step 7, with SweepOrphanFIFOs and the later steps renumbered down by one.
why: It runs after the restoring marker is cleared and immediately before the orphan-FIFO sweep.

cites.section: Fix Component B: Stale-Marker Cleanup Bootstrap Step

text: The step enumerates the live @portal-skeleton-* server-option markers, enumerates the live tmux panes as paneKeys, takes the markers whose paneKey is not in the live pane set, and unsets each (set-option -us @portal-skeleton-<key>).
why: Stale is defined as no live pane for the paneKey.

text: The step is best-effort, mirroring CleanStale's soft-warning semantics: a failure (tmux unavailable, an individual unset error, a live-pane enumeration error) is a soft warning the orchestrator collects and drains after the bootstrap, never a fatal abort.
why: It matches the posture of the existing CleanStale step.

text: The cleanup never treats a silently empty live-pane result as authoritative: when live-pane enumeration fails, or returns zero panes through tmux instability, it skips the unset pass and emits a soft warning.
why: An empty live-pane set would mark every marker stale, including those protecting legitimate hydrate-in-progress panes, destabilising a still-live tmux server.

text: The error-propagating live-pane call is the primary defence against a mass unset; an explicit skip-the-cleanup-on-zero-panes guard is recommended as belt-and-braces if the runtime can plausibly observe zero live panes while markers exist.
why: It guards the same mass-unset hazard should the error-propagating call ever return an empty set.

text: The cleanup step takes no lock or sequencing constraint against the daemon's ticks, though EnsureSaver (step 4) may already have the daemon ticking.
why: The merge filter removes the marker's authority over the merge, so a daemon reading a marker about to be unset cannot resurrect a dead session.

text: Running the cleanup immediately before SweepOrphanFIFOs is intentional: FIFOs whose markers were stale become eligible for that sweep in the same bootstrap, so both halves of a stale-marker / orphan-FIFO pair are reclaimed together rather than the sweep staying blocked by the stale marker protecting the FIFO.
why: SweepOrphanFIFOs removes hydrate-*.fifo files whose paneKey no longer has a live marker.

text: The cleanup does no special-casing of a partially failed restore: it acts only on markers that were set, leaving those whose pane is alive and unsetting those whose pane is not, however the staleness arose.
why: By the time it runs, stale is observably no live pane for the paneKey, which is correct whatever caused it.

text: The bootstrap Orchestrator exposes a new seam for the step (recommended name StaleMarkerCleaner or similar, the final name an implementation detail consistent with adjacent seams), its production adapter in bootstrapadapter wiring the concrete dependencies.
why: It follows the existing bootstrap seam and adapter pattern.

text: The seam exposes three methods, one per responsibility (marker enumeration, live-pane enumeration, marker unset), so each can be mocked independently; one composite interface or three small ones is an implementation choice, and tests use mocks following the bootstrap testing pattern.
why: Each responsibility can then be mocked on its own.

text: Markers are enumerated with state.ListSkeletonMarkers, the canonical source, which already returns a map keyed by paneKey with the @portal-skeleton- prefix stripped, so the marker side needs no further parsing.
why: It is the canonical marker source and already yields paneKeys.

text: (*tmux.Client).ListAllPanes swallows tmux errors, returning an empty list and no error on failure (internal/tmux/tmux.go:551-557), while ListAllPanesWithFormat propagates errors (tmux.go:528-534).
how: Read in the code.

text: Live panes are enumerated with (*tmux.Client).ListAllPanesWithFormat and a format such as #{session_name}:#{window_index}.#{pane_index}, never ListAllPanes; on an error the step degrades to a soft warning and never falls through to unsetting every marker.
why: ListAllPanes's swallowed error would read as no live panes and unset every marker, those protecting live hydrate-in-progress panes included.
rules_out: ListAllPanes: swallows tmux errors.

text: Each live-pane entry, session:window.pane, is converted to canonical paneKey form (session__window.pane) with state.SanitizePaneKey(session, window, pane) before the set difference.
why: Without it the two sides use incompatible separators and the difference is meaningless.

text: A live-pane line is parsed by splitting on its rightmost colon into session and window.pane, splitting the right half on the dot into window and pane, and parsing each with strconv.Atoi; extracting this parse and sanitise as a shared helper or inlining it in the step is an implementation choice.
why: tmux session names may contain a colon, and the rightmost one separates the session from window.pane.

text: A line that fails to parse is skipped, left out of the live-pane set without aborting the cleanup, with a soft warning if the failure is unexpected.
why: A malformed line must never cause a mass unset.

text: A stale marker is unset with (*tmux.Client).UnsetServerOption, given the full option name: the SkeletonMarkerPrefix constant followed by the canonical paneKey.
why: The marker is a server option named by that prefix and the paneKey.

text: The work unit does not modify the marker's set path (internal/restore/session.go:380-384, setSkeletonMarker) or its unset path (cmd/state_hydrate.go:312, UnsetSkeletonMarkerForFIFO): the fix is defensive, accepting that markers leak and making the merge and the new bootstrap cleanup handle stale ones.

text: What lies inside this work unit's scope, and how is it released?

The companion bug killed-sessions-resurrect-on-restart (logged 2026-05-08), the likeliest producer of stale markers in normal use, is out of scope: it lives in cmd/state_hydrate.go / cmd/state_signal_hydrate.go, is scoped independently, and this unit does not depend on it; the fixes are orthogonal.

text: Both changes are in scope and compose without architectural surgery: the merge filter in internal/state/capture.go (estimated about 15 lines) and the new cleanup bootstrap step (estimated about 50 lines with adapter wiring, plus orchestrator sequence and test updates); the estimates are illustrative, not a scope budget.

The test TestCaptureStructureMergeSkippedPanes/merges a skipped pane's session and window from prev when missing from fresh (internal/state/capture_test.go:570-617) is replaced with its inverse: a prev session whose name is not in fresh is not merged, even when its paneKey is in skipSet.

why: It pins the cleanup's unset.

The synthetic reproduction (set the marker, kill the session, wait one daemon tick) does not reintroduce the killed session into sessions.json.

text: Three tmux session managers were compared against ZW (Zellij Workspaces): tmux-session-wizard (shell, ~247 stars, tmux plugin with an fzf popup), tmux-sessionx (shell, ~1.2k stars, tmux plugin with an fzf popup and preview) and sesh (Go, ~1.6k stars, a standalone CLI that delegates its UI to fzf or gum).
how: Research into each project's repository, recorded in the comparative analysis.

text: tmux-session-wizard binds prefix + T to an fzf picker over active tmux sessions (excluding the current one) and zoxide's directories; a selection either switches to the session or creates one named after the directory. It is a handful of shell functions with no custom TUI, no config file and no project registry, and its `t` command also runs outside tmux.
how: Research into the project's repository and source layout.

text: tmux-session-wizard names sessions from directories in three modes, `directory` (basename), `full-path` and `short-path` (intermediate directories compressed to initials, e.g. `/u/l/bin`), through a `session_name()` function whose `_normalize()` helper replaces spaces, dots and colons with hyphens.
how: Research into the project's source.

text: Against tmux-session-wizard, ZW is stronger in its built-in TUI (sections, empty states, mobile optimisation), its exited/resurrectable sessions section, its session metadata (tab count, attached indicator), its layout selection on create, its utility mode inside the multiplexer, and its kill and rename operations; the wizard only switches.
how: Comparison in the research analysis.

text: The research suggests zoxide as an optional project source: rather than building projects.json from scratch, directory suggestions could be pulled from zoxide for a warm start, supplementing the file browser as a discovery mechanism while the manual registry stays for aliases and custom names. It ranks the idea medium effort, medium value (from the wizard and sesh). No line shows it taken up.
how: Recommendation in the research analysis.

text: The research reads tmux-session-wizard as proof that much can be done with zero configuration, reinforcing ZW's already minimal config.
how: Conclusion in the research analysis.

text: tmux-sessionx is a fuzzy session manager over fzf-tmux, configured through 20+ `@sessionx-*` tmux options: a preview pane (a file tree of the session's directory, previews through `bat`), multiple browse modes cycled by Ctrl shortcuts (sessions, windows, tree, config directories, tmuxinator, zoxide, fzf-marks), window-level navigation across sessions, a tree mode nesting windows under sessions, inline rename (Ctrl-r) and inline delete (alt+backspace). Its script orders sessions most-recently-used, applies filter patterns, and dispatches a selection by type: a directory creates a session, `session:window` targets a window, plain text names a session.
how: Research into the project's repository and scripts.

text: Against tmux-sessionx, ZW is stronger in its mobile-first design (sessionx's dense multi-mode interface would be unusable on a phone), its purpose-built TUI not bound by fzf, its session creation flow (a naming prompt and layout choice), its project memory with metadata in projects.json, its simpler two-state mental model (main picker and utility mode) against 7+ modes, and its file browser over sessionx's Ctrl-e expand-PWD.
how: Comparison in the research analysis.

text: The research finds a session preview (file tree, last command and the like, without entering the session) valuable as a concept, ZW already showing tab count, and suggests an optional detail view or preview; its summary lists a preview pane in the picker as not worth adopting, screen space being too precious on mobile.
how: Recommendation in the research analysis.

cites.section: Summary: Ideas Explicitly Not Worth Adopting

text: The research suggests Zellij tab awareness as ZW's equivalent of sessionx's window-level navigation: ZW already queries tab names and could allow navigating to a specific tab from the picker. Its summary ranks tab-level navigation high effort, low value. No line shows it taken up.
how: Recommendation in the research analysis.

text: The research names a tree view, sessions with their tabs nested beneath, as possibly useful for users with many sessions and worth considering as a future enhancement. No line shows it taken up.
how: Recommendation in the research analysis.

text: The research notes the pattern of aggregating several session sources (sessionx integrating tmuxinator, fzf-marks and zoxide at once; sesh more cleanly), while holding that ZW should not bloat itself with integrations; its summary lists tmuxinator and fzf-marks integration as not worth adopting, being the tmux ecosystem's rather than Zellij's.
how: Conclusion in the research analysis.

cites.section: Summary: Ideas Explicitly Not Worth Adopting

text: sesh is a standalone Go CLI of about 20 focused packages that aggregates tmux sessions, configured projects, tmuxinator layouts and zoxide directories into one list, filterable by source (`sesh list -t`, `-z`, `-c`), with no TUI of its own: users wire it to fzf, gum or television through tmux key bindings. A `Connector` interface's `Connect(name, opts)` coordinates session creation; configuration is TOML at `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/sesh/sesh.toml`, defining sessions with paths, startup commands, preview commands and windows; its commands are `list`, `connect`, `last`, `root`, `preview` and `completion`, and it has Raycast and Ulauncher extensions.
how: Research into the project's repository and package layout.

text: Against sesh, ZW is stronger in its built-in TUI, a guaranteed mobile experience rather than one resting on the user's fzf configuration, first-class exited sessions (sesh shows only live tmux sessions), its discoverable interactive layout picker, its interactive file browser, and its lower complexity: sesh needs fzf, tmux key binding syntax and TOML understood, ZW needs `zw` run.
how: Comparison in the research analysis.

text: The research suggests a quick toggle to the previous session, as `sesh last` gives (fixing tmux's detach-on-destroy), as `zw last` or a key binding between the two most recent sessions, ranked low effort, medium value. No line shows it taken up.
how: Recommendation in the research analysis.

text: The research suggests letting users choose the order of session types in the list, whether sessions or projects come first, as sesh lets users control. No line shows it taken up.
how: Recommendation in the research analysis.

text: The research holds that sesh's multi-window session definitions overlap heavily with Zellij's own .kdl layouts, so ZW should lean on Zellij's layouts rather than duplicate them.
how: Conclusion in the research analysis.

text: The research concludes ZW equals or beats all three tools in seven areas: a purpose-built TUI (all three delegate to fzf), mobile-first design for phone SSH, exited session management, interactive layout selection on create, a utility mode inside the multiplexer, session metadata in the picker (tab count, attached indicator), and structured project memory (projects.json with aliases, names and timestamps, richer than zoxide's frequency tracking).
how: Conclusion in the research analysis.

text: The research lists multiple browse modes (7+, as sessionx has) and extensive configuration (20+ options, as sessionx has) as not worth adopting: the modes' complexity is antithetical to ZW's mobile-first simplicity, and ZW is opinionated by design.
how: Conclusion in the research analysis.

text: The research lists delegating the UI to fzf, as all three compared tools do, as not worth adopting: ZW's whole value is its purpose-built TUI.
how: Conclusion in the research analysis.

text: What is the tool, and what problem does it solve?
Portal is a Go CLI that provides an interactive session picker for tmux: it runs at bare shell, before entering tmux, and offers a mobile-friendly TUI for managing tmux sessions.

cites.section: What is CX and what problem does it solve? > Decision

text: The problem it solves: when SSH/Mosh-ing to a machine (e.g. from a phone to a Mac) it is tedious to remember which tmux sessions exist, type session names correctly to attach, and navigate to the right directory to start new sessions; tmux's own session management is command-line only, with no interactive picker.
why: The approved spec's statement of the problem, carrying the log's SSH/Mosh starting point.

text: One command, `x`, does everything: it shows the running sessions, attaches with arrow keys and Enter, remembers project directories for starting new sessions, and works at bare shell, optimized for small screens — in place of `tmux ls` plus `tmux attach -t <name>`.
why: The approved spec's solution and value proposition.

text: The interface is mobile-friendly: clean and minimal, optimized for small screens.
why: A value the approved spec names; the mobile SSH use case drives the layout.

text: Project memory is part of what the tool offers: quick-start new sessions in remembered directories.
why: A value the approved spec names.

text: Remote access itself is not in scope: SSH/Mosh handle it separately.
why: The tool starts once the user is on the machine.

text: Support both syntaxes: `-e` / `--exec` for simple commands and clean aliasing (`x -e claude myproject`), and `--` for compound commands with their own flags, no quoting (`x myproject -- claude --resume --model opus`).

cites.section: Failure Modes That Must Be Covered

text: Layer 1: (*tmux.Client).ListAllPanes (internal/tmux/tmux.go:687-693) swallows every error class (transient transport failures, exit != 0 from a saver-respawn race, server gone) and the legitimate empty case into the same ([]string{}, nil), with no error classification. Its docstring claims this only for the no-tmux-server case. The peer ListAllPanesWithFormat (lines 655-665) propagates errors, a documented, intentional divergence whose cost is this bug.
how: Read the code.

text: Layer 2: cleanStaleAdapter.CleanStale (cmd/bootstrap_production.go:76-83, bootstrap step 11) and portal clean's hook-cleanup tail (cmd/clean.go:75-91) pass the possibly empty live-pane slice straight to hooks.Store.CleanStale, with no guard against an empty live set beside a non-empty store and no adapter-level logging. The adapter's err check is unreachable in practice. hooks.Store.CleanStale (internal/hooks/store.go:130-159) is correctly scoped, so the defect is the caller's, not the store's.
how: Read the code.

text: Root cause: a dual conflation across two layers, neither of which alone makes the bug appear, which together silently destroy hooks.json whenever `tmux list-panes -a` returns an empty result for any reason during a bootstrap-triggering command: the helper's swallow (Layer 1) and the unguarded destructive consumer (Layer 2). All three hypotheses (error swallowing, no hazard guard, no adapter logging) were confirmed present together.
how: Read the code.

text: The swallow was a convenience for the no-tmux-server case, where portal clean should not error. It was kept when the helper was reused in bootstrap step 11, whose context guarantees a tmux server is running, so the swallow became a vector for silent destruction without the docstring or implementation being revisited.
how: Read the code and its docstrings.

text: Bootstrap step 9 (CleanStaleMarkers, cmd/bootstrap/stale_marker_cleanup.go) does the same diff-then-delete work against tmux server-option markers and is immune by construction: it calls the error-propagating ListAllPanesWithFormat (line 119) and has an explicit mass-deletion hazard guard (lines 126-141) that skips with a WARN when the parsed live set is empty but markers exist, its comment block (lines 80-92) calling the deferral a successful soft outcome. Step 11 has the same shape of work and neither safeguard: the architectural inconsistency is the bug.
how: Read the code.

Change 1 — Repurpose `ListAllPanes` to Wrap the Error-Propagating Helper

text: How should bootstrap step 11 and portal clean stop wiping hooks.json when tmux is transient?

When `list-panes -a` exits non-zero or returns empty, the cleanup treats the live-pane set as unknown, not empty: it skips the destructive call, logs a Warn at ComponentBootstrap, and continues, the next bootstrap retrying, as step 9 and Component B's orphan sweep already do.
why: A transient tmux failure means the live set is unknown; treating it as empty deletes every persisted hook.

text: Fix in depth across both layers, lifting step 9's pattern verbatim where possible: the helper propagates errors (closing mode a) and both callsites carry a mass-deletion hazard guard (closing mode b), with adapter logging. Both changes are required; either alone leaves one failure mode open.
why: Matching the prior art is structurally cleaner than any single-layer fix, and the cost of defence in depth is low; the user prefers it and wants the step-9 shape lifted, not re-derived.
rules_out: Option A, switching the helper only: leaves mode (b) open in the documented high-risk saver-respawn window.
Option B, hazard guard only: closes both modes but leaves ListAllPanes a footgun for future consumers.
alternatives: A — switch helper only
B — hazard guard only

text: Repurpose (*tmux.Client).ListAllPanes, rather than delete or deprecate it, into a thin wrapper over ListAllPanesWithFormat("#{session_name}:#{window_index}.#{pane_index}") that propagates errors and parses with the existing parsePaneOutput.
why: Repurposing removes the swallow contract structurally while every call site keeps compiling, and new consumers inherit the safe behaviour by default.
rules_out: Deletion: forces every call site, production and test, to change in this unit; high blast radius for a contract-narrowing change.
Deprecation with // Deprecated: keeps the footgun alive, since the compiler does not enforce the tag.
alternatives: Delete ListAllPanes
Deprecate ListAllPanes

text: How wide should the investigation reach?

Wide: verify the dead-branch claim, confirm the markers.go:140 consumer impact, enumerate and assess every caller of GetServerOption / TryGetServerOption, and audit adjacent error-mapping patterns in internal/tmux (ShowAllServerOptions, ListSkeletonMarkers) for the same shape of bug.
why: Confirmed by the user as the investigation's scope.

text: What contract should GetServerOption and TryGetServerOption deliver?

GetServerOption(name) returns ErrOptionNotFound only when tmux reports the option genuinely absent, and a non-nil, non-sentinel error for any other failure (transport, server crash, executable missing, and so on).
why: Its documented contracts promise absence is distinguishable from real failure, and the daemon's restoration-gate reads need a failure to read as a failure.

text: TryGetServerOption(name) returns (value, true, nil) when the option is present, ("", false, nil) when it is absent, and ("", false, non-nil error) for any other failure.
why: Matches its docstring, so callers reading volatile markers such as @portal-restoring can tell a marker absent from a tmux call that failed.

text: Where and how should the stderr distinction be recovered so GetServerOption can discriminate?
A typed CommandError at the Commander layer: RealCommander wraps its errors carrying tmux's stderr, and GetServerOption discriminates on that stderr.
why: Puts the diagnostic shape in the type system where the docstrings already claim it lives; mocks stay trivial struct literals with no os/exec types; future discriminators (such as server crashed versus tmux not installed) get the same channel without API drift; daemon consumer code is untouched.
rules_out: B: fmt.Errorf("%w: %s", err, stderr) at the Commander layer: the discriminator becomes a substring match against a formatted string, brittle if the wrap format changes and harder to test at the boundary.
C: a new Commander.RunWithStderr method: a parallel API surface every mock must stub, and no protection against similar latent conflations elsewhere.

D: an inline type-assert against *exec.ExitError inside GetServerOption: couples internal/tmux to os/exec at the public discriminator site, and mocks would need synthetic *exec.ExitError values whose fields are partly outside Portal's control.
E: string-matching err.Error() with no wrap: mechanically broken, since (*exec.ExitError).Error() is "exit status 1" and the stderr is on .Stderr.
evidence: The user agreed with the structural choice on first pass in a brief, confirmatory findings review; no alternatives were challenged and no edge cases raised.

text: What shape does CommandError take, where does it live, and is it exported?
CommandError is a struct { Stderr string; Err error } with Error() and Unwrap() returning Err, so errors.Is / errors.As against sentinels keep working through it.
why: Carries tmux's stderr alongside the underlying error so callers can discriminate failure modes without coupling to os/exec.

text: CommandError.Error() renders Err.Error() + ": " + trimmed Stderr when Stderr trims non-empty, Err.Error() alone when it is empty or whitespace, and (defensively, Err nil) the trimmed Stderr or "<no error>". The rendered format is not part of the public contract: tests assert behaviour (errors.As extracts a *CommandError, Stderr holds the substring), never the exact string.
why: Readability of the rendered error without making its format a contract.

text: CommandError is a package-level exported type in internal/tmux, constructed as a plain struct literal with no NewCommandError factory.
why: Exported so test code outside the package, and any future package-level helpers, can construct *CommandError literals as mock returns.

text: How does RealCommander produce CommandError?

RealCommander.Run and RunRaw both wrap a non-nil *exec.ExitError into *CommandError, Stderr taken from (*exec.ExitError).Stderr. That field is filled by cmd.Output() only while cmd.Stderr is nil, so the wiring must keep cmd.Stderr nil or capture stderr explicitly (cmd.StderrPipe()) if cmd.Stderr is ever repurposed.
why: Restores the stderr the Commander interface erased, in a type the interface can carry.

text: A non-nil error of any other type (such as the binary not found) is wrapped as *CommandError with Stderr "", the original preserved through Unwrap().
why: An empty Stderr means no signal: a discriminator sees no pattern match and treats the failure as non-absence, the correct conservative behaviour.

text: The Commander interface keeps Run(args ...string) (string, error) and RunRaw(args ...string) (string, error) unchanged: mocks returning a bare error still compile, a mock simulating stderr returns a *tmux.CommandError literal, and one that doesn't care about stderr returns errors.New(...), which discriminators treat conservatively.
why: No external API change, and mocks stay trivial.

text: How does GetServerOption decide between ErrOptionNotFound and propagating the error?

GetServerOption returns (strings.TrimSpace(output), nil) on success; ("", ErrOptionNotFound) when errors.As extracts a *CommandError whose Stderr matches the option-absent pattern family; and ("", err), the original wrapped error, for every other failure (transport, executable missing, server crash, unmatched stderr).
why: errors.As keeps the discriminator working through any future wrapping change at the Commander layer.

text: A non-nil error that is not and does not unwrap to a *CommandError (a mock's errors.New, or a future caller's own wrapping) is non-absence: GetServerOption returns it unchanged whatever its .Error() text, so errors.Is(err, ErrOptionNotFound) and errors.As(err, &cmdErr) both report false.
why: The same outcome as a *CommandError with empty Stderr: no pattern match, propagate.

text: CommandError.Stderr is stored verbatim as captured, trailing whitespace and newlines included; matching is a case-sensitive strings.Contains substring test with no normalisation (no lowercasing, no regex). Only Error() trims.
why: strings.Contains is insensitive to trailing whitespace, so no normalisation is needed.

text: Which stderr phrasings count as the option being absent?

The option-absent family is three substrings: `invalid option:` (unknown @-prefixed or non-prefixed option), `unknown option:` (an alternate form some tmux versions emit) and `ambiguous option:` (an ambiguous prefix match, as the empty name gives).
why: Derived from tmux's observed error surface and tolerant across tmux versions rather than a single literal.

text: The patterns live in an unexported package-level slice in internal/tmux, optionAbsentStderrPatterns, not inlined in GetServerOption, iterated with a plain range loop that short-circuits on the first strings.Contains match: no compiled regex, no alternation.
why: The set is reviewable and testable in isolation and extendable in one place; unexported because internal/tmux already gates the surface and same-package tests can read it; three patterns make iteration cost negligible.

text: With no tmux minimum version pinned anywhere in the project, the pattern set is treated as empirically derived from the tmux probed during investigation and best-effort across the versions users likely run; the discriminator-set unit tests lock it behaviourally, so a new absence phrasing surfaces as a fast test failure and is added to the slice.
why: No compatibility floor exists to confirm the set against.

text: The pattern set is verified only against the tmux probed on Darwin 25.3.0: the `unknown option:` form is attributed to some tmux versions without a version named, and no check against tmux's source or other versions is recorded.
how: The spec states the set is empirical and best-effort; no wider check is recorded.

text: The socket-connect failure (`error connecting to ... (No such file or directory)`), an empty Stderr (non-ExitError wrapping, such as the binary not found) and any other stderr do not match the absent family and propagate as the wrapped *CommandError, never ErrOptionNotFound.
why: Only genuine absence may read as absence.

text: What changes in TryGetServerOption, ErrOptionNotFound and their consumers?

TryGetServerOption's body is unchanged: its errors.Is(err, ErrOptionNotFound) branch becomes exclusive to genuine absence and its `if err != nil { return "", false, err }` branch becomes the live transport-error path, because GetServerOption is now contract-faithful.
why: The wrapper was already written for the contract; only its dependency was wrong.

The person expected sessions whose names start with an underscore to be hidden by default, recalling that convention being decided.

text: The `0` session is not from tmux-resurrect or tmux-continuum: the person removed both plugins and restarted the tmux server, and both `0` and `_portal-saver` still appeared. Portal itself is the source of both unwanted sessions.

The change is benign and is documented so consumers are not surprised.

text: The `built-in-session-resurrection` specification mandates that Portal filter sessions whose names begin with `_` from the TUI session picker, from `sessions.json` capture, and from any future internal-only sessions, since tmux has no mechanism to hide `_portal-saver`. The `tmux.PortalSaverName` doc-comment repeats the claim that the session is filtered from the TUI picker and from capture.

text: Root cause 1: the TUI picker and `portal list` do not filter underscore-prefixed sessions. Of the sites, `internal/state/capture.go` (`keepSessionNames`, `internalSessionPrefix = "_"`) filters, and `internal/restore/restore.go` defensively skips `_*` entries; `Client.ListSessions` returns every running session as tmux reports it, `filteredSessions` in `internal/tui/model.go` excludes only the current session when inside tmux, and `cmd/list.go` prints `ListSessions` output verbatim. So `_portal-saver` shows in every list, and the `PortalSaverName` doc-comment documents an invariant the code does not enforce.

text: Root cause 2: `StartServer` in `internal/tmux/tmux.go` runs `tmux new-session -d` without `-s`, so tmux names the session the lowest unused numeric index from `base-index`, `0` on a fresh server. Portal creates it as a side-effect of `EnsureServer → StartServer` and nothing ever disposes of it, so `0` lingers indefinitely and shows in every list after a fresh server start. The person pressed for full confirmation that `0` was Portal's doing; three lines of evidence converge: the unnamed `new-session` call, commit `bd659a3` capturing the intent in the doc-comment, and the session persisting with both plugins removed.
how: Traced in `internal/tmux/tmux.go` against `man tmux`, with git archaeology on the doc-comment.

cites.section: Root Cause 2 — Bootstrap `0` Session Never Cleaned Up

text: The unnamed bootstrap session was introduced deliberately by commit `bd659a3` (2026-04-07, resume-hooks-not-firing-after-server-kill T1-1), which replaced `tmux start-server` with `tmux new-session -d` so the server has a session and tmux's default `exit-empty on` does not end it before restoration completes. Its rationale relied on tmux-resurrect recognising and cleaning up the `0` session.
how: Git archaeology: `git log -S "tmux-resurrect" -- internal/tmux/tmux.go`, and the `StartServer` doc-comment.

cites.section: Root Cause 2 — Bootstrap `0` Session Never Cleaned Up

text: With Portal's own session resurrection authoritative (bootstrap step 5, `Restore`, rebuilds sessions from `sessions.json`), the delegation of `0`'s cleanup to tmux-resurrect is obsolete and never runs, and nothing else removes it: no bootstrap step targets it by name, `cleanStaleAdapter.CleanStale` prunes only `hooks.json`, `SweepOrphanFIFOs` cleans orphan hydrate FIFOs, and `state.CleanStale` / `state clean` kill no bootstrap session. The `StartServer` comment was accurate when written but was not revisited during the resurrection feature.
how: Traced through `cmd/bootstrap/bootstrap.go`, `cmd/bootstrap_production.go` and the state cleanup code.

cites.section: Root Cause 2 — Bootstrap `0` Session Never Cleaned Up

text: The bootstrap session is redundant the moment bootstrap step 4 (`EnsureSaver`) creates `_portal-saver` or step 5 (`Restore`) creates user sessions: its sole job is keeping the server alive until something else exists. No step removes it, and tmux's `exit-empty` cannot reap it because the server is no longer empty. This is why relying on tmux's native lifecycle after a rename is acceptable: the renamed session has no purpose once real sessions exist, and `exit-empty` reaping, where it applies, targets exactly that condition.
how: Reasoned from the bootstrap sequence in the spec's root-cause analysis.

text: How should `_portal-saver`, and any other session whose name begins with `_`, be kept out of the TUI picker and `portal list`?

`internal/tmux.Client.ListSessions` MUST exclude any session whose name begins with `_` from its returned slice, unconditionally and for every caller, so the TUI picker, `portal list` and any future caller inherit the filter without per-consumer code.
why: The resurrection spec describes `_*` hiding as a Portal-wide invariant, not a per-consumer concern; one chokepoint is a single source of truth future consumers cannot forget: one filter site, one test, one mental model.
rules_out: Filtering at each consumer (`internal/tui` and `cmd/list.go`), mirroring the capture-side pattern: it loses the invariant, the next consumer forgets and the bug repeats, with two edit sites and two tests.

cites.section: 1. Hidden Sessions Showing On Startup > Fix A — Filter `_*` Sessions In `Client.ListSessions` > Behaviour Contract

text: A session is filtered when `strings.HasPrefix(name, "_")` is true, matched on the literal session name tmux reports, with no trimming and no case-folding.
why: The spec defines the filter precisely so the match is unambiguous.

text: The filter is the final post-processing step in `ListSessions` before return, after parsing tmux output and any ordering; any later post-processing (sort, attach-metadata enrichment) runs before it. The contract is that the returned slice never contains a `_*` name.
why: Keeps the contract whatever the rest of the pipeline grows into.

text: `ListSessions` returns an empty, non-nil slice when every underlying session is filtered, never `nil`, so callers may rely on `len(result) == 0` and on JSON serialisation producing `[]` rather than `null`.
why: Callers get one shape for no visible sessions.

text: Apply the filter only inside `ListSessions`; the capture path's `keepSessionNames` double-filters `_*` names as a no-op, no new method is introduced, and `ListSessionNames` keeps its shape as a thin wrapper around `ListSessions`. No new capture test is required beyond the existing regression guard.
why: The smaller change, needing no new internal method.
rules_out: A lower-level raw enumeration that `ListSessionNames` calls directly, bypassing the filter.

text: `ListSessionNames` MUST remain a delegation to `ListSessions` and MUST NOT bypass it to query tmux directly; any future change that decouples them MUST re-evaluate filter placement before landing.
why: The capture strategy depends on the delegation: decoupled, the capture path silently loses the underscore filter and root cause 1 partially regresses for capture.

text: How should a caller that legitimately needs unfiltered session output get it?

A sibling `ListAllSessions` (or `ListSessionsRaw`) on the client is the documented extension point for unfiltered output, and it is not added in this bugfix: it is added when the first legitimate consumer appears, not speculatively, so the default `ListSessions` stays safe by construction.
why: No production caller needs unfiltered output; the only callers want the filter.

text: A `portal list --all` (or equivalent) flag for unfiltered output is deferred and not part of this bugfix; it can be added later if a real diagnostic use case emerges.
why: Users have `tmux ls` for inspecting Portal-internal sessions; a flag now would solve a hypothetical need.

text: How should the user-facing views behave when every session is filtered, as on a freshly bootstrapped server with no restorable state, where only `_portal-bootstrap` and `_portal-saver` exist and `ListSessions` returns an empty slice?

`portal list` MUST emit no output when `ListSessions` returns an empty slice: a silent exit, no "no sessions" message, no trailing newline beyond what the existing iteration produces. The implementer MUST verify `cmd/list.go` against this contract and adjust it if its empty-input path produces output, never assuming no change is needed.
why: The spec fixes the empty-list contract for `portal list` once both fixes land.

text: Does the existing `cmd/list.go` empty-input path already emit no output, or does it need adjusting? The spec leaves this for the implementer to verify.

The TUI picker keeps its existing empty-list rendering (`filteredSessions` returning an empty slice); a dedicated empty-state UX is out of scope for this bugfix, and if the existing rendering is unacceptable to the person it is raised as a separate work unit, not bundled here.
why: Keeps the bugfix to the filter and the rename.

text: Is the TUI picker's existing empty-list rendering acceptable? The spec leaves this to verify.
How should the `0` bootstrap session stop showing in user-facing lists?

`internal/tmux.Client.StartServer` MUST create the bootstrap session with the explicit underscore-prefixed name `_portal-bootstrap`, invoking `tmux new-session -d -s _portal-bootstrap` instead of `tmux new-session -d`, so the underscore filter hides it as it hides `_portal-saver`.
why: The smallest surface change: the chokepoint filter hides it whatever happens to it, so nothing relies on its being reaped. If Restore creates nothing it stays as the keep-server-alive anchor, exactly its job; left beside user sessions it is hidden by the filter, and any reaping by tmux's `exit-empty` is opportunistic, depending on the user's tmux configuration, a nice-to-have rather than a correctness requirement. It also removes Portal's dependence on a third-party plugin for cleanup.
rules_out: An explicit kill step in the bootstrap orchestrator after Restore: it works but adds a new orchestrator step plus a precondition check (never kill the only session, or the server dies); more moving parts than the rename.
Reverting `StartServer` to `tmux start-server`: it reintroduces the failure `bd659a3` fixed, `exit-empty on` killing the server before restoration finishes.

text: The reserved name is an exported package-level constant in `internal/tmux`, sibling to `PortalSaverName`, e.g. `PortalBootstrapName = "_portal-bootstrap"`; every reference to it, `StartServer`'s tmux args, tests and any future diagnostic tooling, goes through the constant, with no literal `"_portal-bootstrap"` elsewhere in the codebase.
why: One canonical reference for the reserved name.

cites.section: 1. Hidden Sessions Showing On Startup > Fix B — Rename Bootstrap Session To `_portal-bootstrap` > Behaviour Contract

text: `StartServer` is called only when no tmux server is running, behind the existing `ServerRunning` gate in `cmd/root.go`, and callers check it first as today; its behaviour against a server already hosting `_portal-bootstrap` (where the create fails with a duplicate session) is undefined and out of scope.
why: The rename keeps the existing calling contract rather than handling a case the gate prevents.

cites.section: 1. Hidden Sessions Showing On Startup > Fix B — Rename Bootstrap Session To `_portal-bootstrap` > Behaviour Contract

text: Portal does not set or modify tmux's `exit-empty` option; reaping of `_portal-bootstrap` is opportunistic, a nice-to-have rather than a correctness requirement. With restorable state, Restore creates user sessions and `_portal-bootstrap` may later be left the only session, the server exiting or not by `exit-empty`; with none, it stays the only session and keeps the server alive; with a server already running, `StartServer` is not called and no bootstrap session is made. Under `exit-empty off` it may persist indefinitely, and the filter hides it in every case.
why: The filter hides the session whatever the user's tmux configuration, so its reaping need not be guaranteed.

text: `_portal-bootstrap` is reserved: no other code creates or reuses a session with that name, and the constant is the canonical reference.

text: A new unnamed `tmux new-session` call is a code-review concern, not a mandated automated check: the underscore-prefix name is the default for any new bootstrap-style session, and reviewers challenge any unnamed `new-session` call.

text: The six other save-trigger events are creates, renames, relayouts and focus changes, none able to leave a consumer seeing a session that no longer exists; the hydration triggers (client-attached, client-session-changed) are an orthogonal mechanism.
