Q2: Signal Propagation from tmux Server to Hosted Processes

text: No existing tool solves shell readiness after pane creation well: tmux-resurrect sends immediately, tmuxinator has a known lost-command bug, tmuxp offers fixed sleeps; shell startup ranges from about 5ms to 2-5s.
how: From the tools' documentation and issues in research.

cites.section: Shell Readiness After Pane Creation — SOLVABLE

text: A detached session dies when its command exits: the window closes, the only window going destroys the session, and with exit-empty on (the default) the server exits when no sessions remain. remain-on-exit is a window/pane option that keeps a dead pane, reusable only via respawn-pane.
how: Read from the tmux man page and source in research.

cites.section: Q1: Session Lifecycle When Command Exits

text: destroy-unattached is a session option (off, on, keep-last, keep-group; default off); per server_check_unattached() in the tmux source, `on` would destroy a `-d` session with zero attached clients immediately. This was never tested: whether a global `destroy-unattached on` kills `_portal-saver` at creation remains unverified, and the saver gets a session-local override regardless.
how: Read from the tmux source in research, which names the edge case not fully verified and worth testing.

cites.section: Q1: Session Lifecycle When Command Exits

text: On `tmux kill-server` the server SIGTERMs itself, destroys sessions, and closes each pane's PTY master with no explicit kill; the kernel then delivers SIGHUP (not SIGTERM) to the hosted process. `kill-session` and an external SIGTERM take the same path; a SIGKILLed tmux has its PTYs closed by the OS, again SIGHUP. SIGHUP is trappable; tmux gives no grace period.
how: Read from the tmux source (cmd-kill-server.c, server.c, window.c) in research.

cites.section: Q2: Signal Propagation from tmux Server to Hosted Processes

text: A detached session shows in `tmux ls` with no way to hide it; `list-sessions -f` can filter, and tmux has no hidden or system session convention. A user attaching to the saver sees its output and Ctrl-C would kill it, to be recreated at the next bootstrap.
how: Read from the tmux man page and source in research.

cites.section: Q3: Interaction with Standard tmux Commands

text: tmux 3.5, 3.5a and 3.6 added no periodic execution primitive; the only timer-like mechanism is status-interval, the pattern continuum piggybacks on. A detached session is the only in-tmux way to run a periodic process without external process management.
how: From the tmux 3.5a and 3.6 CHANGES files in research.

text: tmux-slay, the one public precedent for hosting processes in a detached session, checks idempotency against stored metadata, keeps a permanent init window as keepalive, names its session `bg` by default and has no graceful signal handling; no significant issues were found with the pattern itself, the session-death issues (#2410, #2081, #2626) concerning exit-empty and destroy-unattached. The source review was partial: the plugin entry point returned 404.
how: Read from the tmux-slay source and tmux issues in research.

text: With exit-empty on, if `_portal-saver` is the last session and dies, the tmux server exits; could that surprise a user killing their last real session while the saver is also dying? Research judged it probably not an issue, since the saver dies only with the server, and nothing later settles it.

tmux 3.0+ stores hooks as array-indexed options; `set-hook -a` appends and does not deduplicate, so identical appends accumulate; `set-hook -gu 'EVENT[N]'` removes one entry, tmux does not renumber after removal, and sparse arrays fire correctly.
how: Tested empirically and read from tmux in research.

text: Every tmux-native input command (paste-buffer, send-keys, pipe-pane -I) writes to the PTY master bufferevent, the shell's stdin, where readline reads ESC bytes as meta-key prefixes rather than rendering ANSI. Only a process inside the pane writing its own stdout, or a write to the pane's slave device (`#{pane_tty}`, which races the shell's prompt), reaches the display path.
how: Read from the tmux source (cmd-paste-buffer.c, cmd-send-keys.c, cmd-pipe-pane.c).

cites.section: The research finding that reframed the decision

text: The pre-shell injection mechanism works: on an isolated tmux socket, `cat FILE; exec bash` rendered 1000 lines of ANSI scrollback correctly with a clean `bash-5.3$` prompt; shell history held no helper, cat or scrollback; the blocking-FIFO variant left the pane empty until `echo "go" > fifo`, then rendered the same; default-socket sessions were identical before and after.
how: Measured on an isolated tmux socket during discussion.
command: tmux -L portal-hydrate-validate-<pid> with a pane running `cat FILE; exec bash`, and a blocking-FIFO variant signalled by `echo "go" > fifo`
result: 1000-line ANSI scrollback rendered correctly, clean bash-5.3$ prompt, history clean, FIFO variant identical after signal, default socket unchanged

text: tmux keeps two buffers per pane: the main screen, which is scrollback and what `capture-pane -p -S -` captures, and the alternate screen that programs like vim, htop and less draw into, which is not scrollback. A pane in vim for hours still holds its real shell history in the main screen.
how: From tmux documentation during discussion.

text: tmux's `<prefix>m` marks a pane (used by swap-pane -m), not a scrollback position, and copy-mode position marks have no API to capture or restore; no confirmed tmux format variable exposes a window's last pane.
how: From tmux documentation during discussion.

text: tmux's session-renamed event reliably exposes only the new session name (`#{hook_session_name}`); the prior name is not retrievable from the hook itself.
how: Recorded in the spec's post-implementation note.

text: What should built-in session resurrection deliver, and on what principles?
"Zellij in tmux": after a reboot sessions come back as they were, structure and content, automatically, on by default, with no opt-in.
why: The person's directive: scrollback must be captured or the feature is useless; whatever can be saved should be.
rules_out: Structural-only resurrection
Structural plus scrollback as opt-in (resurrect's model)

text: Portal owns the full lifecycle (server start, restoration, resume hook execution) internally, with no external plugin dependency for resurrection.
why: Relying on resurrect/continuum left Portal no recourse when they broke.

text: Portal's hook system is generic: it stores and fires command strings with no awareness of what consumers do; caller wrapper scripts own process-specific policy.
why: Established design principle carried from research.

text: Portal keeps no separate session registry: live tmux state is read directly (list-panes -a, list-sessions), and saved state mirrors tmux, never diverging from or substituting for it.
why: Established design principle carried from research.

text: Portal captures every session, Portal-created and native tmux alike.
why: list-panes -a sees every session; including them is free and excluding them is extra work, and the picker already shows raw sessions.

text: Session names beginning with `_` are reserved for Portal internals and excluded from capture, restore and the TUI picker (and any future internal-only session), while staying inspectable via `tmux ls`.
why: Without the filter the saver session would be captured and then restored by the next bootstrap, breaking the daemon lifecycle; it keeps internal machinery out of Portal's UX.

text: Bootstrap (PersistentPreRunE, which runs before every user-facing command) is where restoration happens, since Portal is always the entry point.
why: The user never starts tmux directly, always via Portal.

text: Degrade locally, log, continue: no single failure may crash Portal or leave the user stuck; every failure logs to a file and degrades the affected pane or session to a workable state, self-healing where possible.
why: Silent or blocking failure is what made the plugins unusable.

text: YAGNI rigorously: speculative features (ephemeral opt-out, background prefetch, compression, multi-host sync, options capture) wait for concrete user demand.
why: Keeps the implementation surface small.

text: What minimum versions does resurrection require, and how is the tmux version enforced?
tmux 3.0 (February 2020) or later is required; Go, macOS and Linux requirements are unchanged.
why: Array-indexed hooks, the basis of `set-hook -a` coexistence, arrived in 3.0; every mainstream package manager ships newer.

text: Bootstrap runs `tmux -V` once on the first PersistentPreRunE per process, before any set-hook registration, and errors out with a clear message below 3.0 (e.g. "Portal requires tmux ≥ 3.0 (found 2.9). Please upgrade.").
why: Keeps users on older tmux out of a silent "mysteriously not working" failure.

text: What gets saved and restored, and what is excluded?
Captured structure: session names; window indices, names, layout strings, active and zoom flags; pane indices, working directories and active flag.
why: Everything tmux exposes that persists as meaningful state is captured.

text: Only current state is kept: one sessions.json, no snapshots or rotation; a single-slot sessions.json.previous may be added if real corruption appears.

text: signal-hydrate lists the attached session's panes and writes one byte to the FIFO of each marked pane, doing nothing for unmarked panes and never touching the marker.

text: signal-hydrate opens each FIFO with O_WRONLY|O_NONBLOCK, retrying on ENXIO or EAGAIN with short backoff (about 10, 20, 40ms up to about 500ms in all); on exhaustion it logs and moves on, the marker left for the next attach.
why: A blocking open before the helper reads would stall the tmux server, since run-shell is synchronous.

text: On signal the helper closes and removes its FIFO, writes the preamble `\033[?25h\033[?1049l\033[0m`, copies the scrollback file, writes the same reset plus CRLF, sleeps 100ms, removes its marker with `set-option -su`, then reads hooks.json by its --hook-key and execs `sh -c 'HOOK; exec $SHELL'` or `$SHELL`.
why: The reset sequences restore cursor, screen and attributes; the marker clears before the lookup, which does not depend on it, shortening the window in which the daemon skips the pane.

text: If no signal arrives within 3 seconds the helper writes the preamble only, skips the sleep, leaves the marker set so the next attach retries, logs a warning and execs a bare shell with no hook.
why: Degrades fast to a usable pane while keeping the pre-boot scrollback for a retry.

text: If the scrollback file is missing or unreadable on the signal path the helper writes the preamble only, logs, skips the sleep, removes its marker and goes on to the hook or shell.
why: Nothing was dumped, so the empty pane can be captured normally.

text: The FIFO wait times out at 3 seconds.
why: Normal signals take about 10-50ms and slow legitimate cases about 1-2s; 3s is about twice that tail.

text: The helper, not signal-hydrate, removes the marker, after a 100ms settle sleep.
why: tmux parses PTY output asynchronously; an early unset would let a capture take partial scrollback and dedup overwrite the full file. Typical lag is about 1ms; 100ms is unnoticeable against a 500-1500ms dump.

text: A helper crashing mid-dump leaves a stuck pane with partial content, documented as a shouldn't-happen case: the user kills the pane and the next bootstrap re-skeletons it (truncation possible, not corruption); a hook handler crashing before writing leaves the helper to time out with the marker kept; a second signal goes nowhere, harmlessly.
why: Rare enough to document rather than engineer around.

text: The pane command is run through `sh -c` so the `;` chain parses, and the helper's FIFO read implements its own timeout (goroutine plus time.After and select, or equivalent), since a plain read on a FIFO never times out; FIFOs use syscall.Mkfifo on Linux and macOS.
why: Implementation constraints of shells and Go's file reads.

text: Future mechanism verification uses an isolated tmux socket (`tmux -L <unique-name>`).
why: Validation on one left the user's live sessions untouched.

text: How does restoration integrate into Portal's bootstrap, and in what order?
Commands exempt from bootstrap: version, init, help, alias, clean, and every `portal state …` subcommand, user-facing and internal.
why: Internal subcommands run from hooks or as pane commands and would recursively re-bootstrap; the user-facing state commands inspect or tear down what bootstrap sets up.

text: Step 1: EnsureServer() starts tmux if needed and sets serverStarted in the command context when Portal started it.
why: Unchanged job.

text: Step 2 registers the global hooks idempotently, before the saver is created.
why: Creating the saver fires session-created, so the notify pipeline is wired from the daemon's first moment rather than racing registration.

text: Step 3 sets `@portal-restoring 1` before step 4 creates the saver.
why: The saver's session-created and every restore event would otherwise let the daemon's first tick capture mid-build; with it set the first tick no-ops and the first capture after the unset sees complete state.

text: Step 4 sets up the saver idempotently: create if absent, compare daemon.version and restart on mismatch, dev build or missing file, and always set destroy-unattached off.

text: Step 5, Restore(): a missing sessions.json is a no-op; an unparseable one logs, prints a one-line stderr warning and skips restoration; otherwise each saved session not live is created, its saved environment applied with `tmux set-environment -t <name>` after new-session and before any new-window or split-window, its panes armed and laid out and marked; a per-session error logs and skips to the next.
why: Every later pane inherits the saved environment at creation; only plain set values round-trip, not `-r` removals.

text: Step 6 unsets `@portal-restoring`; skeleton markers keep the daemon off unhydrated panes after that.
why: Saving resumes on the next tick.

text: Step 7, SweepOrphanFIFOs, removes on a best-effort basis any hydrate-*.fifo whose paneKey no longer has a live skeleton marker.
why: Cleans FIFOs left by helpers that never got signalled.

text: Step 9 returns to the calling command; a CLI command targeting a saved session finds it already restored, so `has-session` succeeds when attach needs it.
why: Restore is synchronous.

text: Attach after bootstrap: Portal resolves the target, then switch-client inside tmux or exec `tmux attach-session -A -t <session>` via syscall.Exec outside; the tmux event runs signal-hydrate, helpers dump and exec, and the next tick captures the hydrated panes with dedup.

text: What CLI surface does resurrection expose?

text: `portal state status` shows daemon state (pid, version), last save age from saved_at, session and pane counts from sessions.json, disk use under the state dir, and recent warnings from portal.log.
why: Lets users verify resurrection works and diagnose when it doesn't.

text: status exits 0 when healthy and non-zero for a notable problem: daemon not running, last save older than 5 minutes, or recent errors.
why: Scriptable as well as readable.

why: Older entries are history, not recent; a missing log is never itself a warning.

text: `portal state daemon` at startup writes daemon.version and daemon.pid, clears save.requested, checks log rotation and seeds its hash map; it then holds the map, runs the ticker, honours `@portal-restoring` and traps SIGHUP and SIGTERM.

text: No `portal state save` command.
why: Every use case is covered: the SIGHUP flush and 30s max gap cover reboots and risky actions; automation is speculative; reassurance is not a need; debugging can touch the flag.

text: open/x, attach, hooks set/list/rm, clean, alias, init and version keep their user-facing surface; hooks set no longer sets a marker and clean loses its empty-panes guard.

text: How does Portal make resurrection failures observable without nagging?

Portal logs to `~/.config/portal/state/portal.log`, one line per entry as `timestamp | level | component | message` (RFC 3339 UTC; DEBUG, INFO, WARN or ERROR; components daemon, restore, hydrate, notify, hooks, bootstrap), human-readable, not JSON.
why: Silent failure was the plugins' most-cited problem; grep-friendly and modest.

text: Warnings and errors log by default; `PORTAL_LOG_LEVEL=debug` enables verbose tracing. Logged: save failures, restoration warnings, hydrate timeouts, observable helper crashes, and bootstrap events at DEBUG only.
why: Enough to diagnose without noise.

text: Portal rotates the log itself at 1 MiB, renaming portal.log to portal.log.old (replacing it), about 2 MiB in all, no logrotate.
why: Bounded disk use with no external dependency.

text: Only the daemon rotates, at startup or on write; every other writer appends with O_APPEND and never checks size, so with no daemon the log grows until the next daemon start.
why: Two processes rotating at once would clobber portal.log.old; one-line appends are atomic under PIPE_BUF, and daemon downtime is rare and short.

text: Portal is silent by default, `portal state status` being the user's diagnostic entry point; it prints one stderr line only for a genuinely broken bootstrap state: the save daemon failing to start after retries, or sessions.json existing but unusable (corrupt, unsupported version, or unreadable), with the spec's wording.

text: On the TUI path bootstrap warnings are buffered during the loading page and written to stderr after it is dismissed, before the picker or exit; the CLI writes directly; both log the same.

text: Fatal bootstrap failures exit non-zero with a stderr error, never entering or hanging the TUI: tmux -V failing or below 3.0, EnsureServer() failing, set-hook calls failing en masse, and setting or clearing `@portal-restoring` failing; soft failures degrade and continue.

text: No metrics endpoint or telemetry, desktop notifications, syslog, log search tooling, or in-TUI banners about partial restoration.
why: A CLI tool, not a service; failures are rare and nagging adds friction.

text: Disk full during a save fails the AtomicWrite; the daemon logs, keeps ticking and retries, the previous state intact, and never crashes from disk-full alone.

text: No dedup: the target set is taken literally. Duplicate attach targets give mirrored windows of one session; duplicate mint targets each mint a distinct new session; overlapping globs may give a duplicate surface, honored.

text: Each spawned window runs the same open grammar a human would, one pinned target plus hidden --ack: an attach target runs portal open --session <name> --ack <batch>:<token>; a mint target is reduced by the parent to a literal existing directory at resolve time and runs portal open --path <literal-dir> --ack <batch>:<token>.
why: Alias and zoxide queries could re-resolve differently mid-burst; a literal --path can't diverge, so resolution never re-runs in the window, and no burst-only code path exists.

text: Minting happens in each window, not the parent: the atomic guarantee is the read-only resolve of the whole set (any target unresolvable, nothing opens and nothing is created); past it each surface opens or mints itself, and a window that never comes up never mints.
why: Scoping atomicity to the resolve and writes to each surface leaves no orphaned detached sessions.

text: A command rides mint windows only, appended after --ack in the multi-token form (portal open --path <dir> --ack <batch>:<token> -- <cmd> args…); a trigger that is itself a mint target mints locally and feeds the command to CreateFromDir / QuickStart as a spawned mint window does.
why: Attach windows never carry a command.

text: The command is carried to every mint surface as authored, never word-split: -e "npm run dev" stays one unit, so the trigger's local mint and every spawned mint window run byte-identical commands.
why: The same command behaves identically whichever surface a mint target lands on.

text: Past the resolve, per-window failure is leave-what-opened: opened windows stay and failed or un-acked surfaces aren't retried. The trigger connects to its own first target whenever that is viable, whatever other windows' acks do, and skips only if its own target fails at connect, outside tmux returning to the shell.
why: Portal doesn't own or tear down host windows; the trigger's target is unrelated to the others'. The picker's stay-marked-for-retry has no CLI equivalent.

text: The burst records each window's outcome in portal.log, the durable surface; a best-effort stderr summary is still emitted, directly visible only when the trigger's own target failed and Portal returns to the shell.
why: Stderr printed before the trigger attaches is swallowed by the attach, as with resolution feedback.

text: The parent polls for each window's @portal-spawn-<batch>-<token> receipt with a per-window timeout of about 8 s, timed from that window's own spawn; no receipt by then counts the window un-acked and failed.
why: Cumulative sequential delay never eats a later window's budget.

text: The affected path is the cold concurrent-bootstrap route alone: a fresh tmux server and the TUI picker, where the bootstrap orchestrator runs in a goroutine (`progressReceiver != nil`), with a saved `sessions.json` and scrollback present. The warm path, the CLI / direct path and the inside-tmux paths are correct.

text: Severity is low and UX-only: no data or correctness impact, sessions and scrollback restore fine. It reaches anyone who cold-boots (a reboot or a fresh container) into the picker with restorable sessions, and costs one extra keypress (`x`) to reach the sessions just restored.
how: Assessed in the investigation's impact section.

text: `evaluateDefaultPage()` (internal/tui/model.go) picks the landing page: Projects when `commandPending`, else Sessions when `len(m.sessionList.Items()) > 0`, else Projects. It returns early unless both `sessionsLoaded` and `projectsLoaded` hold, and is one-shot latched: it returns at once when `defaultPageEvaluated` is set, which it sets once and nothing resets, so the first call that finds both flags true decides the page permanently.
how: Read from internal/tui/model.go.

text: On the cold route `Init()` batches `fetchSessionsCmd()` and `loadProjects()` while the orchestrator runs in a goroutine, so frame one's `ListSessions()` enumerates tmux before Restore (bootstrap step 6) has created the saved sessions; `ListSessions()` also filters out `_`-prefixed names, so `_portal-saver` never counts, and the snapshot is empty. The maintainers' own comment in model.go confirms the stale snapshot.
how: Read from internal/tui/model.go and internal/tmux/tmux.go.

text: The stale `SessionsMsg` arrives while `activePage == PageLoading`: `applySessions` sets the session list to the empty snapshot (zero live sessions yield an empty list in every mode) but deliberately does not flip `sessionsLoaded`.
how: Read from internal/tui/model.go's SessionsMsg handler.

text: `ProjectsLoadedMsg` (a fast local file read) sets `projectsLoaded` and calls `evaluateDefaultPage()` unconditionally, which during loading bails on the `!sessionsLoaded` guard without latching.
how: Read from internal/tui/model.go's ProjectsLoadedMsg handler.

text: When restore finishes, `BootstrapCompleteMsg` (paired with `LoadingMinElapsedMsg`) calls `transitionFromLoading()`, which sets `activePage = PageSessions` tentatively, sets `sessionsLoaded = true` and calls `evaluateDefaultPage()`; with both flags true it decides on the stale empty list, lands on Projects and latches.
how: Read from internal/tui/model.go.

text: The same handler batches `refetchSessionsAfterRestore()`, which exists to repair the stale snapshot. Its fresh `SessionsMsg` (the restored sessions) lands in a later Update cycle with `activePage` already Projects, so the handler sets `sessionsLoaded = true` and calls `evaluateDefaultPage()`, which returns at the `defaultPageEvaluated` guard: the list contents update, the page stays Projects.
how: Read from internal/tui/model.go.

text: On the warm route (`progressReceiver == nil`, `serverStarted == false`) the orchestrator runs synchronously in `PersistentPreRunE` before the model is built, so Init's `ListSessions()` snapshot is already post-restore and non-empty, `evaluateDefaultPage` lands on Sessions, and `refetchSessionsAfterRestore()` returns nil.
how: Read from internal/tui/model.go.

text: Root cause: on the cold concurrent-bootstrap route the landing decision is made inside `transitionFromLoading` at loading-page dismissal against the stale empty list Init captured before Restore created the sessions, and the one-shot `defaultPageEvaluated` guard latches it; the post-restore refetch updates only the list contents, arriving one Update cycle after the decision, when `evaluateDefaultPage` is a guarded no-op. The page decision and its latch are coupled to a session count that is correct only after the refetch.
how: Concluded from the code trace.

text: The defect is deterministic on the cold route, not a race in the non-deterministic sense: Init always enumerates before restore, so the count is always 0 at decision time and the picker always lands on Projects. The seed's hypothesis, that the decision is captured before the restored sessions are visible to `ListSessions`, was correct.
how: Concluded from the code trace.

text: Co-defect with the same root cause: the `initialFilter` application lives inside `evaluateDefaultPage`, gated on `activePage == PageSessions && !commandPending`. On the bug path the latched page is Projects, so a cold-boot launch carrying a resolution-chain filter (`cmd/open.go` → `WithInitialFilter`) applies it to the project list and zeroes `initialFilter` in the same one-shot call, so it is never applied to Sessions after the refetch repairs the list.
how: Read from internal/tui/model.go; confirmed by the synthesis validation.

text: Contributing factors: the concurrent cold-boot flip runs enumeration before restore by design (race containment, the TUI inert during loading); `refetchSessionsAfterRestore` was introduced for the empty-previews / slow-open incident to fix the list's contents and did not account for the page decision depending on the same count; the decision is one-shot latched; and `transitionFromLoading` decides synchronously, then batches the refetch as a separate command.
how: Read from the code and its history as the log records it.

text: The existing cold-boot test (internal/tui/coldboot_session_refetch_test.go, `driveColdBootToSessions`, `TestColdBoot_PostCompleteRefetch_ReflectsRestoredSessions`) passes for the wrong reason: it builds the model with no project store and never delivers `ProjectsLoadedMsg`, so `projectsLoaded` stays false, `evaluateDefaultPage` returns early without latching, and `activePage` keeps the tentative `PageSessions` set in `transitionFromLoading`. In production `loadProjects` emits `ProjectsLoadedMsg`, so the latch fires.
how: Read from the test; confirmed by the synthesis validation.

text: Why else it was not caught, as the log has it unconfirmed: the startup-ordering tests (cmd/concurrent_*_test.go) cover warm/cold parity and step ordering but appear not to exercise the landing page on a pre-restore-empty cold fetch; the refetch's own test likely asserts list contents, not the active page; the cold route runs once per reboot; and the low UX-only severity kept it out of error tracking until the demo build.
how: Read from the tests; the first two points are stated as 'appears' and 'likely', not verified.

text: Potentially affected, to weigh during the fix: any future consumer of `evaluateDefaultPage` / `defaultPageEvaluated` that assumes the decision reflects post-restore state. The warm and CLI / direct paths are not affected, their decision running on a post-restore snapshot.

text: How should the cold-route landing decision be fixed so it reflects the post-restore session list?

Option A: defer the landing decision on the concurrent cold route to the post-restore refetch's `SessionsMsg`, which already calls `evaluateDefaultPage()`, now against the correct list; the fix changes when the decision is made on the cold route, not its logic.
why: It removes the premature decision at its source, the ordering bug, rather than patching the latch; reuses an existing call site; has the lowest blast radius and keeps the load-bearing warm-path startup ordering untouched (the zero-new-risk contract).
rules_out: Option B: re-open the latch once for the post-restore refetch — patches the symptom rather than the ordering, and adds two decision passes and more mutable latch state.
Option C: gate the cold-route transition on the refetch completing first — the largest restructure of the load-bearing startup ordering, with the most regression risk on a prior-incident surface.
alternatives: B — allow exactly one re-evaluation after the post-restore refetch
C — gate the cold-route transition on the refetch completing first

text: On the cold concurrent route (`progressReceiver != nil`), `transitionFromLoading()` sets an interim `activePage = PageSessions` but neither sets `sessionsLoaded` nor calls `evaluateDefaultPage()`. `sessionsLoaded` is already false then, the stale frame-one `SessionsMsg` never flipping it, so the fix only leaves it unset, never resets it; leaving it false keeps every `evaluateDefaultPage()` call a no-op until the post-restore refetch lands.
why: Nothing can latch against the stale interim list while `sessionsLoaded` stays false.

why: `projectsLoaded` is already true and the latch unset, so the decision runs on correct data.

why: `transitionFromLoading()` no longer decides on this route and `sessionsLoaded` stays false until the refetch, so any interim caller hits the `!sessionsLoaded` early return.

text: What observable behaviour must the fix deliver on each launch route?
AC1: a cold boot into the TUI picker with N>0 sessions restored opens on Sessions, listing all N restored sessions, with no `x` keypress needed.
why: The observable contract of the fix; the fix is correct only if every row holds.

text: AC2: a cold boot into the TUI picker with zero sessions restored opens on Projects; the deferred decision runs the same `len(Items()) > 0` test against the post-restore list, changing when the test runs, never what it tests, so the fix never over-corrects to always-Sessions.
why: Guards against over-correction, a risk the synthesis flagged for Option A.

text: AC3: a cold boot carrying an `initialFilter` with N>0 sessions restored opens on Sessions with the filter applied to, and consumed by, the session list, not the project list.
why: Covers the same-root-cause filter co-defect.

text: AC4: the warm path (server already running) with N>0 sessions opens on Sessions, byte-identical to today.
why: The warm path is already correct and must not change.

text: AC5: the warm path with zero sessions opens on Projects, byte-identical to today.
why: The warm path is already correct and must not change.

text: AC6: a command-pending launch lands on Projects as today; the `commandPending → Projects` arm of `evaluateDefaultPage()` is independent of session count and of the deferral, and is preserved.
why: That branch does not depend on the session count the defect concerns.

text: AC7: on the cold route, between loading-page dismissal and the post-restore refetch landing, a valid `activePage` is held, the interim Sessions page: never an undefined page, a re-entered loading page or a blank frame.
why: Synthesis flagged that deferring the decision must leave a valid interim page so no undefined page flashes.

text: What must hold around the deferral: its predicate, the interim window, error paths and the change's reach?

The deferred decision always resolves on the cold route and is taken by whichever of the post-restore `SessionsMsg` and `ProjectsLoadedMsg` lands second; both handlers' guard shapes are left as they are (the `SessionsMsg` arm suppressed while on PageLoading, the `ProjectsLoadedMsg` arm calling `evaluateDefaultPage()` unconditionally), premature latching being prevented solely by the `!sessionsLoaded` early return, so no path strands the picker on the interim page.
why: `refetchSessionsAfterRestore()` always emits a `SessionsMsg` on the cold route; usually `ProjectsLoadedMsg` has already arrived during loading, and under a late `ProjectsLoadedMsg` its handler is the decision point.

text: A post-restore refetch whose `SessionsMsg` carries an error runs `tea.Quit` before the deferred decision, as a failing Init fetch does today: the cold route exits with the warm route's error UX rather than stranding the picker on the interim page, a single interim frame before the quit being acceptable.
why: Keeps today's error behaviour unchanged.

text: Input during the interim window is not special-cased: the live picker behaves normally (Enter on an empty Sessions list is the existing no-op), and the deferred `evaluateDefaultPage()` overrides any page state reached mid-interim, a user `x` toggle included, since it sets `activePage` directly while the latch is unset. Preserving a mid-interim toggle is out of scope, and the 'TUI is inert during loading' guarantee covers the loading page only, not this interim page.
why: The window is bounded by one post-restore enumeration and opens only after the ≥1.2 s loading screen clears, so input in it is vanishingly unlikely.

text: `progressReceiver != nil` is the single authoritative cold-route predicate for the deferral, identical to `refetchSessionsAfterRestore()`'s guard; the fix introduces no other (no re-probing `serverStarted`, `tmux has-server` or `shouldRunConcurrentBootstrap`).
why: The receiver being wired is definitional of the concurrent route: necessary and sufficient.

text: During the one-Update-cycle interim window the cold route renders `PageSessions` against the not-yet-repaired empty list, which may briefly show the Sessions empty-state signpost, or flip to Projects on an empty restore; this is accepted, not special-cased to suppress the empty state, and eliminating the interim render is out of scope.
why: It is a valid non-blank page and the lowest-risk behaviour; the window is one Update cycle because the refetch is dispatched in the same handler return.

text: A `commandPending` launch never reaches the loading-to-picker transition the fix changes: Init's `commandPending` branch returns before wiring the loading-page dismissal (no `loadingPadTick`, no `progressReceiver` re-issue), so `transitionFromLoading()` is never invoked for it, the deferral never intersects it and no interim Sessions flash occurs on it.
how: Read from Init in internal/tui/model.go, as the spec states it.

text: The change is confined to the cold concurrent-bootstrap landing-decision ordering in internal/tui/model.go: no change to the bootstrap orchestrator, restore engine, scrollback replay, tmux enumeration, or the warm, CLI / direct-path and inside-tmux landing behaviour.
why: Restore is fully correct; the defect is purely the TUI landing decision.

text: The `_portal-saver` `_`-prefix filter in `ListSessions` stays as it is: the saver never counts toward the landing decision.
why: Correct as designed.

text: On a real Mac with portal 0.9.1 and native Ghostty 1.3.1 (no terminals.json override, so the native Ghostty adapter), selecting 3 sessions in picker multi-select and pressing Enter opened zero windows; the notice band showed "'portal-EfVRkk', 'portal-agent-first-3' failed to open — others left open"; portal.log showed `spawn: opened 0/3` for two consecutive batches (17:37:28 and 17:37:33 on 2026-07-16), no `portal attach --spawn-ack` process ever started and no permission-required line appeared. text: Severity is high: multi-window spawn is entirely non-functional on native Ghostty, the primary supported terminal, for every user spawning through the native adapter; a core feature of a shipped release, shipped without live validation.

text: Ghostty 1.3.1's scripting dictionary has no `make` command and no `with properties` terminology: its Standard Suite is trimmed to `count`/`exists`/`quit`; `surface configuration` is a record-type (not a makeable class) carrying `command` (text) and `wait after command` (boolean); and windows are created by the custom `new window` command's `with configuration` parameter of type `surface configuration`.
how: Read from the installed dictionary via `sdef /Applications/Ghostty.app` (318 lines).

text: The shipped template fails to compile against the installed Ghostty 1.3.1: osacompile reports `ghostty_test.applescript:2: error: Expected "given", "with", "without", other parameter name, etc. but found "{". (-2741)` with exit 1. Being a compile failure, it fails identically and instantly for every window regardless of runtime or permission state, which is why the log shows no -1743/-1712 and no --spawn-ack process.
how: Measured by compiling the template with osacompile against the installed Ghostty 1.3.1 in the diagnosing session (transcript 7d88b6b8); the exact command line is not given.

text: From the malformed script to zero windows: ghosttyOpenScript → ghosttyOpenArgv builds `osascript -e <script>`, ghosttyAdapter.OpenWindow runs it, osascript exits non-zero in milliseconds, and mapGhosttyResult maps a non-zero exit whose output holds neither -1743 nor -1712 to SpawnFailed with the osascript error as Detail; every one of the N−1 external windows fails so, the burst reports `opened 0/N` and the trigger self-attach is skipped.
how: Code trace of internal/spawn/ghostty.go.

text: Root cause: the native Ghostty adapter's AppleScript template (internal/spawn/ghostty.go) uses `make new surface configuration with properties {…}` and `make new window with properties {configuration:…}`, a generic Cocoa-Scripting shape that Ghostty 1.3.1's custom verb-style dictionary does not define.
how: Code trace against the installed sdef.

text: The template is a regression away from a researched-and-recorded API, not a guess: the restore-host-terminal-windows feasibility research (deep-dive 001, 2026-06-30, §F1) had recorded `new window with configuration` with a `command` field for Ghostty 1.3.x, and the implementation drifted to `make new … with properties` without re-validation. cites.section: 2. Fix the two destructive callers (the actual bug)

text: How must KillSession and RenameSession build their tmux target so they operate on exactly the named session?

KillSession(name) and RenameSession(oldName, newName) operate on exactly the named session: the `-t` target uses tmux's `=` exact-match prefix, so it binds only to the literal session name and never prefix-matches another. KillSession issues `kill-session -t =<name>`; RenameSession issues `rename-session -t =<oldName> <newName>`. A live prefix-colliding session (`foo-2`) is never killed or renamed when the target (`foo`) is not a live exact match.
why: tmux's default target resolution is prefix-match, which silently kills or renames the wrong session; the core argv fix was never in question.

text: Introduce a centralising `exactTarget` helper, and optionally migrate the existing inline-`=` sites onto it to prevent drift, or make a minimal two-caller patch?

Introduce `func exactTarget(session string) string { return "=" + session }` in internal/tmux, the session-level sibling of the pane-level PaneTargetExact; together they are the two canonical ways to build an exact-match `-t` target, and exactTarget is the canonical session-level exact-match target builder.
why: The user's explicit steer: "do it properly, not a hack… clean, as if it was never there." The user prioritised cleanliness and maintainability over minimal diff; a helper removes the repeated-inline-string drift surface that allowed the bug.
rules_out: A minimal two-caller patch with inline `"="+name` (Option 1): leaves the drift surface that allowed this bug, a hack rather than a clean fix.
alternatives: Option 1: minimal two-caller patch, inline `"="+name`: smallest diff, consistent with the current inline style, lowest surface.
Option 2 variant: the helper with no migration, Claude's initial recommendation, superseded because it leaves a mixed inline/helper state.

text: Fix the two destructive callers through the helper, each with a rationale godoc block mirroring the already-fixed sites: KillSession builds `kill-session -t exactTarget(name)`, RenameSession builds `rename-session -t exactTarget(oldName) <newName>`.
why: These two are the actual bug; the godoc mirrors the rationale the fixed sites carry.

text: Users with a single saved session are unaffected (one session, one attach, one signal), as is a hot-path portal open of an existing session after the cold-start bootstrap, since Restore builds no skeleton for live sessions.

text: Restore's skeleton arm phase, per saved pane, mkfifos <state>/hydrate-<paneKey>.fifo, respawn-pane -k's the pane into the wrapper sh -c 'portal state hydrate --fifo X --file Y --hook-key Z; exec $SHELL', then sets @portal-skeleton-<liveKey> for every live pane; the helper blocks in an O_RDONLY open of its FIFO up to a 3 s timeout; signal-hydrate, run by the global client-attached and client-session-changed hooks, enumerates only the panes of #{session_name}'s session and writes one byte to each marked pane's FIFO with O_WRONLY|O_NONBLOCK; hooks fire only on the signal-arrived and file-missing paths, the latter also unsetting the marker.

text: Root cause: a missing trigger, not a race with the helper's open. signal-hydrate is fired by per-session hooks scoped to the session being attached or switched to, while bootstrap step 5 skeletons every non-live saved session, so on a cold start with N saved sessions the other N-1 sessions' helpers never receive a signal during that server lifetime and time out after 3 s.

text: Symptom A: a stuck marker made the daemon's merge (mergeSkippedPanes) re-inject a killed session from the previous index into sessions.json; the companion daemon-merge fix on main requires the session, window and pane to be live before merging, so the user-visible resurrection is already structurally neutralised on main, though the marker still leaks without this fix.

text: Symptom C: the daemon's captureAndCommit skips scrollback capture for any pane whose marker is set, so a timeout-stuck marker suppresses that pane's scrollback save for the server's lifetime; CleanStaleMarkers does not close it, its predicate being a marker without a live pane while these markers sit on live panes.

text: Does the fix push hydration into bootstrap (eagerly signalling every skeleton pane after step 5), redesign the timeout path (fire hooks and unset the marker on timeout, possibly drop the wrapper), or both?

text: A new bootstrap step writes the single-byte hydrate signal to the FIFO of every pane in the freshly set @portal-skeleton-* marker map right after Restore, so every armed helper is signalled within milliseconds and proceeds through the success path (marker unset, scrollback replayed, hooks fired, exec $SHELL).

cites.section: 2. The Save Path Stops Trusting an Unconfirmed Session List

text: Root cause: every save treats the session list tmux reports at that instant as complete and authoritative and acts on it irreversibly in the same step: a session the capture does not see is dropped from sessions.json, the housekeeping pass inside every commit (gcOrphanScrollback) deletes every scrollback file the new index no longer names, and a pane whose scrollback read comes back empty has its saved file overwritten with zero bytes. Nothing in the pipeline tells the user ending a session apart from tmux or the machine going away.
how: Code trace and the sandbox experiments.

text: The save pipeline rests on two premises that hold during interactive use and fail at teardown: that a session disappearing from tmux means the user removed it (the premise of the per-kill synchronous commit and of housekeeping as self-healing by construction), and that an untrustworthy tmux read reports itself as an error (assumed by the all-sessions-failed guard, the restore marker's fail-closed read and the commit lock). Because deletion is coupled to the commit, the moment Portal is most wrong is the moment it destroys the only copy of the scrollback.

text: What does a cycle do when it stands down?

A cycle stands down on a failed session listing or a refused confirmation: it writes no commit and runs no housekeeping, so sessions.json stays as it was, no scrollback file is deleted or emptied, and the saved state names only files that exist. It then ends as a failed cycle through each committer's existing route: the tick logs its failure and re-touches save.requested so its next tick retries; commit-now logs, touches save.requested and exits non-zero (failCommitNow); the shutdown flush logs and reports flush_completed=false.
why: A transient failure on a healthy server then delays a save by one tick, and saves never stall.

text: How does an install choose between eager resumption and lazy prompting, and at what scope?

Every registration resolves to one of two modes at restore time: eager, today's behaviour, firing as soon as scrollback replay finishes with no panel; or lazy, holding the hook behind the waiting panel until the user answers.
why: The install must be able to keep today's behaviour or prompt.

text: The mode comes from an install-wide default with a three-state per-registration override: a registration carries eager, lazy or nothing; nothing inherits the install's default and changes with it, and an entry setting either mode holds it regardless of the install.
why: A thing that must be up whether anyone looks (a dev server, a tunnel, a watcher) behaves differently from one the user walks up to; the measured install has only the latter, so the finer model covers the case at a cost small enough that betting against it was the worse trade.

text: The install-wide default is lazy: an install that upgrades and reboots meets panels rather than processes.
why: Defaulting eager leaves the feature switched off behind a setting with no UI; lazy is not a silent change, since a panel says what it is and what key answers it, so the worst first-boot outcome is a few keypresses landing the user where eager would have.
rules_out: Defaulting eager, the conservative choice that changes nothing on upgrade.

text: A registration is written whole: `portal hook set` writes exactly what it is handed, carries no attribute forward from the entry it replaces, and the store's wholesale overwrite of an event's value is correct behaviour.
why: A registration replaces its predecessor completely; inheriting configuration from a dead one makes a writer's output depend on state it never saw. Policing re-registration is not Portal's job.
rules_out: A `hook set` with no mode flag leaving an existing mode alone.

text: A pin lives on the registration, not on the pane: anything that re-registers without the flag drops it, and that is the contract rather than a defect; the one collision, a pinned pane re-registered, resolves by re-passing the flag.
why: It follows from a registration being written whole; the external SessionStart hook writes only for panes running a session and its SessionEnd counterpart usually removes the entry first, so the exposure is small.

text: The install-wide default lives in `prefs.json` as the key `resume_mode`, holding `eager` or `lazy`, decoded tolerantly and independently: missing, empty, corrupt or unrecognised gives the shipped default, and the key is `omitempty` on write.
why: `prefs.json` already holds the install's UI preferences and decodes every field this way.

text: A `prefs.json` that cannot be read at all resolves to the shipped default too, so such an install meets panels rather than processes.
why: The shipped default arriving by the ordinary route, in the safe direction: a panel is answered in a keystroke, while an unwanted resume cannot be taken back.

text: Which keys answer the panel, and what does every other input do?

Nothing the user did not send may answer the panel: the waiter swallows every byte but Enter and `d`, including Ctrl-C, Ctrl-\ and Ctrl-Z, which would signal a foreground process, and Ctrl-D; a paste cannot answer with its line breaks, since tmux delivers a pasted line feed as Enter's carriage return. why: A safety property: a stray paste or a key pressed in the wrong window cannot spend the offer and unfreeze the pane; the recovery tail bounds the damage of a dying waiter but is no reason to let a stray byte answer.

why: A waiting pane must not be killed or stopped by a key the swallow rule claims to swallow; Ctrl-\ kills with a core dump and was missing from the original list.

text: A freeze that cannot be lifted holds the answer: the pane leaves the panel's screen first, and if the marker then cannot be cleared the panel is drawn again with the reason on its report row; neither the hook nor the shell fall-through runs while the marker stands, and the key can be pressed again.
why: Handing over with the marker set would freeze the pane's saved scrollback for the rest of its life with nothing reporting or reclaiming it; what the screen claims and what the pane holds never disagree.
rules_out: Handing the pane over anyway.

text: A panel redrawn after a discard whose marker clear failed comes back as drawn, the removed command under its label and both keys live, with the reason on its report row; it is not a fresh decision to draw. Enter reads the store again: usually it finds nothing and drops to a shell once the marker clears, and a registration naming a different command that replaced the entry during the wait is run.
why: A redraw that re-read the store would find no registration, paint nothing, and leave a pane that swallows keys with its transcript frozen for good.

cites.section: 7.2 The pane stays frozen for as long as its resume is unanswered

text: A waiting pane keeps its place in the saved set throughout: the freeze suppresses its scrollback write alone, and the structural capture enumerates it and merges its previous record into the fresh index, matched only against panes found in the same enumeration, so a stale marker cannot resurrect the waiting pane once it is gone (`internal/state/capture.go:96-127`); it restores on every later reboot with its original content and a fresh panel.

9.1 What was measured and needs nothing

text: A waiting pane whose session the capture misses keeps its place: when the enumeration lists a live waiting pane whose token no fresh record carries but a previous record does, that previous session is carried into the committed index whole, under its previous name, for that cycle, with no token on a second record; a carry onto the name of a session the capture reached refuses the whole commit for the caller to retry. The carried copy is the previous topology rather than the live one, so for that one cycle it can hold a sibling that has since closed or moved: the guard against resurrecting a gone pane still holds for the waiting pane itself, which the same enumeration lists live, but not for the rest of the carried session.
why: A session renamed, killed or failing its environment read mid-capture drops out, and housekeeping would delete the waiting pane's transcript with nothing to re-capture it.

cites.section: 7.2 The pane stays frozen for as long as its resume is unanswered

text: The merge finds a frozen pane's previous record by its durable `@portal-pane-id`, not its position, and keeps pointing at the scrollback file holding its bytes; this covers the whole hand-over from restore to wait (a mid-restore pane with a token matched by token, one without by address unless a live pane carries that record's token), and every committing capture, saver tick and `portal state commit-now` alike, reads the mid-restore markers itself.
why: Matched positionally, one rearrangement during the wait leaves the old file unreferenced for housekeeping (`ComputeReferencedSet`, `internal/state/commit.go:64`) and the pane restores empty; a tokenless pane at a tokened pane's old address would otherwise take its record and bake one hook into two panes.

cites.section: 7.2 The pane stays frozen for as long as its resume is unanswered

text: The helper writes the pane's saved token itself, with no read first, before it pins and marks the pane, the same value restore would have written.
why: Restore's re-stamp is best-effort, so a parked pane could carry none and its registration look stale; one live pane answers to a token, so there is no collision to arbitrate.

cites.section: 7.2 The pane stays frozen for as long as its resume is unanswered

text: The saved scrollback file name is a second address that does not survive the pane moving: restore and housekeeping read the record's stored path verbatim, but the saver's write derives its path from the pane's live address (`state.WriteScrollbackIfChanged(dir, paneKey, …)` → `state.ScrollbackFile(dir, paneKey)`, `internal/state/paths.go:84`), so the next pane to occupy a frozen pane's vacated address is captured into its file, undetected by `ComputeReferencedSet`.

cites.section: 7.2 The pane stays frozen for as long as its resume is unanswered

text: A frozen pane's bytes leave the positional namespace for as long as it waits: at the tick it is first frozen its scrollback is re-filed as `scrollback/pane-<PortalPaneID>.bin` and the merged record carries that path; when the wait ends it is re-filed under its current address and the token file is reclaimed on the next commit. A pending pane with no token keeps the positional path and today's exposure.
why: The namespaces are disjoint by construction (every positional key ends `__<window>.<pane>`), so no later occupant can claim the file.
rules_out: Refusing a write to a path another record claims, which loses the intruder's scrollback instead.

cites.section: 7.2 The pane stays frozen for as long as its resume is unanswered

text: When a mid-restore pane with a token-shaped token holds a record naming a positional file another record in the same capture also names, the capture hard-links that file to the pane's token name (refusing an existing name) and points the record there before any scrollback is written that cycle.
why: A renumbered restore can point the pane at a path another live pane writes; a link rather than a move lets a helper that has not opened its baked path still find it, and acting only on a shared name keeps a file only this record names referenced through housekeeping.

cites.section: 7.2 The pane stays frozen for as long as its resume is unanswered

text: How is the daemon multiplication closed?

The invariant is exactly one `portal state daemon` per state directory, which in practice is one per user; a user running two tmux servers against one state dir shares one daemon, the second server's bootstrap hitting the lock and recovering through the contention path. Isolating daemons per tmux server is not in scope.
why: `stateDir` resolves per user through XDG config resolution, and multi-tmux-server-per-user is an unusual configuration.

text: The fix is a coordinated pair: a daemon-side singleton lock as the structural invariant, and a synchronous kill barrier in the saver bootstrap so the common-case recycle is quiet.
why: The lock alone closes the bug but logs a contention WARN and leaves a briefly empty `_portal-saver` on every recycle; the barrier alone narrows the race but a sweep can outlast its timeout and it guards no other double-spawn path; together the barrier keeps the common case quiet and the lock makes every edge case safe. The user wanted a structural fix, and the pidfile-as-singleton gap is closed properly by flock.
rules_out: Singleton flock alone, without the barrier: noisy on every recycle.
Synchronous kill alone, without the lock: leaves 'no two daemons can coexist' a comment, not an enforced property.

text: How does the daemon enforce that at most one daemon writes to a state directory?

cites.section: 1. Multiple State Daemons Running Concurrently > Fix Part 1: Daemon-Side Singleton Lock > Purpose

text: At daemon startup, before `WritePIDFile` and before the tick loop, the daemon takes an advisory `flock` on `<stateDir>/daemon.lock`, guaranteeing N ≤ 1 daemons write to the state directory however they were started.
why: It is the floor that holds even if every other guard fails; flock is the right primitive for 'held while the process is alive'.
rules_out: A pidfile created with `O_EXCL`: a one-shot atomic create, not a held lock, it leaks on crash and blocks startup until cleaned, needing its own cleanup-on-startup dance.

cites.section: 1. Multiple State Daemons Running Concurrently > Fix Part 1: Daemon-Side Singleton Lock > Purpose
1. Multiple State Daemons Running Concurrently > Fix Part 1: Daemon-Side Singleton Lock > Behaviour
Why a lock and not `O_EXCL` pidfile create

text: The lock is taken exclusive and non-blocking, `unix.Flock(fd, LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB)`, failing fast.
why: The loser runs as the initial process of a tmux session, so a blocking acquire would hold tmux's `new-session` synchronously; fail-fast keeps contention to one log line and an immediate exit, and the next bootstrap's tolerant-kill-and-recreate branch recovers.
rules_out: Blocking `LOCK_EX`.

cites.section: 1. Multiple State Daemons Running Concurrently > Fix Part 1: Daemon-Side Singleton Lock > Behaviour

text: On acquiring the lock the daemon proceeds normally (writes its pidfile, enters the tick loop) and holds the lock for its whole life, the kernel releasing it on any exit: clean exit, non-zero exit, signal kill or crash.
why: Kernel fd cleanup makes release on crash automatic, with no stale-lockfile dance.

cites.section: 1. Multiple State Daemons Running Concurrently > Fix Part 1: Daemon-Side Singleton Lock > Behaviour

text: The lock fd must be held in a variable that lives as long as the daemon process (a package-level var, or a field on a struct the run loop keeps alive) and must never go out of scope while the daemon runs; any future wrapper with a finalizer must not close the fd.
why: A finalizer closing the fd would release the lock while the daemon still runs, silently reintroducing the race.

cites.section: 1. Multiple State Daemons Running Concurrently > Fix Part 1: Daemon-Side Singleton Lock > Behaviour

text: When the lock is held (EWOULDBLOCK), the daemon logs one WARN line such as 'another daemon holds the lock; exiting' and exits with status 0; the line's presence matters, not its wording.
why: Exit 0 keeps tmux from treating it as an abnormal session termination.

cites.section: 1. Multiple State Daemons Running Concurrently > Fix Part 1: Daemon-Side Singleton Lock > Behaviour

text: The lock fd is set `FD_CLOEXEC`.
why: So it does not leak into any child process the daemon forks.

cites.section: 1. Multiple State Daemons Running Concurrently > Fix Part 1: Daemon-Side Singleton Lock > Behaviour

text: The lock file is opened with mode 0600.
why: It matches the mode of Portal's other state files.

text: The lock helper does not create `<stateDir>`; the state directory's existence stays the caller's responsibility, whichever step ensures it today.
why: The daemon-startup path already writes other state files and already ensures the directory.

text: An `open(2)` failure on the lock file (EACCES, ENOSPC, ENOENT, EMFILE, ENFILE and the like) is fatal: the daemon logs an ERROR line describing it and exits non-zero, distinct from the contention path's WARN and exit 0.
why: An open failure is a genuine misconfiguration or system problem to surface loudly, not absorb silently.

text: Lock acquisition runs in `cmd/state_daemon.go` on the daemon-startup path, before the `state.WritePIDFile` call and before any state-directory write.
why: The pidfile must never be written by a daemon that loses the lock.

text: Which package does the lock helper live in? It may live in `internal/state` beside the pidfile helpers for symmetry; final placement is left to planning.

The lock acquire call is seamed for tests through a package-level var such as `var lockAcquire = unix.Flock`, matching the `daemonRunFunc` / `daemonShutdownFunc` seam pattern, so tests can fake success, failure and inspect FD_CLOEXEC.
why: It follows the existing test-seam style.

text: A loser daemon exiting 0 as `_portal-saver`'s initial process closes its window and so, by default (no `remain-on-exit`), the session; the next bootstrap sees no session and creates one with no barrier. With `remain-on-exit` the next bootstrap sees a dead pane, takes the stale-pidfile branch, whose barrier returns at once on the dead PID, and recreates. Both paths converge.
how: Reasoned in the spec from tmux's default session behaviour.

text: `daemon.pid` is kept for `BootstrapAliveCheck` and written by each lock-winner only after the lock is held, so it becomes informational and authoritative, always naming the one daemon that won the lock.
why: With the lock in place the pidfile can no longer be overwritten by a racing daemon.

text: How does the saver bootstrap synchronise a kill with the prior daemon's exit before respawning?

cites.section: 1. Multiple State Daemons Running Concurrently > Fix Part 2: Synchronous Kill Barrier > Purpose

text: The barrier wraps the kill: before `KillSession(_portal-saver)` it reads the prior PID with `state.ReadPIDFile(stateDir)`, issues the kill as today, then polls `state.IsProcessAlive(prior_pid)` until it reports dead.
why: Waiting for the prior daemon to exit keeps the lock's contention WARN from firing on every recycle.
rules_out: Treating `_portal-saver`'s presence as the singleton signal and letting the daemon detect a version mismatch and self-exit: it would teach the daemon to manage its own version lifecycle, far larger surgery; the kill-respawn protocol is sound and needs only a barrier.

text: The barrier's total wait is bounded by a 5-second timeout.
why: 5 s sits above the 3.9 s cold-sweep ceiling measured at the affected profile with margin; 3 s would fire WARN-and-proceed on ordinary cold restarts there, so 5 s keeps the WARN for genuinely stuck daemons or heavier scrollback.
rules_out: A 3-second timeout.

why: There is no prior daemon to wait for.

text: When is the fix correct?

At most one `portal state daemon` exists per state directory at any time, however many bootstraps have run, verified by a real-tmux integration test of two back-to-back `EnsurePortalSaverVersion` calls, one forcing a version-mismatch recycle, asserting exactly one live daemon, and manually by `pgrep -P <tmux-server-pid> -f 'portal state daemon'` counting 1 after repeated bootstraps.
why: Singleton-ness is a structural property future seams may depend on, and the lock holds it even under code paths not yet written.

text: The common case is a single bootstrap invocation triggering a recycle (version mismatch, stale pidfile, manual session kill): the prior daemon has exited before the new one begins its first tick, and no lock-contention WARN is logged. Two bootstraps in close succession are not the common case and may log one WARN on the loser, which is accepted.
why: The barrier makes the single-invocation recycle quiet; the lock keeps concurrent invocations safe.

cites.section: Clean handover on the common case

text: Clean handover is verified by the barrier unit tests (the prior PID dying within the timeout returns cleanly with no log) and a manual recycle test against the affected scrollback profile.
why: Those cover the common-case path the criterion names.

cites.section: Clean handover on the common case

text: Past the 5 s timeout the bootstrap respawns rather than block; the new daemon's flock either succeeds or fails cleanly with one WARN and exit 0, and the next `portal` invocation recovers through `BootstrapPortalSaver`'s tolerant-kill-and-recreate branch with no manual intervention.
why: Degradation under timeout must stay bounded and self-healing.

text: With the saver present and the version matching, `EnsurePortalSaverVersion` never enters the barrier and its latency is unchanged, verified by barrier unit tests confirming it is entered only from the kill sites; no broad timing test is needed.
why: The fix must not regress the steady-state critical path.

cites.section: No regression on the steady-state critical path

text: After every successful bootstrap `daemon.pid` names the lock-winning daemon while it runs; it need not be cleaned up on graceful shutdown, since `BootstrapAliveCheck` finds the holder alive or the PID dead and takes the stale-pidfile branch. Verified by the existing pidfile and `BootstrapAliveCheck` tests passing, with acquisition before `WritePIDFile`.
why: `BootstrapAliveCheck`'s signal-0 probe already tolerates stale-after-exit content.

text: A daemon that crashes (panic, SIGKILL, reboot) releases the lock through kernel fd cleanup and the next startup acquires cleanly, verified by a regression test simulating abrupt exit.
why: No stale-lockfile handling should ever be needed.

text: The fix adds at most two new WARN lines, one per event: the losing daemon's lock contention and the barrier's timeout. Their wording is illustrative; tests assert one line's presence at WARN per event, never its text, and a rewording is no regression.
why: The two WARN paths are enough to surface the abnormal cases.

text: The clean-handover path logs nothing new; silent success is the expected behaviour.
why: The common case should be quiet.

text: No diagnostic or INFO line is added at the recycle decision point, so the existing recycle path stays silent, an acknowledged trade-off; recurrence diagnostics, if needed, are a follow-up observability work unit.
why: The two WARN paths surface the abnormal cases; recycle diagnostics are a separate concern.

text: What tests does the fix require?
The fix's tests never use `t.Parallel()`.
why: The cmd package injects mocks through package-level mutable state cleaned up with `t.Cleanup()`, per project convention.

text: Unit tests in `cmd/state_daemon_test.go` through the `lockAcquire` seam cover: acquire succeeds → pidfile written and tick loop entered; EWOULDBLOCK → one WARN, exit 0, no pidfile, no tick loop; the lock fd has FD_CLOEXEC set, by flag inspection or a recorder.
why: These pin each path of the lock's behaviour.

text: That `lockAcquire` runs before `WritePIDFile` is asserted through filesystem state: after a failed acquire the pidfile keeps its previous value, or stays absent in a fresh state dir; no `WritePIDFile` seam is added for it.
why: The reverse order would let a loser overwrite the pidfile before exiting, and observable state tests it without a new seam.

text: Unit tests in `internal/tmux/portal_saver_test.go`, with `ReadPIDFile`, `IsProcessAlive` and the clock injected, cover: the PID dying within the timeout → nil, no WARN; never dying → returns non-fatally with one WARN after about the timeout on the injected clock; no PID file, a dead PID, or an unreadable or corrupted PID file → returns at once with no log.
why: These pin each branch of the barrier without real processes or waits.

text: The barrier is exercised through both call sites, the version-mismatch branch and the stale-pidfile branch, each triggered independently and recording that the shared helper ran.
why: Both paths must invoke the shared helper.

text: A new real-tmux integration test in `internal/tmux/portal_saver_integration_test.go` (`restoretest`/`tmuxtest` conventions, skipped where tmux is unavailable) creates the saver with `EnsurePortalSaverVersion`, writes a different value into `<stateDir>/daemon.version` directly, calls it again to force the recycle, and asserts `pgrep -P <tmux-server-pid> -f 'portal state daemon'` counts exactly 1.
why: It is the load-bearing test for the bug: the `BootstrapAliveCheck` seam tests cannot model a pidfile overwritten while the prior daemon runs, and writing the file directly exercises the real mismatch comparison with no new seam.

how: Assessed in the investigation and the spec.

text: `unix.Flock(LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB)` advisory locking works on darwin, the affected platform, and Linux, CI's; Windows is not a supported Portal platform.
how: Read from the spec's regression-risk section, which states it without citing documentation.

text: How does the fix ship, and how do affected servers converge?

The fix ships in a regular release with no hotfix; affected users have the workaround `tmux kill-session -t _portal-saver` then `pkill portal`, or `tmux kill-server` at the heaviest impact. The version ldflag interacts with how often the mismatch trigger fires, not with the fix.
why: Few users are likely affected at about one orphan per 34 hours of tmux uptime, needing long-lived servers, and the workaround is well defined.

text: On a server already holding orphans, the first post-fix bootstrap may log several WARN lines and need several `portal` invocations to settle, which is accepted: killing `_portal-saver` SIGHUPs only its own daemon, the orphans keep their locks until their cancelled sweeps end, so each new daemon loses the lock and exits until they drain and one acquires it. A server not in that state upgrades silently: one kill, a clean exit, the lock taken, no logs.
why: It is the correct convergence behaviour and no worse than the existing workaround.

text: No user-facing documentation changes are needed; the fix is internal to the saver-bootstrap subsystem.
why: Nothing the user sees changes.

text: Completion cannot turn one shape into the other only where the shell honours `ShellCompDirectiveNoFileComp`: the filename fallback is switched off by the shell, not Portal, in zsh and fish always (fish registered `complete -c <name> -f`), and in bash only where `compopt` is a builtin (4.0 and later) and the `bash-completion` package is installed, because cobra's script gates the switch-off on `type -t compopt` and reaches `_get_comp_words_by_ref` from that package first. On macOS's stock `/bin/bash` 3.2 the standing `complete -o default` registration supplies filenames, for `portal open` as much as for `x`.
how: Read from cobra v1.10.2's generator (`bash_completionsV2.go:132-138`, `:432-438`), as the implementation's corrigendum records.

text: The trailing slash that keeps an argument a path is always one the user types: a single-segment absolute directory typed without it is a sigil however it was reached.
why: On a shell that honours the no-file directive, `portal open /tm<TAB>`, and `x /tm<TAB>` once the corrected `portal init` output is live, never becomes `/tmp/`; where the shell cannot honour it, the fallback supplies filenames for `portal open` exactly as for `x`.

text: Both bash and zsh will define a function whose literal name is `x/port` and dispatch that word to it.
how: Measured in GNU bash 5.3.15 and zsh 5.9.
command: bash --noprofile --norc -c 'x/port() { echo RAN-FUNC; }; x/port'; zsh -f -c 'x/port() { echo RAN-FUNC }; x/port'

text: The form is a positional with a space after the command, `x /port` or `portal open /port`, the character after the `/` beginning the term; the seed's no-space `x/port` is ruled out permanently.
why: Claiming the no-space shape buys nothing: the function name must be the search term, so it would take a function per term, and without one the word falls through to a path; the only other interception, a global unknown-command hook, would put Portal in the path of every mistyped command on the machine.
rules_out: the no-space form `x/port`
a global unknown-command hook

text: The shape makes a positional a sigil wherever it sits on the line, so `portal open ~/Code/api /tmp` is a usage error rather than a two-mint burst.
why: Recognising the shape only as the sole positional would make the outcome depend on argument order, `portal open /tmp ~/Code/api` erroring while `portal open ~/Code/api /tmp` succeeds, which no user can hold and no message can explain.
rules_out: recognising the shape only as the sole positional

text: Recognition applies to the arguments `open` parses as targets and stops at a `--` separator: a `/word` among the trailing command's words is that command's argument, never a sigil (`portal open ~/Code/api -- ls /tmp` is unaffected), and a command carried as a flag value was never in reach.
why: A sigil line carries no command at all, so stopping at the separator loses nothing.

text: Accepted cost: single-segment absolute directories typed without a trailing slash, `x /tmp`, `x /opt`, `x /srv`, stop minting and start filtering; the escape is `-p` (`portal open -p /tmp`, and `portal open -p ~/Code/api -p /tmp` bursts two mints unchanged).
why: Minting a session directly in a root-level directory is not something the user does, so the shadowed directories are ones nobody opens a session in.

text: The recognition rule stays a test of the argument's shape and never consults the filesystem.
why: A rule that minted when the single-segment path happened to exist would read the same command differently on two machines.

text: `x /`, the sigil with no term, opens the picker with the filter open and empty, the cursor in it, ready to type: not plain `x`, not an error, and not "mint at root".
why: `-f`'s refusal of an empty value does not transfer: `-f ""` is a flag given no argument, while `/` on its own is the gesture that opens a filter. Nothing about using `/` errors.
rules_out: a usage error for the bare `/`, following `-f`'s refusal of an empty value
evidence: "Using `/` with no string is not an error. That's an empty filter, ready to be typed into in the TUI."

text: No `+` mint sigil is built.
why: "Add new" is already the bare form's behaviour; the one gap it could fill, forcing a mint when a live session is named exactly the term, is covered by `-p`, `-a` and `-z`; a fourth mint route is the surface accretion the work set out not to cause.
rules_out: a `+` mint sigil alongside the search sigil

text: No configurable sigil is built.
why: A command string is a shared artifact, unlike a keystroke: under a configurable sigil `x /tmp` mints on one machine and filters on another. It would also be the first Portal setting to change parsing rather than appearance, every field `prefs.json` carries being UI state (`grep -n 'json:"' internal/prefs/store.go`).
rules_out: making `/` configurable, opt-in via global config

text: How does the search form resolve: what does each match count do, and when is the count taken?
A sigil argument never enters the bare-positional resolution chain, reaches no path, alias or zoxide domain, and can never mint: its term is a search over live sessions and nothing else.
why: Declaring the domain is what makes eager resolution safe: the sigil has the same K=1/K=2 cliff as project-prefix matching, but both sides of it are session-domain, so the worst case is a picker the user was already heading for, not a stray session.

cites.section: 3.1 The sigil is session-domain by declaration

text: When exactly one live session matches the term, it is attached directly, with no picker.
why: The single-match attach is the one shortcut past the pre-filtered picker, and is consistent with the shipped `-s <glob>` route, which already attaches a lone match.

text: When two or more sessions match, the picker opens on the Sessions page with the cursor on the first matching row, the narrowed list holding the matching sessions except where the target-collision carve-out withholds some.
why: It degrades to exactly the screen the user was heading for.

text: The sigil never fails: zero matches opens the picker on the Sessions page with no session surviving the term, indistinguishable from filtering to nothing inside the picker, where `Esc` clears the filter; nothing is written to stderr and the exit status is not a failure.
why: The form is the pre-filtered picker and a count of zero is a filter result, not an error; a message at the shell strands the user having done nothing, where an empty list is one keystroke from recovery.
rules_out: zero matches as a hard failure at the shell
evidence: "Nothing errors from using `/`. Worst case it populates a filter with zero results. The same as me opening the TUI now and filtering to zero results. No difference."

text: A term-less sigil takes no count: `x /` opens the picker on the whole live session list as the bare-slash rule sets it, whether one session lives or twenty.
why: It carries nothing to match.

text: The searched set is the set the picker lists: Portal's internal sessions, `_portal-saver` and `_portal-bootstrap`, are never search candidates, count toward no K and can never be attached by a sigil.
why: They are absent from the picker's list.

text: Whenever a term opens the picker, at K = 0 and K >= 2 alike, it lands as `-f` lands it: filter text set and committed rather than focused, the cursor re-anchored onto the post-filter visible set, so arrows, `Space` and `Enter` work at once; the bare slash alone lands with its filter focused and empty.
why: The user is not left inside a live filter input; `x /` carries no term to commit.

text: K is taken once the tmux server can answer for the live session set: at once on a warm server; on a cold one once the concurrent bootstrap has run every step to completion, not merely the restore, the loading page standing until then and replaced by the attach at K = 1 or the picker at any other count.
why: Acting at the end of restore would replace the process mid-bootstrap and abandon the steps after it, among them clearing the `@portal-restoring` marker, which must not outlive bootstrap.

text: The loading page's minimum display span is untouched: where the count can be taken before it elapses, the page stands for the remainder and the attach or picker follows when it lifts.
why: The concurrent path's own behaviour is unchanged for the sigil.

text: Accepted cost: the user cannot predict before typing whether they land in a session or in the picker.
why: The wrong side of the cliff costs a screen they were already opening.

text: The sigil emits no `resolve` component log line.
why: That component records one INFO line per bare positional resolved through the guessing chain, deterministic targets (globs, domain pins) emitting none, and a sigil declares its domain as a pin does. Derived from the component's own rule, not decided in discussion.

text: An attach under K = 1 uses the connector the invocation already selects (`syscall.Exec` into `tmux attach-session` outside tmux, `switch-client` inside it); the sigil introduces no third connection mode.
