text: What should Tab offer after the sigil, `x /po<TAB>`?

Before this feature the sigil form completed to nothing: the slash is part of the word, no session name begins with one, and the filename fallback is off, so Tab was silently inert rather than misleading (the review's predicted fallback to root filenames did not happen).
how: Measured with Portal's completer.

text: Completion looks past the sigil: `/po<TAB>` completes the term after, and excluding, the `/` against live session names, leaving the sigil in place; offered words carry it (`/portal-a1b2`, never `portal-a1b2`).
why: A completed full name normally leaves one match, which attaches, so `/po<TAB><Enter>` becomes the whole interaction; a word without the slash would replace the whole word and drop the sigil the user typed.
evidence: "`/` is the command, followed by the string; we complete on the string after and excluding the `/`"

text: Completion is prefix-shaped while the form matches by containment: the words offered are the searched set's session names the typed term prefixes, so `/ort<TAB>` offers nothing while `/ort` still finds `portal-a1b2` on Enter.
why: The shell discards any candidate that is not an extension of the word being completed.

text: What is offered is the set the sigil can reach: inside tmux the session the caller is attached to is never offered; outside tmux, or when the attached-session read fails or answers nothing, nothing is held back on that account. `/<TAB>` offers every session in the searched set.
why: Completing to the attached session would land on a picker filtered to zero rows; degrading rather than dropping is the count's own rule, and completion carries no channel for a failure. Accepting a completion of the bare slash narrows to one session and attaches it.

text: Completion is bounded by the `--` separator and by nothing else: a `/word` among the trailing command's arguments is answered with no candidates and the shell's own filename completion left on (`ShellCompDirectiveDefault`); the word immediately after the separator keeps the sigil arm, being indistinguishable at the flag layer from the next ordinary positional.
why: Past the separator the word is not a search form, so offering sigil candidates would complete to a term the parser will not honour and suppress the filenames the user wanted.

text: Everywhere else a search form could be typed, one is offered, including on a line the composition rule refuses (`open api /po<TAB>`, or a line carrying `-f`, a pin, `-e` or `--ack`); Enter on that line is then refused by `validateSearchFormCollisions`.
why: Completion judges the word in front of the cursor, which genuinely is a search form; only its company is illegal, and the user may delete the other target before pressing Enter.

text: Directories are never offered as completions, though they count for matching.
why: A completed `/Users/leeovery/Code/portal` reads as a path and trips the no-second-slash rule straight back into path territory.

text: A live session name carrying a `/` (tmux permits one; `ValidateSessionName` refuses only `:`, a leading `$` and a leading `-`) is never offered; it stays reachable by a term stopping short of the slash.
why: Completing `/foo` to `/foo/bar` would produce a second slash, which the recognition rule reads as a path.

text: Cobra's emitted script asks the typed word for its completions rather than a registered command name (zsh builds the same request from `${words[1]}`), so Tab after `x`, which expands to `portal open`, runs `portal open __complete …`, a real `open` invocation carrying `__complete` as a positional, and Portal's completer is never consulted.

text: `spawn.UnsupportedNoopMessage` for a named-unsupported terminal is rewritten to `can't open new windows in <name> · <bundleID> — nothing opened`, keeping the name and bundle id.
why: In the CLI there is no banner, so that line is the only place the user gets the bundle id, the `terminals.json` key.

text: The blocked-entry flash is distinct from the reactive no-op: it carries no `— nothing opened` and says "isn't available", while `— nothing opened` stays on the reactive no-op alone.
why: A pre-emptive block attempts nothing, while the reactive no-op follows an attempt.

text: Rewriting `UnsupportedNoopMessage` is in scope, widening the fix into `internal/spawn`; since its wording is shared with the CLI open burst, the rewrite must read correctly for the CLI's something-was-attempted case and be coordinated with `cli-verb-surface-redesign` so the two surfaces stay coherent.
why: The plain-language rewrite covers the whole unsupported-terminal family, and that message is shared.

text: The two blocked-entry strings live in `internal/tui`, rendered by a new TUI-local helper (e.g. `multiSelectBlockedFlashText(id)`) that picks the shape by `m.detectIdentity.IsNull()`, mirroring `unsupportedFlashText`; this copy is not shared with the CLI and needs no `cli-verb-surface-redesign` coordination.
why: The pre-emptive block is a picker-only surface.

text: The blocked-entry flash uses the existing notice-band flash slot and self-clears on the next actionable key (the authoritative trigger, matching `setFlash`/`isActionableKey`; "next keypress" is shorthand for it); inheriting that slot's auto-clear timer is expected and not forbidden.
why: The existing flash lifecycle already satisfies the self-clear requirement.

text: On a named terminal the blocked-entry flash co-renders two-row with the persistent banner: banner on the section-header row, flash on the notice-band row.
why: The flash's slot is a separate row from the header the banner claims.

text: Repeated `m` while the blocked flash shows clears the flash, then re-blocks and re-flashes; this is intentional.
why: An actionable key clears the flash before its handler runs, and that behaviour is fine.

text: In the named two-row state both rows carry the shared `⚠` glyph (banner through `renderUnsupportedHeader`, flash through the warning-flash slot's unconditional glyph), so two `⚠` show until the flash clears; the block flash is not special-cased to drop its glyph.
why: The glyph is a consistent warning marker, not duplicated information (the non-repetition constraint governs text only); each row is independently a warning and the flash is transient.

text: Does the double `⚠` in the named two-row state hold up at the implementation visual gate? The spec accepts it subject to that confirmation.
Setup guidance stays with the named-unsupported banner (terminal name, bundle id and `see docs`); NULL/remote has no remedy, so it gets no pointer, only the plain explanation.
why: Only the named case has a `terminals.json` remedy.

text: `see docs` is left unchanged here; making it a real (ideally clickable OSC 8) link to a new custom-terminal setup page is out of scope, logged as the separate quickfix `custom-terminal-docs-and-clickable-see-docs`.
why: It renders no concrete URL or path today and no `terminals.json` setup doc exists in the repo.

text: Accept the minor imprecision of "over a remote connection" for NULL: NULL is almost always remote/mosh but can rarely be a detection error folding to a null identity.
why: It stays directionally correct, and the actionable truth ("multi-select isn't available" / "nothing opened") holds either way.

text: Adjacent spawn messages for other scenarios (session killed mid-burst `'…' is gone — nothing opened`, a window `failed to open`, macOS permission guidance) are not rewritten.
why: They are already plain and separately owned.

text: What test changes does the fix require?

Rework `TestBurstUnsupported_NonNullAtomicNoOp` and `TestBurstUnsupported_NullFlash` in `burst_unsupported_noop_test.go` to enter multi-select before resolving detection (the in-flight path), since a post-resolve `m` is now blocked; `TestBurstUnsupported_DeferredThenUnsupported` and `TestBurstUnsupported_SupportedStillDispatches` stay valid, and the deferred-Enter → reactive no-op coverage is kept.
why: Their `markTwo` precondition fails once entry is blocked post-resolve.

text: Invert `TestApplySectionHeader_UnsupportedNullShowsHonestLine` in `unsupported_banner_test.go`: a resolved NULL now renders the standard `Sessions ··· N` header.
why: It asserts the old NULL banner, which the banner split makes false.

text: Remove the render-level `TestUnsupportedHeader_NullIdentityNoHostLocal`.
why: It exercises the deleted NULL render branch.

text: New banner-split coverage: a NULL identity renders the standard `Sessions ··· N` header, not the banner, and the By-Tag "no tags yet" signpost returns (the mirror of `TestActiveNoticeBand_SuppressesSignpostWhenUnsupported`, which uses a named identity and stays valid); a named identity's banner is unchanged.

text: New `m`-entry block coverage: `m` on a resolved-unsupported terminal (NULL and named) does not enter multi-select and sets the blocked flash, which self-clears on the next actionable key; plus a named co-render assertion that a blocked `m` yields the two-row state (banner on the header row, flash on the notice-band row) with both rows carrying `⚠`.

text: New help-suppression coverage of three cases: unsupported and not in multi-select omits `m`; supported lists `m`; unsupported in multi-select mode (the A1 state) lists `m`. `keymap_dispatch_guard_test` stays green.

text: Guard the unchanged supported (native/config) path: banner absent, `m` enters, help lists `m`, burst dispatches.

text: Add a NULL-identity capture fixture `sessions-unsupported-null`, seeded through the existing detection seed seam with `InitialDetection = &spawn.Identity{}`, rendering the standard header with no banner (visually identical to `sessions-flat`), with a committed reference PNG; the render-level banner-split test stays the primary NULL assertion, and the named `sessions-unsupported-terminal` fixture stays valid.

text: Before this work, `internal/state/logger.go` was a thin printf-style wrapper around `os.File`: line format `timestamp | level | component | message`, levels Debug/Info/Warn/Error, component constants, file-mutex serialisation, no structured fields or handler abstraction. It rotated `portal.log` to `portal.log.old` when a daemon write would push the file past 1 MiB; only the daemon rotated (`OpenLogger(path, rotate=true)`), other writers appended, and `os.Remove(oldPath)` ran before every rename, so only one rotated file was ever kept.
how: Read from the code of `internal/state/logger.go` during the discussion.

text: The 2026-05-28 evidence loss (a `hooks.json` wipe at 08:18 BST, then a saver disappearance, with `portal.log` later at 0 bytes) was rotation churn, not literal truncation: at the 1 MiB threshold the file rotated every few hours under load, and a second rotation overwrote the single `.old` that held the 08:18 wipe before the user looked. WARN-only logging also left no INFO breadcrumbs around the wipe or the saver's disappearance, and silent destruction (no line on rotation or deletion) multiplied the loss.
how: Reasoned in the discussion from the old logger's code and the incident's evidence.

text: A second destruction path is unidentified: the user's `portal.log` was found at 0 bytes with no `.old` on disk, and `logger.go` holds no `O_TRUNC`, so something other than rotation zeroed it. Its root cause was left to investigation during implementation and is unverified.
how: Read from the incident's state on disk and the old logger's code; the cause was never found.

text: What zeroed `portal.log` on 2026-05-28, with no `.old` left and no `O_TRUNC` in the old logger? The design makes such destruction detectable and recoverable, but the root cause stays the implementation-phase investigation target.

Estimated log volumes: WARN 50-200 KB/day steady, 1-10 MB/day in an incident; INFO 1-5 MB/day steady, 10-50 MB/day stressed; DEBUG 5-20 MB/day steady, 50-500 MB/day in a stuck loop. The rolling 30-day window peaks at about 600 MB even at DEBUG. A reboot burst on a 30-pane install at INFO is about 50-100 lines over the first 10 seconds, and steady state with 1 Hz cycle summaries peaks at about 8 MB/day under churn, so no rate limiting or sampling is needed.
how: Estimated in the discussion; no figure was measured.

text: How wide is the observability work's scope: the inbox's seven logging patterns, or wider?

The scope is wider than the inbox's seven patterns: use logging anywhere it aids debugging or insight, under a disciplined level taxonomy. That makes level discipline and the subsystem prefix taxonomy foundational subtopics, decided ahead of the further pattern decisions.
why: Without a level contract, logging everywhere devolves into noise, and the INFO baseline has to be greppable by subsystem prefix.
rules_out: Limiting the work to the inbox's seven patterns

text: What logging foundation replaces the bespoke printf logger, and what API does it expose?
Adopt Go's standard-library `log/slog` as the logging foundation, replacing `internal/state/logger.go` wholesale.
why: Standard library with no new dependency, structured fields native, handler-based so one set of call sites emits text for tail/grep or JSON for tooling, and future-proof as call sites multiply; migration cost is small today.
alternatives: Keep the printf wrapper and extend it with structured field conventions

text: A new package `internal/log` is the single owner of all logging machinery; no `*slog.Logger` is constructed anywhere outside it.
why: One owner keeps the handler, taxonomy and rendering consistent across every process.

text: `internal/log` exposes `Init(stateDir, version, processRole string) error` (builds the custom rotating handler and swaps it in behind the stable root logger, called from `main` before other portal code), `For(component string) *slog.Logger` (a component-bound child, safe before `Init`, cached at package init), `Close(exitCode int)` (emits the `process: exit` marker; never calls `os.Exit`) and the test-only `SetTestHandler(t, h)` (swaps a handler for a test and restores it via `t.Cleanup`, so no subprocess is needed).
why: A small fixed surface: configuration once, a factory per component, an exit marker that owns no control flow, and an in-process test seam.

text: `Init` is idempotent and re-entrant: a second call re-points the handler and does not panic. The configured-once-in-production invariant is held by convention (only `main` calls `Init`) plus the test-only `SetTestHandler` seam.
why: Panic-on-second-call fought slog's grain (`slog.SetDefault` is re-settable) and forced every log-asserting test into a subprocess.
rules_out: Enforcing a single Init by panicking on a second call

text: The root `*slog.Logger` is built in `internal/log`'s own package `init` over a small custom handler whose inner delegate is replaceable (mutex- or `atomic.Pointer`-guarded); `Init` swaps the configured handler into it, so loggers cached at package init before `Init` route to the configured handler once it lands, with no nil returns. The cost, one synchronized read per `Handle`, is accepted.
why: Every consumer imports `internal/log`, so its `init` runs first and the root exists before any `For`; the swap avoids stale cached loggers and rides on the custom handler already needed for rotation.

text: Before `Init` runs, the indirection holds a safe default handler that writes INFO and above as text to stderr.
why: Pinned from the discussion's 'discard or stderr-text' so any unexpected pre-`Init` log surfaces rather than vanishing; `main` calls `Init` first, before any TUI rendering, so the window carries no expected output.

text: Baseline attrs (`pid`, `version`, `process_role`) are injected by the configured handler per record, not via `root.With(...)` at construction.
why: Package-init children created before `Init` would otherwise miss them.

text: The one custom handler also owns rotation, the retention sweeps, the `component:`-prefix text rendering and the lifecycle-marker level-filter bypass.
why: A single seam for every handler concern; the text-mode format is specified with the taxonomy.

text: `main` resolves `process_role` before Cobra parses argv, by a longest-prefix match of the leading `os.Args[1:]` subcommand tokens (flags ignored) against a static table: `state daemon` → `daemon`; `state hydrate` / `state signal-hydrate` → `hydrate`; `hooks …` → `hooks_cli`; `clean` → `clean`; `open …` / `x …` / `attach …` / bare `portal` → `tui`; anything else → `bootstrap`. First match wins, and the value is passed to `log.Init`.
why: `Init` runs before any other code and before the parse, so a lightweight inspection is needed; `bootstrap` as the explicit default leaves no invocation unmapped in the closed 6-value space.

text: A package that logs binds each component it emits under once, at package init, as `var logger = log.For("<component>")`, and call sites use `logger.{Debug,Info,Warn,Error}` with `"key", value` attrs drawn from the closed vocabulary.
why: The factory string is the only place a component name appears in Go code, so the typo surface is small and reviewable.

text: The binding rule is once per package, per component, not one package per component: a component may be bound by several packages (it names a subsystem, whose code need not live in one package) and a package may bind several components; what is forbidden is a second binding of the same component inside one package.
why: A second binding in one package is invisible at review, every call site still looking correct.

text: A package handed an already-bound logger through a seam binds nothing: `internal/theme` emits the `theme` component through an injected logger whose single `log.For("theme")` binding lives in `cmd`, and `internal/spawn`'s shared emission helpers take an injected logger that `cmd` passes for the CLI burst and injects into `internal/tui` for the picker burst, beside `internal/spawn`'s own binding for detection and the `terminals.json` load.
why: The seam case of the bind-once rule.

text: The migration deletes the `internal/state.Logger` type, the `internal/state.Component*` constants, the pipe-delimited line format and `state.NopLogger()`; tests needing a silent logger use `slog.New(slog.NewTextHandler(io.Discard, nil))`.
why: No sentinel or legacy surface survives; `log.For` always returns non-nil.

text: What does a portal log line look like: how is the subsystem rendered, which components and attr keys exist, and which attrs does every line carry?

`component` is a structured slog attr at every call site; the custom handler renders text output with `component:` as a literal prefix at the start of the message body, timestamp and level before it, and JSON output and programmatic filtering use the attr unchanged, so `grep "<component>:" portal.log` yields the per-subsystem trail.
why: Keeps the intuitive grep idiom for tail-and-eyeball use and the structured attr for JSON and filtering, at essentially no cost since a custom handler is already needed for rotation.
alternatives: Standard slog TextHandler (`component=hydrate`), noisier by eye
A manual `<component>:` prefix in the message text only, losing the structured attr

text: The component value space is closed at 21: `bootstrap daemon restore hydrate notify hooks preview saver capture signal log-rotate clean aliases projects process spawn resolve theme attach sessions migrate`. This list is the single source of truth for the count; mid-move to zmx, production code binds 18 of them (`notify` went with `portal state notify`, `signal` with the FIFOs, and nothing binds `preview` since the preview reads zmx's history).
why: A closed, enumerated set makes every subsystem's prefix predictable for grep and keeps names from being invented at call sites.

text: Component `daemon` owns the `portal state daemon` runtime: the tick loop and self-supervision.
why: One subsystem per component.

text: Component `bootstrap` owns the six-step bootstrap orchestrator, its gate and `bootstrap.lock`: DEBUG `bootstrap owed` (`reason` `latch`, `zmx dir` with `error`, `no saver`, `saver unknown` with `error`); INFO `restoring flag lowered` (`detail`); INFO `saver ended` (`detail`) when a saver Portal can't use is ended; INFO `step skipped` (`step`, `detail`) for Restore and WriteLatch when an earlier step left the restore unfinished, and for WriteLatch alone when the old daemon couldn't be replaced; INFO `bootstrap skipped` (`detail`, `took`) when a bootstrap that waited finds nothing owed; ERROR `bootstrap.lock unavailable` (`error`, `took`). Bound again in `internal/state`: WARN `latch unsynced` (`error`, `error_class` `write-failed-fsync`) and INFO `zmx dir recorded` (`path`).
why: Each bootstrap decision leaves one greppable line under one prefix.

text: Component `restore` covers `internal/restore` under its caller's logger: one INFO `restore complete` (`restored`, `failed`, `anomalous`, `took`) per bootstrap restore; per session a DEBUG `session skipped` (`session`, `reason` from a closed set: `it is live`, `another spelling of its name is live`, `it is one of Portal's own`, `it ended this boot`, and for a retry `its entry is gone` or `its entry records another creation`), a DEBUG `session restored` (`session`, `path`), and WARNs counted in `anomalous` (`restore session failed` with `detail` for a retryable failure, `record session creation failed`, `clear hydrating flag failed`, `scrollback file refused`); a DEBUG `restore retry failed`; once a run a WARN `sessions.json unreadable` or `list sessions failed`, the post-pass and post-retry recount WARNs, and a WARN `restore cancelled` (`detail`, `error`) when its context ends with sessions left. `open` bringing back one kept session (`BringBack`) logs the same lines for that entry, including `its name is one the backend can never create`, and one INFO `restore complete` with `session`. Bound again in `cmd` (`open.go`) for the WARN `sessions.json unreadable` / `list sessions failed` (`session`, `error`) when resolution can't judge a kept session.
why: The restore's outcome and every anomaly are reconstructible from `restore:` lines.

text: Component `hydrate` owns the per-pane `portal state hydrate` helper (FIFO open, scrollback replay, exec chain); on zmx it logs an INFO `scrollback kept for the next restore` (`session`, `path`) when a transcript it couldn't replay is kept with its hydrating flag left raised.
why: The helper's whole trail sits under one prefix.

text: Component `notify` owns the notification helpers.
why: One subsystem per component.

text: Component `hooks` owns `hooks.json` mutations (`hooks set/rm`, `CleanStale`), `portal migrate`'s rewrite of `hooks.json` from its backup (`RekeyFrom`: DEBUG `rekey-move` and `rekey-rm` per key, one INFO `rekey` with `op`, `entries`, `via`, `took`, a WARN `rekey` for a refused or failed rewrite, which writes nothing, and a DEBUG `rekey-noop` with no backup), and the hook-staleness cycle in `internal/hooksweep`: a DEBUG `clean-stale-skipped` (`op`, `via`, `reason`) for a stand-down, at WARN for `reason` `tmux-keys` (`entries`), which lasts until migration moves the tmux state aside, and for `reason` `mass-reap` (`entries`: three or more keys, at least half of `hooks.json`).
why: Every change to `hooks.json`, and every refusal to change it, is greppable as `hooks:`.

text: Component `preview` owns the TUI scrollback preview page.
why: One subsystem per component.

text: Component `saver` owns the `_portal-saver` session lifecycle.
why: One subsystem per component.

text: Component `capture` owns the daemon's capture loop (promoted from inside `daemon`); on zmx, the saver's scrollback capture in `internal/saver`: DEBUG `capture skipped` (`session`, `error`) for history unavailable, timed out, gone, on the alternate screen or too large after the first warning; WARN `capture too large` the first time in a run; WARN `capture failed` for other failures; WARN `write failed` (`session`, `path`, `error`, `error_class`); WARN `unsynced` (`error_class` `write-failed-fsync`); and from the clean of unnamed scrollback and stale temp files a DEBUG `removed` (`path`) per file, a DEBUG `cleaned` (`reaped`), a WARN `remove failed` and a WARN `clean failed`.
why: Capture anomalies are signal; per-file detail stays at DEBUG under the poll's INFO summary.

text: Component `signal` owns the FIFO signalling mechanism (`EagerSignalHydrate`, `portal state signal-hydrate`'s diagnostics, and the FIFO send/receive plumbing in `internal/state`), whichever binary writes it; `signal-hydrate`'s `process_role` stays `hydrate`, and the hydrate helper's own exit-path lines, `signal timeout` among them, stay under `hydrate`.
why: Homing the mechanism under one component lets `grep "signal:"` reconstruct it whole; process role and component are orthogonal.

text: Component `log-rotate` owns rotation and retention events.
why: One subsystem per component.

text: Component `clean` owns the sweep paths: bootstrap's orphan-daemon and stale-flag sweeps (a DEBUG `stale flag lowered` with `session` and `detail` per flag) and `internal/state`'s orphan-FIFO sweep. It is named for the retired `portal clean` command, whose user-invoked repairs live on `portal doctor --fix`.
why: Sweeps share a prefix whatever runs them.

text: Components `aliases` and `projects` own the `aliases` and `projects.json` store mutations.
why: Added for the state-mutation audit trail.

text: Component `sessions` owns the session index (`sessions.json` version 2) in `internal/sessionindex`, its lines carrying `op`, `session`, `value`, `detail` and `via`: a WARN with `error` and `error_class` when an `Update`'s write fails, a DEBUG `update-noop` (`op`, `via`) for an `Update` that changed nothing, and a WARN `unsynced` (`error_class` `write-failed-fsync`) when the directory sync after the rename fails, the write landed all the same. Bound again in `internal/state` for `Forget` (an INFO `forget` naming what went, a WARN `forget` per removal that failed or file refused) and `ClaimRule`'s once-a-process WARN `claim-rule` when the boot time can't be read; in `cmd` for the WARN `forget` when `hooks.json` can't be found and the WARN `unrecorded` (`open_mint.go`) when a minted session can't be claimed; and in `internal/saver` for the WARN `drops-held` (`op`, `sessions`, `detail`, `via`) on a mass vanish and the DEBUG `claim-skipped`. Whether each committed change, a drop the saver's poll lands among them, is also its own line is the point the sessions question names as at odds.
why: What went with a dropped entry, and every failure to write the index, is reconstructible from `sessions:` lines.

text: `Forget`, removing what Portal keeps beside an entry a committed `Update` removed or replaced, removes the entry's hook only while the hook still holds the command it read, removes every hook of a batch under one hold of the hooks lock, and logs each removal as the `hooks` component's `discard`, carrying the caller's `via` and, in `value`, the command it removed.
why: So `Forget` takes only the hook it read with the entry, and each removal is greppable under `hooks:` with where it came from.

text: Is the `hooks` component's `discard` an `op` value? The `sessions` row names each hook `Forget` removes a `discard`, and the `value` key's row says a `discard` carries the command it removed, yet neither the state-mutation trail's closed `op` value space nor the `op` key's row in the closed attr-key space lists `discard`.

text: Component `migrate` owns `portal migrate`'s run in `internal/migrate`, under the `bootstrap` process role: INFO `no tmux server`, `tmux hooks removed` (`unset`), `tmux saver killed`, `tmux daemon exited` (`target_pid`, `took`), `hooks backed up` (`path`), `state built` (`path`, `sessions`), and one INFO per run not refused (`migrated`, `migration finished`, `already migrated` or `nothing to migrate`, each with `path` and `took`); a WARN `unsynced` when a parent's sync after a rename fails, the first rename's logged only after the second; and an ERROR `stopped` (`error`, worded for the user) whenever a run stops or fails to start. The `sessions` and `hooks` components record what it writes.
why: A migration's every step and its refusal are greppable as `migrate:`.

text: Component `process` is reserved for portal-binary lifecycle and diagnostic markers (`start`, `exit`, `exec`, `panic`, `log-level resolved`) regardless of subcommand; subsystem-level lifecycle events have their own components.
why: Keeps the binary's lifecycle tripwires distinct from subsystem milestones.

text: Component `spawn` owns the multi-window spawn service, bound in `internal/spawn` and in `cmd`, both burst surfaces emitting through `internal/spawn`'s single-sourced renderers. Detection emits exactly one line: INFO `detection resolved host terminal` (`terminal`, `bundle_id`, `detail`), INFO `detection resolved no host-local terminal` (`detail`), INFO `detection could not tell the host terminal` (`detail`) or WARN `detection transient failure` (`detail`). The ack channel logs a WARN `spawn ack write failed` (`batch`, `error`), a WARN `spawn ack clean failed` (`batch`, `error`) and a DEBUG `stale spawn ack removed` (`path`).
why: Single-sourced renderers keep the picker and `open` burst paths from drifting.

text: Component `resolve` owns `portal open`'s resolution decision: one INFO per bare positional resolved through the guessing chain (glob and domain-pinned targets emit nothing), and one more when a kept session judged again under `bootstrap.lock` is kept no longer and resolves again. It is bound and emitted only in `cmd/open.go`; `internal/resolver` stays pure and log-free.
why: Records the chain's guess without making the resolver library impure.

text: Component `theme` owns theme load, enumeration and persistence outcomes, emitted from three sites in two packages: the loader in `internal/theme` (through an injected logger), `cmd/config.go`'s one-shot `appearance` → theme translation, and `cmd`'s theme persister behind the panel's commit.
why: The theme loader has outcomes worth a passive record; its full catalog is its own section.

text: Component `attach` owns the attach runner in `internal/runner` and its key config in `cmd`. Per attach: DEBUG `started` (`session`, `target_pid`) and `ended` (`session`, `took`), then one INFO `outcome` on every end (`session`; `reason` from {`detach`, `detach_to_shell`, `kill`, `switch`, `take`, `exit`, `signal`, `context`, `panic`, `goexit`}, a panic outranking a signal, which outranks other ends; `code`, `detail`, `target`, `error` as they apply). As they happen: DEBUG `terminal input ended`, WARN `child did not exit`, WARN `resize failed`, WARN `panic`, DEBUG `terminal reset` (`reason` `exit` or `drain`), DEBUG `switch seen`, DEBUG `kill unconfirmed`. Bound again in `cmd`: WARN `key config`, WARN `register failed`, WARN `leader unknown`, WARN `take failed` (`detail` from {`lock`, `read`, `record`, `detach`, `wait`, `lead`}), INFO `clients detached`, and one INFO `drop judged` (`result` `taken` or `shell`, `detail`, `error`). Bound again in `internal/runnerreg`: one INFO per request a caller sends (`switch`, `detach to picker`, `take`, `confirm session`, each with `result` from {`accepted`, `refused`, `failed`, `no runner`}), DEBUG `stale runner` (`reason` `dead` or `orphan socket`), DEBUG `runner entry left` (`reason` from a closed set), DEBUG `take record unreadable`, DEBUG `stale take removed`; and from a runner DEBUG `request`, `listed`, `unlisted`, WARN `register failed`, `unregister failed` and `serve failed`. Every key is cross-listed from its own group.
why: Every attach's end, and every take or switch request, can be told apart from the log when a landing surprises.

text: `tmux` is deliberately not a component; tmux-call detail rides as DEBUG breadcrumbs under the caller's component.
why: `internal/tmux` is a thin wrapper, and logging at that layer produces extreme volume per call.

text: All attr keys are snake_case.
why: The slog/JSON ecosystem convention.

text: The message string is a terse phrase and data lives in attrs (`logger.Info("ok", "pane_key", k, "took", d)`, never `logger.Info(fmt.Sprintf(...))`), with sticky context via `.With(...)` when several events share it.

text: In text mode a string value containing whitespace is quoted with `"`, and a single-token value is emitted unquoted (`raw=trace`, `raw=`); the `raw="<v>"` forms in example lines elsewhere in the spec are sketches, not the contract.
why: Pins quoting against the spec's illustrative lines.

text: JSON mode is standard `slog.NewJSONHandler` output with no special handling; `component` is an ordinary JSON field.
why: Tooling gets standard slog JSON.

text: New components and new attr keys require explicit amendment of the specification's closed lists; spec writers and code reviewers may not introduce component or attr names ad hoc, and the space is genuinely closed.

text: What does each log level mean, and what is the production default?

Use slog's four levels with this contract: DEBUG is the kitchen sink for reconstruction (swallowed-error breadcrumbs, per-event changes under summaries, transient values, decision inputs), off in production; INFO is decision and terminal-point summaries, cycle summaries and lifecycle events, one line per meaningful choice; WARN is unexpected-but-recoverable conditions, every line a signal; ERROR is genuinely unrecoverable, the process about to exit, rare.
why: Without a contract DEBUG and INFO blur and `PORTAL_LOG_LEVEL` stops predictably changing what you see.
rules_out: Custom sublevels such as Trace or Notice

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > Log-level discipline > Decision

text: Daemon lock contention, where the losing daemon exits because it lost `daemon.lock`, is logged at ERROR, unlike the non-contention lock-acquire failure, which stays WARN.
why: ERROR is for "we're exiting because we cannot continue", and the loser daemon exits because it lost the lock.

text: The production default is `PORTAL_LOG_LEVEL=info`, changed from the historical WARN.
why: WARN-only was the posture that left no evidence on 2026-05-28; INFO trades trivial disk for a continuous forensic baseline.
alternatives: Keep WARN as the default

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > Log-level discipline > Decision

text: Because INFO is the production baseline, the prefix taxonomy is designed so a grep on a prefix yields a useful trace at INFO, and state-mutation breadcrumbs are INFO, not DEBUG, so they survive at production level.
why: The two implications the level contract carries forward.

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > Log-level discipline > Decision

text: An idempotent no-op is DEBUG, unless the no-op is the user-visible decision (such as a saver kept at its version, skipping the respawn), which is INFO.
why: A purely internal skip clutters the INFO baseline; an operator wants to see an upgrade considered and declined.

text: A failure inside a hysteresis window (such as the saver probe inside the 3-tick self-supervision window) is DEBUG per tick, with one INFO or WARN when the threshold trips.
why: WARN per tick during transient contention would fire continuously and break the 'every WARN is signal' promise.

text: A recoverable-but-rare condition (a corrupt `sessions.json` falling back to empty, a decode failure dropping one item) is WARN; rarity never bumps it to ERROR.
why: ERROR is strictly a process exiting because it cannot continue.

text: Each call site's level follows the code shape mechanically: an expected swallow → DEBUG with `error_class=expected`; an unexpected error swallowed where work is dropped or the postcondition unmet → WARN with `error_class=unexpected`; one where the postcondition still holds → DEBUG with `error_class=unexpected`; a terminal line before a meaningful successful return → INFO; a cycle-end summary → INFO; an idempotent no-op → DEBUG unless user-visible, then INFO; a probe failure inside a hysteresis window → DEBUG; a hysteresis trip → INFO, or WARN if anomalous; an unexpected-but-recoverable condition → WARN; the line before `os.Exit(N)`, `return err` from `main` or a panic → ERROR.
why: Spec writers and reviewers apply it without judgment.

text: Whether an unexpected swallowed error is WARN or DEBUG is the single question 'did swallowing it lose something?': WARN if the function dropped a unit of work or failed its postcondition, DEBUG if the postcondition still holds.
why: Anchored to the function's contract, not the author's sense of importance; it replaces the judgment row 'DEBUG or WARN if production visibility is wanted'.

cites.section: Log-level discipline (DEBUG/INFO/WARN/ERROR contract) > Mechanical rule (spec-phase intake)

text: A `PORTAL_LOG_LEVEL` that is not exactly `debug`, `info`, `warn` or `error` after lowercasing falls back to `info` with one WARN at process start: `bootstrap: invalid PORTAL_LOG_LEVEL raw="<v>" resolved=info`.
why: Invalid config falls back to the default and is signalled.

text: The default flip affects only the unset case: an explicitly set `PORTAL_LOG_LEVEL`, `warn` or `error` included, resolves unchanged. No in-band 'default changed' line is emitted; how the flip is communicated is a release-notes concern outside the spec.
why: `portal.log` is read after the fact, so an in-band notice is invisible when it would matter.
rules_out: An in-band log line announcing the default change

text: How should `portal.log` rotate so evidence is not churned away?
Rotation is calendar-daily as the primary boundary, with a configurable size-cap safety valve, all encapsulated in the `internal/log` handler.
why: Realistic volumes make a day the right forensic unit; a WARN burst can't push out yesterday, and the size cap only guards against disk fill in a runaway, where capping wouldn't help debugging anyway.
alternatives: Calendar-only daily rotation with no size threshold

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > Log rotation mechanism > Decision

text: Every process's handler is date-aware: each write computes today's filename and ensures the open fd points at it; the first write of a day across all processes creates the file with `O_CREAT|O_EXCL`, and losers of the race open it `O_APPEND`, race-safe for slog-sized writes under `PIPE_BUF`. If something deletes today's file mid-day, the next writer's create-or-append recovers observably.
why: Library-level ownership closes the daemon-down-at-midnight and multi-writer boundary concerns (review F1, F2).

text: A daemon down across midnight, or a multi-day downtime, needs no catch-up logic: any waking process's first write opens today's file, and the day-roll sweep seals every past-day file at once.

why: Settles the `.N` ordering edge.

why: Never fires in normal use even at DEBUG steady state (about 20 MB/day), yet catches a runaway within about a day before the disk fills.

text: Rotated files are immutable: `chmod 0400` once they are no longer today's, so even a buggy library can't overwrite past evidence and the destruction surface narrows to today's file.

text: Each `Handle` computes today's date and reuses the open fd only while the date is unchanged and its inode still matches the current `portal.log` symlink target (`fstat` the fd, `stat` the target, compare `st_dev` and `st_ino`); a date change runs the full new-day path plus the retention sweep.
why: A long-lived `O_APPEND` fd would otherwise keep writing into an orphaned inode.

text: An inode mismatch or `ENOENT` on the target the same day (today's file unlinked or replaced mid-day, or a peer's size-cap rotation) reopens by following the current symlink target `O_APPEND|O_WRONLY`, else recreates the file, and runs neither the retention nor the `chmod` sweep. An already-open writer such as the daemon thereby recovers onto the live file, so a mid-day deletion is detectable and non-lossy going forward.
why: Defends against the unknown zeroing scenario without treating it as a new day.

text: On a reopen, before swinging the symlink, a `portal.log` that is a regular file (by `lstat`) is removed, and so is any `portal.log.old`: the first run under the new system starts clean and pre-migration history is not preserved. After that `portal.log` is always a symlink and the guard never fires.
why: Settles the first-startup migration edge.

text: A reopen opens `${stateDir}/portal.log.<today>` with `O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_APPEND|O_WRONLY`, mode `0600`, retrying `O_APPEND|O_WRONLY` on `EEXIST`.
why: The race-safe create-or-append.

cites.section: Mechanical rule — per `Handle(record)` into the `internal/log` handler

text: The symlink swing uses a pid-scoped temp link `portal.log.<pid>.symlink.tmp` (removed and recreated if this pid's own is left from a crash), then `os.Symlink` and an atomic, last-writer-wins `os.Rename`; concurrent swings are benign since every racer's target is the same. A temp leaked by a crash between the two is reclaimed best-effort by the same pid's next swing; no sweep reclaims it.
why: Cross-process swings never collide on the temp name, and one process swings at most once at a time.

cites.section: Mechanical rule — per `Handle(record)` into the `internal/log` handler

text: On a new day, `chmod 0400` every other `portal.log.<date>*` file not today's and not already 0400, by strict date parse: only names whose date portion parses as `YYYY-MM-DD` (`portal.log.<date>` and `portal.log.<date>.<N>`) are candidates, and any other sibling (the swing temp, the `portal.log.swept.<date>` sentinel, any future one) is skipped.
why: Keeps a leaked swing temp writable so its reclamation isn't bricked.

cites.section: Mechanical rule — per `Handle(record)` into the `internal/log` handler

text: When `current_size + len(serialized) >= PORTAL_LOG_ROTATE_SIZE`, rotate to `portal.log.<today>.<N>`: N is the highest existing for today plus 1 (or 1), opened `O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_APPEND|O_WRONLY`, retrying `N+1` on `EEXIST`, and the symlink swung to it as above; then write the record to the current fd.
why: The disk-fill valve's mechanics.

cites.section: Mechanical rule — per `Handle(record)` into the `internal/log` handler

text: A size-cap rotation does not `chmod 0400` the previous same-day segment; same-day segments are sealed only at the day roll. A peer that missed the rotation keeps appending to the prior segment, splitting today's writes across two readable files, which is accepted.
why: A peer may hold an open `O_APPEND` fd on it that `chmod` doesn't evict, and the cap is a disk-fill valve, not a correctness boundary.

cites.section: Mechanical rule — per `Handle(record)` into the `internal/log` handler

text: Rotation lives in one seam, the `internal/log` handler; no call site outside that package implements rotation logic.
why: Library-encapsulated ownership.

text: A portal version upgrade mid-day writes to the same day's file, only the per-record `version` attr changing.
why: Same date, same file; no special handling.

text: Logging never crashes portal: on an open or write failure (disk full, `EACCES`) the handler tries one stderr fallback write for the record, otherwise drops it, and the process continues; `chmod` and `unlink` failures in the day-roll and retention sweeps are WARN-and-skip; a failed symlink swing leaves the prior symlink and writes continue to the open fd.

text: The per-`Handle` rotation logic stays on the hot path, including the daemon's 1 Hz tick goroutine: steady state is about one unbuffered `write(2)` a tick, and the once-a-day midnight maintenance (swing, past-day seal, retention sweep) costs sub-ms to low single-digit ms, within the 1 s tick and 3 s self-supervision budget, often paid by another process thanks to the single-winner sweep gate.

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > Retention policy and audit > Decision

text: The sweep runs on the first `Handle` of each calendar date, after today's file is opened, so its deletion lines and retention WARN land in today's file, never in the file being aged out.
why: Settles where the breadcrumbs land across midnight.

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > Retention policy and audit > Resolved operational edges

text: Only one process runs a day's sweep: it creates `${stateDir}/portal.log.swept.<today>` with `O_CREAT|O_EXCL`, and on `EEXIST` returns at once, running and emitting nothing; only today's sentinel is meaningful.
why: Every process's first line of the day is its `process: start`, so without the gate a reboot morning's ~32 processes would each emit the deletion lines and 31 would WARN on files already gone.
rules_out: A re-entrant sweep every process runs as a no-op

text: The sweep lists `${stateDir}/portal.log.*` and keeps only names that parse as `portal.log.<YYYY-MM-DD>[.<N>]`, skipping and never deleting any other sibling; each kept file dated before `today - PORTAL_LOG_RETENTION_DAYS` is deleted.
why: A new non-log sibling is safe without being remembered.

text: The sweep unlinks every `portal.log.swept.<date>` sentinel not dated today, WARNing and continuing on error.
why: Prior-day sentinels are dead weight, pruned by an exact 'not today' rule rather than the retention cutoff.

text: The sweep is best-effort and runs synchronously inside the winner's first-of-day `Handle`, the `process: start` line emitted during `log.Init`, so even a short-lived winner finishes it before any work or exec. why: Retention is a disk-space bound, not a correctness boundary.
rules_out: A resumable sentinel with takeover of a dead winner's partial sweep

text: `portal doctor` preserves rotated logs and never sweeps; `portal doctor --fix` runs the same sweep function with `cutoff = today` (deleting every rotated file but the current one), bypassing the single-winner gate and removing every `portal.log.swept.*` sentinel, today's included, as unconditional maintenance with no stale-logs check to fail.
why: An explicit user invocation must always run; the gate exists only to dedupe the automatic sweep.

text: A retention `unlink` never races a live writer's fd: no writer holds an fd older than the current day, since every `Handle` reopens onto today's file within about a tick of midnight, and retention deletes only files at least 30 days old.
why: Resolved by construction; no zombie writer into a deleted inode.

text: How is destruction of today's log, by an unknown cause, made detectable after the fact?

cites.section: Defensive invariants against unknown-cause log destruction > Context

text: Every portal process emits one INFO line at the very start of its execution and one on termination; these are the tripwires, the first line of a damaged day's file timestamping when destruction must have happened.
why: With rotated-file immutability and the `O_EXCL` first-of-day open, they make destruction detectable and recoverable without root-causing it.

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > Defensive invariants against log destruction > Decision

text: `log.Init`, as its final action, emits exactly one `process: start` INFO with `cmd` (`filepath.Base(os.Args[0])`) and `args` (the rest of argv); the baselines are injected, not passed.
why: The start tripwire.

text: `log.Close(exitCode)` emits one `process: exit` INFO with `code` and `took` (from the `startTime` captured at `Init`) and does not call `os.Exit`.
why: The logger owns no control flow, mirroring slog's omission of `Fatal`.

cites.section: Mechanical rule — `process: exit` and the `main` exit shape

text: `main` owns the single `os.Exit`: it calls `log.Init`, runs `rootCmd.Execute()` (which maps to a return code rather than exiting) inside a function whose deferred recover logs `process: panic` with `reason` at ERROR and sets code 2, calls `log.Close(code)` unless it panicked, then `os.Exit(code)`. Exactly one terminal marker fires per run, `process: panic` alone on the panic path.
why: `os.Exit` skips deferred functions, so a deferred `Close` would miss Cobra's error path, the most interesting termination.
rules_out: Deferring `Close`, or calling it before an `os.Exit` scattered elsewhere

cites.section: Mechanical rule — `process: exit` and the `main` exit shape

text: Bare `os.Exit` outside `main` is prohibited and rejected at PR review; every other function returns an error or code.
why: The enforcement mechanism for 'every termination is marked'.

cites.section: Mechanical rule — `process: exit` and the `main` exit shape

text: The one sanctioned exception is the daemon's self-eject, which calls `os.Exit(0)` directly: it first emits `daemon: self-eject ticks=N threshold=N`, then `log.Close(0)`, then exits, and runs no `daemonShutdownFunc`, so no `daemon: shutdown` line fires on that path.
why: It must not unwind through another capture or commit cycle, and stays fully paired.

cites.section: Mechanical rule — `process: exit` and the `main` exit shape

text: Every binary entry point (today only `main.go`) calls `log.Init` before any other portal code that might log and routes all termination through the `main` shape.
why: Coverage of the markers.

cites.section: Mechanical rule — `process: exit` and the `main` exit shape

text: Every `syscall.Exec` call site emits a plain `exec` INFO immediately before the exec, under its owning component, with no logger-owned helper: `AttachConnector` emits `process: exec target=tmux args=…` (with `args` by `shellquote.Readable`), and the hydrate helper's marker is `hydrate: exec`.
why: `syscall.Exec` runs no deferred code and never returns, so without a marker a benign handoff, portal's most common termination, looks like a destructive kill.

text: A `process: start` is classified by what follows it: `process: exit` is a normal return, `process: exec` a benign handoff, `process: panic` a recorded crash, and nothing at all is alarming.
why: The termination markers make every run's end readable.

text: An unpaired `process: start` is alarming only if no `saver:` or `daemon:` line names that pid as an external kill: a process killed by an uncatchable signal emits nothing, but the killer records it (the tmux version's `saver: kill-barrier started/escalated target_pid=X` and `saver: placeholder died`).
why: A deliberate kill is recorded by its killer.

text: The rotation handler writes directly to the `*os.File` (`O_APPEND`) with no `bufio`, so a marker is in the kernel when `Info` returns and survives `os.Exit` and `syscall.Exec`; no `Sync`/flush API or atomic exit/exec helper exists. An unbuffered writer is a locked constraint on the handler.
why: Flush reduces to not buffering.

text: The `process` lifecycle set (`start`, `exit`, `exec`, `panic`, `log-level resolved`) is written by the handler regardless of `PORTAL_LOG_LEVEL`, while staying semantically INFO for every other purpose.
why: At `warn` or `error` a filtered tripwire would falsify the always-present guarantee and hide the line proving the resolved level.

cites.section: Lifecycle markers bypass the level filter

text: `SwitchConnector` (the in-tmux path) needs no exec marker: it runs `tmux switch-client` as a subprocess and returns, getting `process: exit` via `Close`.
why: Only true replace-process sites need the exec marker.

text: The `args` attr logs the whole argv, quoted only where a shell would need it, hook commands included.
why: Acceptable for portal's single-user threat model.

text: How is it verified that `PORTAL_LOG_LEVEL` actually reaches spawned processes such as the daemon?

`log.Init` emits one `process: log-level resolved` INFO immediately after `process: start`, with `resolved` (`debug` / `info` / `warn` / `error`), `source` (`env` for a valid set value, `default` for unset, `fallback` for an invalid value, which also emits the invalid-level WARN) and `raw` (the env value as observed, empty if unset); it bypasses the level filter. Every entry point calling `log.Init` emits it with no extra work.
why: A positive marker closes the gap where a level fails to propagate and coverage silently degrades while tests still pass.

text: Any integration test that sets `PORTAL_LOG_LEVEL` must find the spawned process's `process: log-level resolved resolved=<expected> source=env` line (matched by `pid`) and fail if it is absent or not `source=env`, through the helper `AssertLogLevelResolved(t, logPath, pid, expected)` in `internal/portaltest`.

text: How is failure context (stderr, errno, phase) kept when an external call fails, so it reaches the log?

cites.section: Diagnostic context preservation at boundaries > Context

text: Every external-boundary call site preserves stderr, errno and phase-of-failure context in the wrapped error it returns; the level discipline and call-site pattern then decide how that error reaches `portal.log`.
why: Discarding stderr is the most common way debug context is lost exactly where it is needed.

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > Diagnostic context preservation at boundaries > Decision

text: Every `exec.Cmd` call site uses `cmd.CombinedOutput()` or captures `cmd.Stderr` into a buffer before `Run`/`Output`, and on error wraps the exit status (or signal) and the trimmed stderr, as `fmt.Errorf("%s %v: %w (stderr: %s)", cmd.Path, cmd.Args[1:], err, stderr)`. Prohibited: `_, _ = cmd.Run()`, `cmd.Output()` without `cmd.Stderr`, or any wrapped error without the stderr text.
why: Boundary class 1.

text: `internal/tmux.RealCommander.Run`/`RunRaw` capture stdout and stderr on every invocation; on non-zero exit the error embeds the exit code, the tmux argv and the trimmed stderr, and tmux sentinels (`ErrNoSuchSession`, `ErrEmptyPaneList`) are detected from stderr and wrapped as `fmt.Errorf("%w: %s", sentinel, stderr)`. A generic error without stderr is prohibited.
why: Boundary class 2.

text: Errors from `os` syscalls keep their path and errno: added context wraps with `%w` so the original is preserved and unwrappable; replacing a `*os.PathError` with something like `errors.New("file operation failed")` is prohibited.
why: Boundary class 3.

text: For `io`/`bufio` and scrollback FIFO reads, EOF and timeout are expected outcomes classified `expected`; other I/O errors wrap as `fmt.Errorf("read %s: %w", path, err)` to keep the path.
why: Boundary class 4.

text: At the log site the `error` attr is the wrapped error itself (`err`, never `err.Error()`), and the handler renders the whole wrapped chain, stderr text included.
why: slog handles the serialisation and the context survives to the line.

cites.section: slog attr usage at the eventual log site

text: A shared helper in `internal/log` (such as `CombinedOutputWithContext(cmd) ([]byte, error)`) may be added only once 3 or more identical wrapping patterns exist in production code; until then each site wraps directly.
why: No helpers ahead of need.

text: `defaultIdentifyPS` (`internal/state/daemon_identity.go`), which discarded stderr on failure, embeds the trimmed stderr in its wrapped error per boundary class 1.
why: A pre-identified defect a mechanical pass could skip.

text: When does a cycle emit a summary, what does it carry, and what falls below or beside it?

cites.section: Cycle-level summary cadence and shape > Context

text: Every cycle emits one INFO summary at completion, with per-item events at DEBUG in the steady state or WARN on an anomaly.
why: An operator reconstructs a window from summaries without per-event lines.

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > Cycle-level summary cadence and shape > Decision

text: A cycle is a loop iterating distinct items, a sequence running discrete named steps (the six-step bootstrap orchestrator, the restore engine), or a ticker-driven periodic loop (the daemon's 1 Hz loop).
why: Defines which functions owe a summary.

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > Cycle-level summary cadence and shape > Mechanical rule

text: A cycle captures `start` before its body, counts items and per-item anomalies, and at its end emits exactly one INFO `<verb> complete` with `<unit>` from the closed keys `sessions`, `panes`, `entries`, `steps` (sweeps reporting `reaped`/`killed`/`skipped`/`unset`, the saver's poll and final flush `claimed`/`dropped`/`captured`/`reaped`, restore `restored`/`failed`), sub-counts such as `natural_churn` (items that ended cleanly mid-cycle), `anomalous` (items that failed without ending the cycle, each with its own WARN) and `entries_failed`, and always `took`.
why: A uniform verb + counts + `took` triplet; a new unit key needs an amendment.

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > Cycle-level summary cadence and shape > Mechanical rule

text: Inside a cycle, a per-item DEBUG breadcrumb is always emitted where the per-item path is interesting, and a per-item WARN only for an item that fails anomalously, counted in `anomalous`.
why: DEBUG floods only when enabled; the summary is the INFO truth.

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > Cycle-level summary cadence and shape > Mechanical rule

text: The cycle catalog: `capture: poll complete claimed=N dropped=N captured=N reaped=N took=T` for the saver's 5 s poll, only when it claimed, dropped, captured or removed something; `capture: flush complete captured=N took=T` at shutdown, only when it captured; `bootstrap: orchestration complete steps=6 warnings=N took=T`; `bootstrap: step complete step=<StepName> took=T` per step; `restore: restore complete restored=N failed=N anomalous=N took=T`, and with `session=S` for `open` bringing back one kept session; `clean: orphan-fifo sweep complete reaped=N skipped=N took=T`; `clean: orphan-daemon sweep complete killed=N took=T`; `clean: stale-flag sweep complete unset=N took=T`; hooks `CleanStale` in the batch-summary shape; `hooks: rekey op=rekey entries=N via=V took=T` for `portal migrate`'s rewrite; the retention sweep in its own shape.
why: Spec writers produce one INFO call site per catalogued cycle.

text: Which saver and daemon lifecycle events are logged, and with what?

cites.section: Saver and daemon lifecycle event taxonomy > Context

text: Saver and daemon lifecycle events form a closed catalog, each site emitting exactly one INFO at the moment described; adding an event requires amending the specification, and per-tick summaries stay with the cycle catalog.
why: The 2026-05-28 saver disappearance was undiagnosable for want of INFO lifecycle events.

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > Saver and daemon lifecycle event taxonomy > Decision
1. Portal Observability Layer > Saver and daemon lifecycle event taxonomy > Mechanical rule

text: The tmux version's `saver` events, emitted by bootstrap: `placeholder created` (`tmux_pane`), `destroy-unattached off` (`tmux_pane`), `respawn-daemon` (`from_pid`, `to_pid`, `tmux_pane`), `daemon ready` (`target_pid`) after the 2 s readiness barrier, `kill-barrier started` (`target_pid`), `kill-barrier escalated` (`target_pid`, `reason=kill-session-timeout`) and `placeholder died` (`target_pid`, `reason` `signal` / `exit` / `unknown`) when bootstrap observes a saver pane's host process exited.
why: Bootstrap observes the saver from outside, a different observer than the saver's own `process:` lines.

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > Saver and daemon lifecycle event taxonomy > Mechanical rule

text: On zmx the saver's lifecycle is `internal/saverhost`'s (EnsureSaver and the stop it shares with `portal uninstall`, each under `saver.lock`): INFO `session created` (`target_pid`), `daemon ready` (`target_pid`, `took`), `daemon kept` (`target_pid`; a recycle considered and declined), `recycle` (`target_pid`, `reason`), `stop started` (`target_pid`) at the proved SIGTERM, `stop escalated` (`target_pid`, `reason=term-timeout`) at the re-proved SIGKILL, and `daemon exited` (`target_pid`, `took`) just before the session kill. Beside them a WARN `stop refused` (`target_pid`, `error`) when the stop refuses its pid or a proof fails, so no signal is sent, and a DEBUG `session created elsewhere` (`error`) when another process created `_portal-saver` first.
why: The zmx saver observed from outside, as bootstrap's tmux events did.

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > Saver and daemon lifecycle event taxonomy > Mechanical rule

text: `daemon` events: `lock acquired` (`session`, the zmx session it runs in, empty outside one) on taking `daemon.lock`; no INFO as the self-supervision counter climbs (DEBUG); `self-eject` (`ticks`, `threshold`) when it trips; `shutdown` (`reason` `sighup` / `signal` / `exit`, `flush_completed`, false when the final flush failed, stood down for a restore or was cut by the bound or a second signal) on the normal return path, emitted once by the flush or the bound, whichever is first, and never on the self-eject path.
why: Covers only moments `process:` cannot express.

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > Saver and daemon lifecycle event taxonomy > Mechanical rule

text: `process:` owns the OS-process boundary for every role, the daemon included; `daemon:` and `saver:` lines are additive milestones, never a substitute. A `daemon: spawn` event is dropped as redundant with `process: start process_role=daemon`, its unique attr moving onto `daemon: lock acquired` (on zmx, `session`).
why: No two lines for one instant carrying the same data.
rules_out: A `daemon: spawn` event

text: Reason spaces are closed per event: `kill-barrier escalated` `kill-session-timeout`; `placeholder died` `signal` / `exit` / `unknown`; `recycle` `version` (another version recorded, a dev build's naming its build) / `unknown` (after ReadyWait no `daemon.pid` naming the session's process or no `daemon.version`, or this build is the unidentified `dev`); `stop escalated` `term-timeout`; `daemon shutdown` `sighup` / `signal` / `exit`, not `self-eject`. New values require amending the catalog.
why: Closed values keep lifecycle lines mechanically readable.

text: Tick-rate events are not INFO: the saver poll's summary is the cycle catalog's, logged only for a poll that did something, and per-tick probe failures are DEBUG, only the self-eject trip being INFO.
why: Keeps the INFO baseline at meaningful events.

text: The catalog's calling code: `cmd/bootstrap/` for the tmux `saver:` events; `cmd/state_daemon.go` for `lock acquired`, `self-eject` and `shutdown`; `internal/tmux/portal_saver.go` for the kill-barrier escalation; `internal/saverhost/` for the zmx saver events.
why: Spec writers walk these files row by row.

text: What does the `theme` component log, when, and from where?

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > The `theme` component event catalog > Decision

text: `theme` events form a closed catalog amended only through the specification; the component exists so a launch that could not use the theme asked for leaves a passive record.
why: The panel's row and doctor's line are seen only when the user goes looking; the log is the record that exists without that.

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > The `theme` component event catalog > Decision

text: Theme rejections log at WARN, not INFO.
why: 'Your config did not work' is a warning in a log; doctor's advisory exit code is a separate decision that need not agree.

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > The `theme` component event catalog > Decision

text: The component records where a theme is used, never where one is diagnosed: `portal doctor`, `portal theme export` and the offline `capturetool` emit no `theme` event; the emitting processes are TUI launches.
why: Those commands are the user looking; doctor would put the most WARNs where they are least needed; a read-only diagnosis writing WARNs breaks its read-only claim; and it makes the per-process dedup determinate.

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > The `theme` component event catalog > Decision

text: The catalog: `loaded` INFO, one per resolved slot at TUI construction plus the newly live slot when a commit turns a constant into an adaptive pair, not deduplicated, the panel's re-resolutions emitting none (`slug`, `slot`); `enumerated` INFO once per panel open, absent or unusable directory alike and on an open refused by the post-enumeration floor re-check, but not on an entry-gate refusal (`count`, `rejected`); `rejected` WARN per rejected file, deduplicated per process on `slug`+`reason` or `path`+`reason` for a file with no slug (`slug` or `path`, `reason`, `token`); `directory unusable` WARN from both the panel's enumeration and the construction-time read, deduplicated on `path`+`reason`, nothing for an absent directory; `fallback applied` WARN, deduplicated on `slug`+`reason` (`slug` the failed nomination, `slot`, `reason`); `appearance migrated` INFO only on a persist that wrote a theme key (`slug`), its absence the failure signal; `commit failed` WARN per failed panel commit write (`slug`, `slot`, `reason`), not emitted by the migration path.
why: Each event's cadence and dedup keeps the trail forensic rather than running commentary.

text: `fallback applied` is emitted before its paired `loaded`, and `loaded` carries the slug of the palette that actually rendered, the fallback's where one applied.
why: A reader meets the cause before the consequence, and `grep "theme:"` can say which palette is on screen.

text: The dedup key is `(event, identity, reason)`.
why: The event keeps catalogs from colliding on a shared identity, and the same file failing for a different reason is a different problem.

text: Whether anything is written is the caller's decision: the loader emits unconditionally through its logger seam; `cmd`'s one direct construction of the seam uses the real component logger on the used paths (TUI construction, the panel, the persister), and `portal doctor`, `portal theme export` and `capturetool` take `theme.NewSilentLoader()`, the same loader over a discarding seam.
why: A silent caller runs the identical code path, with no branch, flag or second implementation.

text: The per-process dedup state lives on the injected logger, not in the leaf package: one TUI process shares one scope across every enumerating path, concurrent processes each own theirs, tests inject a fresh one, and check-and-record is one critical section.
why: The construction-time read and the panel hit the same conditions and must not double up.

text: `internal/theme` binds nothing; the single `log.For("theme")` binding lives in `cmd` and constructs the seams on the used paths, and a guard test catches a second binding inside `cmd`.
why: The seam case of the bind-once rule.

text: `internal/theme` emits `loaded`, `enumerated`, `rejected`, `directory unusable` and `fallback applied` through the seam; `cmd/config.go` emits `appearance migrated` from the translation's persist; `cmd`'s theme persister alone emits `commit failed`. The exec path (`portal open <target>`) emits nothing, constructing no TUI and never running the loader.
why: `prefs` must not import `internal/log`, and the TUI emitting would make `internal/tui` a fourth site; the exec path stays free of cost.

text: How is hook firing observed, given that the hydrate helper hands off through `syscall.Exec` and never sees the hook's exit status?

No wrapper envelope: the architectural limit is accepted, everything up to the exec is instrumented, and post-exec is silent by design. A shell envelope capturing the hook's exit status to a file for the daemon to read is deferred to a separate work unit, the next layer if the lookup and exec lines prove insufficient.
why: The envelope brings shell-quoting hazards, signal-handling complications and a new file-cleanup concern.
alternatives: A shell envelope recording the hook's exit status before chaining to `$SHELL`

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > Hook-firing observability limit (syscall.Exec) > Decision

text: The hydrate helper (`cmd/state_hydrate.go`, `execShellOrHookAndExit`) emits a DEBUG `hook lookup` with `hook_key` and `result` (`hit` / `miss` / `error`, plus `error` on an error) after querying `hooks.json` and before the exec.
why: Distinguishes a drifted hook key (miss) from a failed lookup (error) from a helper that never reached the lookup (no line).

cites.section: 1. Portal Observability Layer > Hook-firing observability limit (syscall.Exec) > Mechanical rule

text: Firing a multi-window spawn burst from a remote tmux client (Blink on iPhone/iPad over SSH/mosh) while a host-local terminal client (Ghostty on the Mac) is also attached opens the N-1 spawned windows on the host-local terminal; the trigger window self-attaches to the Nth session remotely, so it reads as a partial success while host windows, which Portal never tears down, linger on the machine the user isn't at.
how: Reported by the user in the inbox bug capture and recorded as the symptoms, with reproduction steps for both burst surfaces.

text: Severity is moderate: nothing is destroyed, but host windows open silently on the wrong machine and linger, and the triggering user gets no indication; it hits the user's routine remote workflow on both burst surfaces. The pure-remote case (no local client attached) already resolves NULL and correctly no-ops.
how: From the user's report as the log records its environment and impact.

text: What should a spawn burst do when its triggering client is remote but a host-local client is attached to the same session?

A remote-triggered burst resolves unsupported and takes the same atomic no-op as the pure-remote case, even with host-local clients attached; windows never open on a machine or display the triggering user isn't at.
why: Opening windows on a screen the user isn't looking at is a silent wrong-machine action, a trust and correctness fault.

text: Which burst surfaces does the fix cover, and does it extend to supporting mobile terminals as spawn targets?

The fix covers both burst trigger surfaces, the TUI multi-select picker burst and the CLI multi-target `portal open <a> <b> ...` (N>=2) burst, since both share the identical `internal/spawn` detection gate.
why: The CLI-verb redesign re-homed the burst under `open`, sharing the same `detect_inside.go` gate as the picker.

text: A mobile-terminal (Blink) spawn adapter is out of scope: this fix is about the detection locality gate only.
why: Supporting mobile terminals as spawn targets was judged infeasible elsewhere (no host-to-device control channel) and is independent of this bug.

text: Both burst surfaces resolve the host terminal through the same `spawn.Detector.Detect()`: the CLI burst at `cmd/open_burst_run.go:158` and the TUI multi-select at `internal/tui/spawn_detect.go:90` (run once per picker session, cached at startup); `portal doctor`'s host-terminal line (`cmd/doctor.go:406`) is a third consumer. Inside tmux, `resolve()` reads the triggering pane's session and calls `detectInsideTmux`.
how: Code trace of the detection path.

text: `detectInsideTmux` (`internal/spawn/detect_inside.go:86-105`) decides locality in the wrong order: a client whose walk resolves NULL (remote/mosh) is dropped before the activity comparison, and `client_activity` is only a tiebreak among the surviving local clients. It answers 'is any host-local client attached to the triggering session?' rather than 'is the client that triggered this burst host-local?', so in the mixed case the remote, most-active trigger is discarded and the local client's identity is returned as supported.
how: Code trace of the per-client loop (NULL-drop at line 98 before the comparison at line 100).

text: The bug fires only when a host-local client is attached to the same session as the remote trigger: `ListClients` runs `list-clients -t <session>`, which lists only clients connected to that session, and the session is the triggering pane's (`display-message -p '#{session_name}'` with no `-t`). A local client on another session isn't listed, giving a clean NULL and the correct no-op. The precondition is natural, since `tmux attach` with no `-t` lands on the most-recently-used session.
how: Code read of `internal/tmux/clients.go` and `internal/tmux/tmux.go`, against the tmux 3.7b man page for list-clients.

text: Recent spawn bugfixes did not fix this: `detect_inside.go` has one commit ever (`45010cf3`, restore-host-terminal-windows); the spawned-window-dead-ends-on-session-exit fix touched `ghostty.go` and the persistent-no-host-terminal-banner fix is TUI-side. The bug still lives in current main. This settles the discovery's first task, whether it still reproduces, by reading the history, not by a live reproduction.
how: git log of the detection files.

text: A plain pane-run `display-message -p '#{client_pid}'` resolves to the highest-`client_activity` client attached to the pane's session, tmux's best-client resolution (`cmd_find_current_client` -> `server_client_best`). Since the user acts on their client immediately before detection, that most-active client is the triggering client: a strong tmux-native heuristic, not a hard binding.
how: Read-only probe on tmux 3.7b.

text: `client_activity` tracks a client's sent input, not the redraws it receives from mirroring: tmux mirrors output, never input, so a trigger keystroke on the remote client bumps only the remote's activity and an idle mirroring local client stays stale. Detection runs immediately after the trigger action (picker startup for the TUI, command entry for the CLI), so the triggering client is still the freshest.
how: Measured in a sandbox `-L` socket on tmux 3.7b: a client on a session printing `date` every second, sent no keystrokes, held a flat `client_activity` (1784808119) across about 4 s of mirrored output; one injected keystroke advanced it to 1784808123.

text: The inside-tmux client walk introduced by restore-host-terminal-windows (`45010cf3`) solved NULL-filtering for the pure-remote case but framed activity as a local-only tiebreak, assuming that any attached local client means the user is at a local terminal; and tmux gives a pane-run command no hard binding to the client that launched it, so the design leaned on enumeration and under-used the most-active heuristic.
how: Code and history read, recorded as contributing factors.

text: The buggy outcome is codified as intended in a unit test: `internal/spawn/detect_inside_test.go:133` ('it drops remote clients but still resolves a mixed local+remote client set') seeds a remote at activity 9999 and a local at 1 and asserts the local wins. No test models the remote client as the user, and the real scenario needs an actual remote plus host-local client on one session, outside unit-test reach and easy to miss when the developer sits at the local terminal.
how: Read of the test suite.

text: The TUI's proactive multi-select `m`-entry block keys on `DetectUnsupported()` (`m.detectResolution == spawn.ResolutionUnsupported`), which is false in the mixed case because detection resolves a supported local terminal, so the block is silently defeated and the user walks the full flow into a wrong-machine burst. Fixing detection re-arms it with no separate change: the mixed case resolves NULL, `DetectUnsupported()` is true and `m` is pre-blocked.

text: How should inside-tmux detection decide whether the host terminal is driveable when several clients are attached to the triggering session?

`detectInsideTmux` selects the triggering client first, the client with the highest `client_activity` across all clients enumerated on the triggering pane's session (local and remote alike, enumeration unchanged as `ListClients(session)`), then locality-checks that single winner, inverting the filter-then-tiebreak order.
why: It is the only option correct in both mixed directions: a remote trigger with an idle local bystander no-ops, and a local trigger with an idle remote bystander still drives, which the user routinely hits with both attached. It is one localized change that corrects every `Detect()` consumer.
rules_out: Any remote client on the session means a no-op (option B): refuses a legitimate local spawn because an idle remote is attached.
Drive only when every client is local (option C): the same defect, a single remote bystander disables local spawn.
alternatives: B: any remote client on the session -> no-op
C: only drive if all clients are local

cites.section: The Fix: Gate Locality on the Triggering (Most-Active) Client

text: On an exact `client_activity` tie the first-listed client wins the selection, a deterministic rule that keeps the existing multi-local tie-break behaviour.
why: The code must apply some deterministic rule, and this one keeps the existing multi-local tests green.

cites.section: The Fix: Gate Locality on the Triggering (Most-Active) Client

text: Only the winner's process tree is walked; a winner that resolves to a local `.app` bundle is driven, its `Identity` returned as a supported host terminal.
why: The winner is the client the user is acting through, so its locality alone gates the burst.

cites.section: The Fix: Gate Locality on the Triggering (Most-Active) Client

text: A winner whose walk reaches a clean NULL (remote/mosh, ancestry never reaching a local `.app`) gives a NULL identity and nil error: the honest no-op, the same atomic no-op as the pure-remote case.
why: A remote trigger must never open windows on the host.

cites.section: The Fix: Gate Locality on the Triggering (Most-Active) Client

text: A winner whose walk fails transiently (a `ps` or `defaults` error) gives NULL plus an `ErrDetectTransient`-wrapped error, which `Detect()` logs as a `spawn` WARN and folds to the unsupported no-op: never open windows on uncertainty.
why: The fail-safe principle agreed in discussion: when the winner's locality is indeterminate, the honest no-op beats risking a wrong-machine spawn.

cites.section: The Fix: Gate Locality on the Triggering (Most-Active) Client

text: An empty client list gives a clean NULL with nil error: no winner to select, the honest no-op, not a transient error.

text: By scenario the fix gives: pure remote -> NULL no-op (unchanged); single local -> drive (unchanged); mixed with the remote most active -> NULL no-op (the bug fixed); mixed with the local most active -> drive (legitimate local spawn kept); 2+ all-local -> drive the highest-activity local, first-listed on a tie (unchanged); enumeration failure -> NULL and WARN (unchanged); winner's walk transient -> NULL and WARN (fail-safe); empty list -> clean NULL. The change is only ever 'no-op where it used to drive', never a new false drive.
how: The spec's scenario table, with fix validation confirming no new false drive.

text: Should the most-active winner be computed in Go over the existing `ListClients` set (A1), or delegated to tmux's best-client via `display-message -p '#{client_pid}'` (A2)?

Compute the winner in Go over the existing `ListClients(session)` enumeration, which already returns each client's PID and `client_activity`, then walk only the winner, keeping the `clientLister` seam and the `detectInsideTmux(session, lister, walker, reader)` signature intact.
why: It reuses data already fetched with no extra tmux round-trip and keeps the unit tests and their deterministic tie-break assertions meaningful.
rules_out: Delegating to tmux's best-client via `display-message -p '#{client_pid}'`: adds a round-trip, exposes no controllable tie-break, and would restructure the seam.
alternatives: A2: delegate to tmux's best-client resolution and walk that pid

The dropped walk-resilience property is accepted explicitly as an owned behaviour change: a local burst with 2+ local clients whose most-active client's `ps` transiently flakes now refuses (NULL and WARN) rather than driving a resolvable lower-activity local, and a regression test locks it in on purpose.
why: It is the deliberate fail-safe of never spawning on uncertainty, a trade of resilience for correctness that must be owned, not slipped in.
