text: A cleanup failure logs WARN and retries at the next cadence; it never escalates or crashes the daemon.
why: Mirrors the tick loop's existing 'tick failed' handling.

text: Accepted residue: if a cold boot's marker or FIFO cleanup soft-fails, the residue isn't retried until the next full bootstrap.
why: Markers and FIFOs are inert (the daemon-merge live-set filter already prevents dead-session resurrection), and version-stamped upgrades add full-bootstrap cleanup passes beyond restarts.

text: Accepted residue: with hooks cleanup moved from the per-command bootstrap to the conditionally alive daemon, the worst case (daemon dead, revival failing and no portal clean) leaves inert hooks bloat until the daemon next revives.
why: Stale hooks can't fire on the wrong session; the person weighed keeping a bootstrap-time pass and rejected it, since it would only help when the daemon can't start at all, already a capture-down state.

text: Accepted residue: a daemon that repeatedly self-ejects and is revived within less than the cleanup interval resets its in-process lastCleanup each time, so cleanup can be starved indefinitely while liveness probes report it alive.
why: The residue is inert hooks bloat, and a flapping daemon is a rare pathological state whose real problem is the flapping.

text: Where is the latch stored, what does it hold, and when is it satisfied?

The latch is @portal-bootstrapped, a tmux server option whose value is the binary version (version-stamped, not a presence flag), set with SetServerOption and read with TryGetServerOption, on the @portal-restoring mechanism and the internal/state/markers.go seam vocabulary (RestoringChecker, ServerOptionWriter).
why: A server option dies with the server, so a restart clears it and the next command full-bootstraps. Version-stamped because the person upgrades Portal often and restarts tmux rarely: a presence latch would keep RegisterPortalHooks from re-running mid-lifetime, so a new binary's hook bodies would lag for weeks; version-stamping re-converges hooks and recreates the daemon on the first post-upgrade command, then re-stamps.
rules_out: A bare presence latch

text: The latch is satisfied only when present and its stored value equals the running binary's cmd.version, a plain string equality. One TryGetServerOption read decides: absent, mismatched, or a read error or down server is not satisfied (full bootstrap); present and matching is satisfied (abridged). No separate ServerRunning() probe.
why: The read fails gracefully on a down server; the person: 'single read is fine.'

text: The latch's value is exactly cmd.version, a bare version string; forensic extras such as a set-timestamp or pid are out of scope.
why: The satisfied test is plain string equality, so the format must stay parse-free; extras would need a delimiter and a parse-and-compare rule, so they are deferred rather than left an ambiguous implementation detail.
rules_out: Adding set-timestamp or pid to the latch value

text: Accepted: local and unversioned builds carry a constant version string, so version-stamping re-bootstraps only on real version bumps, not local rebuilds; testing local hook changes uses the escape hatch tmux set-option -u @portal-bootstrapped.
why: The person rarely runs local builds, which interfere with the brew-installed version.

text: The latch needs no explicit invalidation code: a server restart clears it, and a version mismatch after an upgrade is 'not satisfied', so the first post-upgrade command full-bootstraps (re-registering hooks, recreating the daemon) and re-stamps.
why: Guiding principle: don't program around anything that self-heals through an idempotent, no-op full bootstrap.

text: The manual escape hatch is exactly tmux set-option -u @portal-bootstrapped, forcing the next command back to a full bootstrap. Production code never unsets the latch; no portal command, portal clean flag, subcommand or help text for unsetting it is added.
why: The raw tmux path is the whole user-facing contract for forcing a re-bootstrap; UnsetServerOption is a reused mechanism only for it.
rules_out: A portal-level unset command or flag

cites.section: Out of scope (planning must not invent)

text: When is the latch set, and what counts as a successful bootstrap?

The latch is set as the final action of a successful Orchestrator.Run, inside Run rather than by its callers, so the synchronous path and the concurrent cold+TUI goroutine set it identically: latch present means a full bootstrap ran to completion.
why: No second set-point to keep in sync.

text: The latch is set at the end, never early. A pure cold burst, N commands hitting a serverless tmux at once outside the picker, is not collapsed by this and is accepted as a non-goal.
why: Set early, a concurrent command would take the abridged path before Restore recreated the sessions and attach to one that doesn't exist yet. End-setting suffices for the reopen burst, which fires only from the picker, shown only after the bootstrap completes. The pure cold burst is already tolerated by the daemon flock and idempotent hook convergence; the latch only reduces its frequency.
rules_out: Setting the latch early, such as right after the server is up

cites.section: Discussion: Skip Bootstrap When Warm > Context

text: Successful means no fatal error: soft warnings (SaverDownWarning, CorruptSessionsJSONWarning, a partial restore) still set the latch; only a fatal step (EnsureServer, RegisterPortalHooks, SetRestoring, ClearRestoring) leaves it unset, so the next command retries the full bootstrap.
why: Soft warnings either self-heal on the abridged path or are non-retryable; requiring a clean run would let one transient SaverDownWarning force every command back to a full bootstrap for the whole lifetime.
rules_out: Requiring a warning-free run to set the latch

text: In Run, the latch write goes after the last soft step and the fatal-error gate but before the 'bootstrap: orchestration complete' summary and the return; on the concurrent path it is therefore written before the terminal completion event (BootstrapCompleteMsg / the progress pipe's Done).
why: Latch present means a full bootstrap ran to completion by the time the picker transitions and any reopen burst could fire.

text: The latch write is best-effort: on failure it logs WARN and is swallowed, never fatal; the next command reads not satisfied, re-runs the full bootstrap and retries the write.
why: It self-heals through the idempotent, near-no-op full bootstrap.

text: A latch-write failure is only a WARN log line under the bootstrap component, on both paths: it is not appended to the returned warnings and not routed through the progress channel or the bootstrapWarnings sink.
why: It self-heals, so nothing is actionable for the user.

text: Because the latch is set only after EagerSignalHydrate and the clearing of @portal-restoring, latch present guarantees hydrate signalling finished and @portal-restoring was cleared: the latch and @portal-restoring are never both set on an abridged command, a late-arming skeleton pane can't be stranded unsignalled, and a crash mid-bootstrap leaves the latch unset so the next command re-clears a leaked restoring marker.

text: Where does the latch check sit in the entry path, and how does the abridged path plug into the existing plumbing?

In PersistentPreRunE, after the tmux client is built, one latch read and version compare branches: satisfied goes to the abridged path; not satisfied goes to the full bootstrap, concurrent with the loading screen on the TUI path (open with no args) and synchronous otherwise.
why: Single read chosen for minimalism.

text: The verdict is computed once into a latchSatisfied bool and threaded, never read twice. The abridged gate sits upstream of shouldRunConcurrentBootstrap and returns before the orchestrator; on the not-satisfied path shouldRunConcurrentBootstrap drops its ServerRunning() probe and reduces to the TUI-path test (isTUIPath && client != nil).
why: The not-satisfied verdict already establishes that a full bootstrap is needed, and a full bootstrap on the TUI path should always show the loading screen.

text: The concurrent loading path fires whenever a full bootstrap runs on the TUI path, keyed on latch-not-satisfied rather than server-down: a hand-started tmux server hit by x now gets the loading screen and progress instead of a synchronous stall. What the full bootstrap does is unchanged.

text: The abridged path runs through the same entry-path plumbing as the synchronous full path, differing only in its reduced step set: it injects serverStartedKey (false) and tmuxClientKey into cmd.Context() without running the orchestrator.

text: Why do the N-1 windows a multi-select burst spawns dead-end on "Process exited. Press any key to close the terminal." when their session exits or detaches, while the trigger window lands back at a shell prompt?
What shape of work is this report, and which phase does it route to first?
The work is a bugfix (present-broken behaviour with a concrete symptom and error text, a root cause still to confirm, nothing new to build) and routes to investigation first.
why: The report is a concrete broken behaviour, not a new capability.

text: When the session running in a spawned (N-1 external) Ghostty window exits or detaches, the window shows tmux's `[detached (from session <name>)]` then `Process exited. Press any key to close the terminal.`, and a keypress closes the window. Reproduced by multi-selecting 2+ sessions in the picker, dispatching the burst, and exiting the session in a spawned window; reported as always reproducing, on macOS with Ghostty, after the multi-window spawn feature started working.
how: From the bug report captured 2026-07-17 and the investigation's symptoms.

text: The seed's and discovery's references to `portal attach <session> --spawn-ack` and `cmd/attach.go` are stale: a spawned burst window now runs `portal open --session <name> --ack <batch>:<token>`; the rest of the seed's hypothesised mechanism holds.
how: Code trace during investigation.

text: Per the restore-host-terminal-windows spec, the spawn layer composes the command and hands `{command}` to the adapter verbatim; the adapter only opens a window running it (`OpenWindow(command)`).
how: From the restore-host-terminal-windows spec, read during investigation.

text: Root-cause factor 1: `internal/spawn` composes the spawned window's command as a single one-shot, env-self-sufficient argv, `/usr/bin/env -u TMUX -u TMUX_PANE PATH=<picker PATH> <exePath> open --session <name> --ack <batch>:<token>`, deliberately a real argv run verbatim so it drops cleanly into `terminals.json` recipes; Ghostty runs that command string through bash, so the window's root process is a single non-interactive command with no surrounding interactive shell.
how: Code trace of `composeOpenArgv`, `renderCommandString` and the Ghostty adapter.

text: Root-cause factor 2: a spawned window is always outside tmux (composition strips `TMUX`/`TMUX_PANE`), so `portal open --session` writes its ack marker and then `AttachConnector.Connect` `syscall.Exec`s into `tmux attach-session`, replacing the process image; the tmux client becomes the window's one and only process, with no Portal or shell frame left behind.
how: Code trace of `cmd/open.go`.

text: Root-cause factor 3: the Ghostty adapter opens the window with `wait after command:true`, so when the exec'd tmux client returns Ghostty holds the dead window awaiting a keypress ("Process exited. Press any key to close the terminal.") instead of closing or dropping to a shell. The flag came in with the ghostty-spawn-zero-windows fix (2026-07-16) as "the normal-detach window lifecycle for a spawned session", which is why the dead-end appeared only once the multi-window spawn feature started working. Together with the one-shot exec chain (`bash -c` -> `env` -> `portal open` -> `tmux attach-session`), no factor alone is the whole bug.
how: Code trace of `internal/spawn/ghostty.go` and the ghostty-spawn-zero-windows spec.

text: The trigger window's clean landing is structural: the trigger self-connects in-process from the already-running Portal, a child of the user's interactive login shell, so exiting the tmux attach returns to that shell's prompt; it never goes through the Ghostty adapter or `composeOpenArgv`. Confirmed for both burst entry points, the `portal open` multi-target burst and the picker multi-select burst.
how: Code trace of `cmd/open_burst_run.go`, `internal/tui/model.go` and `cmd/open.go`.

text: Ghostty runs a window's `command` as `/usr/bin/login -flp <user> /bin/bash --noprofile --norc -c "exec -l <command>"`: `exec -l` replaces the outer bash with the command's first token.
how: Revealed live in the sandbox by a failed implicit-append attempt.

text: Affected: every burst-spawned (N-1 external) window on the native Ghostty adapter, through both burst entry points, which share the same `internal/spawn` composition and adapter. Not affected: the trigger window, single-session `portal open`/attach run from a shell, and detection, pre-flight, the ack channel and selection mutation; the bug is purely post-exit window lifecycle.
how: Code trace during investigation.

text: The osascript / Ghostty boundary has no automated coverage: the only real-Ghostty test is `//go:build manual`, so neither the unit nor the integration lane sees what a spawned window does after its command exits.
how: Read from the ghostty-spawn-zero-windows work and the test tree.

text: The dead-end is a post-exit lifecycle behaviour, not a spawn failure: the burst succeeds (windows open, acks land, `spawn: opened N/N`) and the defect shows only later, when the user exits the session, outside anything the spawn feature's tests or logs observe.
how: Reasoned from the code trace and the spawn feature's tests and logs.

text: `wait after command:true` was composed days before the report, and its interaction with the one-shot exec chain was never exercised end to end on a real Mac before shipping.
how: Read from the ghostty-spawn-zero-windows dates and its manual-only test.

text: How should a spawned window land when its session exits, and by what mechanism (chain a shell after the attach, have a shell run portal, or lean on the host terminal's post-command behaviour)?

A spawned window whose session exits behaves "as if the user opened Ghostty themselves": it lands at a normal interactive shell prompt, the session having been launched into it, as the trigger window does. A clean close is an acceptable fallback, but a usable prompt is the goal.
why: The dead-end feels broken and is inconsistent with the trigger window's landing.

text: Portal's job ends at "open a window running this command": how the window behaves when the command ends belongs to the command and the terminal, so Portal shapes end-of-window behaviour only for the command it authors, the native Ghostty adapter's, and leaves custom-terminal users in full control of their recipes.
why: Portal centrally controlling the lifecycle would override custom-terminal users' own choices, such as a deliberate close-on-exit.
rules_out: Option A: Portal fork/waits tmux and then execs `$SHELL` behind a spawned-only flag, centrally owning the window lifecycle for every terminal (also carried tty/signal-proxy risk from Portal parenting a full-screen tty app)

text: The spawned window is not closed when its session exits: it stays visible, and a live shell makes it visible and usable.
why: With several scattered Ghostty windows an abrupt close loses track of which one vanished, which the user judged worse than the dead-end.
rules_out: Option C: `wait after command:false`, closing the window cleanly on exit

text: The implicit-append form `<argv>; exec "$SHELL" -il` fails under Ghostty: `exec -l` replaces bash with the first token, so the `; exec` fallback is unreachable, and a first token not found is fatal (`exec: <cmd>: not found`, window "failed to launch").
how: Tried live in a sandbox (throwaway `-L` tmux socket).

text: The explicit wrapper `bash -lc '<composed open argv>; exec "$SHELL" -il'` works under Ghostty: `exec -l bash -lc '…'` replaces the outer bash with the inner one, which runs the session command as a child and then execs `$SHELL`; after the session was killed the window landed at the user's normal prompt, `/bin/zsh` as an interactive login shell with Oh My Zsh sourced and `$SHELL` propagated, not bash.
how: Run end to end in a sandbox (throwaway `-L` tmux socket, no live tmux server touched).

text: The native Ghostty adapter composes its window command as the explicit wrapper `bash -lc '<composed open argv>; exec "$SHELL" -il'`, so after the session's `portal open` exec chain finishes the window lands in the user's interactive login shell. Both burst entry points, picker multi-select and `portal open` multi-target, get it through the shared adapter.
why: The wrapper runs the session command as a child and then execs the shell, keeping the window visible and usable; the explicit form is the one that survives Ghostty's `exec -l` command model.
rules_out: The implicit-append form `<argv>; exec "$SHELL" -il`, unreachable under Ghostty's `exec -l`
evidence: Sandbox-validated live: the window landed at the user's zsh prompt after the session was killed

text: `wait after command` is dropped from the Ghostty osascript.
why: Once the exec'd shell keeps the window alive the flag is not needed, and it is what produced the "Press any key to close" dead-end.

text: The wrap lives only in the native Ghostty adapter (`internal/spawn/ghostty.go`); the shared `composeOpenArgv` and `renderCommandString` are not changed.
why: A wrap in shared composition would put shell metacharacters (`;`, `exec`) into the `{command}` handed to `terminals.json` adapters, which work only if the terminal runs `{command}` through a shell, a guarantee `terminals.json` does not make; a direct-exec custom terminal would silently break.
rules_out: Option B in shared composition: the same shell wrap placed in `composeOpenArgv`

text: Custom `terminals.json` terminals get no change: one whose own post-command behaviour waits after its command can still dead-end as the Ghostty adapter did before the fix, and this is a known, accepted residual.
why: How a custom terminal's window ends is the user's own recipe's business, and covering it would have meant the shared-composition wrap that breaks the `{command}` contract.

text: The wrap is argv-agnostic: it wraps whatever argv the adapter is handed, so mint surfaces (`open --path <dir> --ack <batch>:<token>`, optionally with a `-- <command…>` passthrough) get the same fallback shell as attach surfaces, and a passthrough element survives the same quote nesting as any other.
why: The change lives at the adapter, below the choice of surface.

text: The sandbox's implicit attempt also showed `tmux: not found`, a test artifact: the hand test left out the `PATH=<picker PATH>` the real composed argv always carries, and Ghostty's `--noprofile --norc` bash with its login default PATH can't find tmux without it.
how: Seen live in the sandbox attempt.

text: The composed open argv inside the wrapper is unchanged from today for both surface kinds, keeping its `/usr/bin/env … PATH=<picker PATH> -u TMUX -u TMUX_PANE` prefix, so `tmux` resolves; the wrap must not strip PATH.
why: Ghostty's inner bash runs `--noprofile --norc` with a login default PATH, so a PATH-less command can't find tmux.

text: The `bash -lc '…'` form is schematic, not a byte template: the wrapper is built as the real argv `["bash", "-lc", <payload>]`, the payload being the rendered composed argv followed by `; exec "$SHELL" -il`, and that 3-element argv is rendered through the existing shell-quote helper, which nests the inner single quotes with the POSIX `'\''` idiom; the osascript `command:"…"` double-quote/backslash layer then wraps the result as today.
why: The composed argv is already single-quoted per element, so pasting it inside an outer single-quoted string would terminate the quote and emit a corrupted command that fails at Ghostty launch.
rules_out: Hand-rolled string concatenation of the illustrative form

text: The `--ack` marker ordering is unchanged: `portal open` still writes its `@portal-spawn-<batch>-<token>` marker before the attach handoff, and the burst still confirms each window and logs `spawn: opened N/N`.
why: The wrapper only adds a shell after the command; it does not alter what the command does before its handoff.

text: The `syscall.Exec` attach path is untouched: no change to `AttachConnector`, connector selection or the exec into tmux; the fix lives entirely in the Ghostty adapter's command composition.
why: Keeping the exec path avoids any tty/signal-proxy risk and keeps the trigger and bare-shell landing as they are.

text: `$SHELL` in a Ghostty window is populated by `/usr/bin/login`, which Ghostty launches the window through.
how: From the observed Ghostty launch command and the sandbox's `$SHELL` propagation.

text: No fallback for `$SHELL` is specified; should `exec "$SHELL"` ever fail, the inner bash exits and the window closes rather than landing at a shell, which is acceptable since a clean close is an accepted fallback and no "Press any key" dead-end returns.
why: `$SHELL` is reliably set by `/usr/bin/login`, so the failure is only theoretical.

text: The trigger path gets no change: the trigger window self-connects in-process and already lands cleanly.
why: Any fix must add a fallback to the spawned path without touching the correct trigger path.

text: Single-session `portal open`/attach, detection, pre-flight, the ack channel and selection mutation get no change.
why: They are correct; the bug is purely post-exit window lifecycle.

text: The fix ships in a regular release, not a hotfix: severity is low, a cosmetic/UX rough edge with no data loss.
why: UX polish on a shipped feature; fix complexity and regression risk are both low, the change being adapter-local.

text: Closing a spawned window from the fallback prompt shows Ghostty's close confirm; what should be done about it?

After landing at the fallback zsh prompt, closing the Ghostty window shows Ghostty's standard confirm, "Close Window? All terminal sessions in this window will be terminated.", which is normally suppressed at an idle prompt.
how: Seen live in the sandbox.

text: The close confirm is not caused by `wait after command`: it still fires with the flag omitted. Nor is it a nested subprocess: the exec chain replaces bash -> bash -> zsh in place, same pid, no children at the prompt.
how: Re-ran the explicit wrapper in the sandbox with `wait after command` omitted.

text: The close confirm's cause is inferred, not verified (Ghostty's source is not in the repo): missing shell integration. Ghostty suppresses `confirm-close-surface` at an idle prompt only when shell integration it injected on launching the shell tells it the shell is idle, and a surface launched through a custom `command` gets none. The suggested check, a `Cmd-N` window at idle not prompting where a command-launched one does, is not recorded as run.
how: Inference from Ghostty's documented behaviour; unverified against Ghostty's source.

text: The close confirm is intrinsic to landing in a shell Ghostty did not launch itself, whatever the approach (the rejected Option A included), and can't be switched per window: the sdef exposes only `command` and `wait after command`.
how: Read from Ghostty's AppleScript sdef and reasoned from the inferred cause.

text: The close confirm when closing from the idle fallback prompt is accepted as is, a known residual and not a defect; no shell-integration workaround ships.
why: The fix turns a dead-end into a usable shell, the goal; one extra click is minor and honest, since a live shell really is running.
rules_out: Re-injecting Ghostty shell integration into the fallback (restoring `ZDOTDIR`/`GHOSTTY_RESOURCES_DIR`): Ghostty-version-specific, fragile, risks double-sourcing or config breakage on updates
Setting `confirm-close-surface = false`: the user's global Ghostty config, dropping the prompt for windows with real running processes too; not Portal's call

text: How is the fix tested, given the Ghostty osascript boundary has no automatable lane?
No new automated real-Ghostty test lane: the osascript boundary stays `//go:build manual`.
why: The boundary has no automatable lane.

text: Unit tests at the command-composition seam, beside the existing `ghosttyEmbed` / template tests, assert the Ghostty adapter emits the wrapper against the correctly escaped expected string (the `'\''` nesting, not the schematic form).
why: The composition seam is the one automatable place that sees the wrapper, and the implicit-versus-explicit shape is what a regression could bring back.

text: Unit tests assert the Ghostty adapter no longer emits `wait after command`.
why: Dropping the flag is half of the fix.

text: Unit tests assert the composed argv inside the wrapper still carries its `PATH=<…>` / `-u TMUX -u TMUX_PANE` prefix.
why: The wrap must not strip PATH, or tmux won't resolve.

text: The quote-nesting test uses a quote-sensitive fixture, an argv element holding shell-special characters (a single quote, `;`, `$`, `"`), ideally the mint `-- <command…>` passthrough such as `-- sh -c 'echo hi'`, and asserts the embedded argv round-trips uncorrupted through the added `bash -lc` layer.
why: An attach-only argv carries no special characters and would never exercise the `'\''` double-escaping path.

text: No further manual-validation deliverable is required: the mechanism was validated live, sandboxed, during the investigation, so only the code change and its unit coverage remain to build and verify.
why: The functionality is already tested end to end.
rules_out: Shipping the sandboxed Ghostty test commands as the fix's manual validation

text: On the detach path tmux's own `[detached (from session <name>)]` line still prints above the fallback prompt; that is expected tmux client-detach output, outside the fix's scope, not a sign the fix failed.
how: tmux client-detach output, read from the code trace and the sandbox.

text: Any re-validation against tmux runs on a throwaway `-L <socket>` tmux server, never the live default server hosting the user's real sessions, so earlier Ghostty spawn misfires are not repeated.

text: The bug came from an inbox seed Claude surfaced at the end of the portal-observability-layer implementation; the person had no first-hand awareness of it, so its shape was settled from the seed plus a quick code check, as a single self-contained bugfix: one scope (the status reader's format assumption), no new behaviour to design, its root cause located.
how: Read in discovery session 001's exploration and the log's references.

text: How should the work proceed from discovery: straight to a fix, or investigation first?
Investigate first; if the root cause is not easily identifiable, stop the work; if it is, proceed to the fix.
why: The person's directive, carried from discovery into investigation.

text: `portal state status` always reports `Recent warnings: 0 (last: none)` whatever WARN/ERROR lines `portal.log` holds, where it is expected to report the warnings the daemon and other Portal processes logged. The failure is silent: no error, no crash, the section permanently empty in production, masking real daemon, bootstrap and restore warnings.
how: Read in the investigation's symptoms and the spec's bug statement.

text: It reproduces always, being a deterministic format mismatch: run Portal so the daemon logs at least one WARN line to `portal.log`, run `portal state status`, and the Recent warnings section reports zero. It affects every environment running the post-observability-layer build, independent of platform.
how: Read in the investigation's reproduction steps and environment.

text: Severity is medium: a diagnostic/observability regression, the command lying by omission, not data loss or a crash; it affects anyone relying on `portal state status` to surface recent warnings.
how: Read in the investigation's impact and the spec's severity section.

text: Root cause: `internal/state/status.go` parses `portal.log` assuming the legacy pipe-delimited layout (`timestamp | level | component | message`, `logFieldSeparator = " | "`, 4 fields), while `internal/log`'s handler now writes slog text (`<RFC3339Nano> <LEVEL> <component>: <msg> <attrs k=v…> pid=… version=… process_role=…`) with no pipes. `logEntryQualifies`'s `strings.SplitN(line, " | ", 4)` yields a one-element slice for every line, so it returns false unconditionally: `RecentWarnings` is always 0 and `LastWarning` always empty. The format contract was broken on the writer side with no matching reader update.
how: Read by tracing `portal state status` through `cmd/state_status.go`, `CollectStatus`, `scanRecentWarnings` and `logEntryQualifies`, verified against the real writer in `internal/log/handler.go`.

text: The pipe parser came in with `507f7308` (built-in-session-resurrection T6-4), when `internal/state`'s legacy logger wrote pipe-delimited lines and reader and writer agreed; `08980e61` (portal-observability-layer T1-10, deleting the legacy `internal/state` logger) changed the writer to slog text and is the introducing change. The status reader appeared in no observability task's file list, so the sweep that changed the format never touched it.
how: Read in the git history.

text: Only the two warning-derived fields are affected: the Recent warnings line always reads `0 (last: none)`, and `isUnhealthy`'s `RecentWarnings > 0` branch in `cmd/state_status.go` can never fire, so a daemon actively logging WARN/ERROR still reports healthy and exits 0. This answers how deep the mismatch goes, which discovery deferred to investigation.
how: Read in the code trace of `warningsLine` and `isUnhealthy`.

text: Every other status field (daemon running/PID/version, last save, session and pane counts, state size) reads `daemon.pid`, `daemon.version`, `sessions.json` or the state-dir tree, not `portal.log`: `collectDaemonState`, `collectIndexState` and `computeStateSize` do not read the log. No other production code reads `portal.log`: `scanRecentWarnings` is the only non-test caller of `PortalLog(`.
how: Read in `CollectStatus`'s collectors and by grepping for `PortalLog(`.

text: The status tests seed the legacy pipe format (`internal/state/status_test.go`'s `writeLogLine`, and two cases in `cmd/state_status_test.go`), so they validate the parser against input only it understands and stayed green through the writer change; no test, unit or integration, feeds a genuine `internal/log` line into `CollectStatus`/`scanRecentWarnings`. This answers whether the tests give a false green, which discovery deferred to investigation.
how: Read in the two status test files.

text: No shared format constant couples producer and consumer: the line format lives implicitly in `internal/log/handler.go`'s `Handle`, and the reader re-derives it independently with its own constants.
how: Read in the writer and the reader.

text: The scanner swallows malformed lines by design, so a 100% mismatch reads the same as no warnings logged: no error, no panic, nothing to notice.
how: Read in `scanRecentWarnings`.

text: Go's `time.Parse(time.RFC3339, …)` accepts both fractional-second and whole-second input, so the reader's `time.RFC3339` parse of the writer's RFC3339Nano timestamps is not a second defect; the only functional break is the field separator and field extraction.
how: Read in the investigation, which says it was verified empirically; no command is given.

text: How is the status reader's format mismatch fixed?
Migrate the status reader (`internal/state/status.go`) to parse the slog text format the writer emits.
why: The reader is the side that drifted; the writer is correct.

text: The writer/handler in `internal/log` is not changed: only the reader is fixed.
why: The writer is correct and out of scope; only the reader drifted.
rules_out: Changing the writer to match the reader.

text: How are the reader and writer kept in sync so the drift can't recur?

Export a parse helper from `internal/log`, the writer's package, defined alongside the writer as the single inverse of its line format, and consume it from `internal/state/status.go`: one format definition, one place to change.
why: It removes the contributing factor of writer and reader each defining the format independently; the import direction state → log already exists and log never imports state, so the coupling is legal, cycle-free and free.
alternatives: Fork 1A: an independent parser in `status.go`; smallest diff, but it re-derives the format a second time, leaving the same drift able to recur.

text: What is the shared parse helper's contract and parsing rules?

The helper (e.g. `internal/log/parse.go`) is `ParseLogLine(line string) (parsed LogLine, ok bool)`, returning a `LogLine` of `Time` (from the RFC3339Nano timestamp token), `Level` (DEBUG, INFO, WARN or ERROR), `Component` (the subsystem prefix, trailing `:` removed, empty if absent) and `Message` (the human message only, contextual attrs and the pid/version/process_role baselines excluded); `ok` is false for any line not matching the writer's layout.
why: Defined alongside the writer so any future writer-format change forces this parser to change too.

text: `Time` is the first whitespace-delimited token, parsed with `time.RFC3339Nano`; an unparseable timestamp gives `ok == false`.
why: The writer emits RFC3339Nano, so the helper uses the matching layout for producer-consumer symmetry; whole- and fractional-second inputs both parse, `time.RFC3339` being equivalent.

text: `Level` is the second whitespace-delimited token, verbatim.
why: The writer's layout puts the level second.

text: `Component` is the text between the level token and the first `:` in the line, surrounding whitespace trimmed; an empty or all-whitespace run gives `Component == ""` with `ok == true`.
why: The writer emits one space after the level and, for an empty component, a space before the colon; component names carry no spaces or colons, so the first `:` reliably ends the component.

text: `Message` is the text after `<component>: ` up to, excluding, the first whitespace-delimited token of the form `key=value` (matching `^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_.]*=`).
why: This one boundary rule drops both the contextual attrs and the trailing baselines in one pass.

text: Only the first `:` in the line delimits the component; later colons belong to the message, so `… WARN daemon: flush failed: disk full pid=…` parses as component `daemon`, message `flush failed: disk full`.
why: A message may itself contain `:`.

text: A plain whitespace split finds the message boundary even when an attr value is quoted and holds spaces (`version="3.6 beta"`).
why: The boundary token always begins a fresh whitespace-delimited token and a genuine attr key always precedes any value content, so the first match lands at the first real attr and a `key=value`-shaped substring inside a quoted value can never shift it earlier.

text: An empty message, the component's colon-space followed at once by the first attr token, parses with `ok == true` and `Message == ""`.
why: The line still matches the writer's layout.

text: The helper documents the assumption that log messages hold no `key=value`-shaped token; if ever violated, the only effect is the displayed `LastWarning` summary truncating early, never the `RecentWarnings` count or the health signal.
why: The codebase's messages are short human phrases from closed per-component catalogs, so the assumption holds.

text: `ParseLogLine` returns `ok == false` when the line holds no `:`, has fewer than two whitespace-delimited tokens, or its first token does not parse as an RFC3339Nano timestamp; an empty line falls under these.
why: These are exactly the shapes the malformed-line test treats as not matching the new layout.

text: How does the status reader change to use the helper?
Remove the `logFieldSeparator = " | "` and `expectedLogFieldCount = 4` constants from `status.go`.
why: They define the legacy pipe format the reader no longer parses.

text: `scanRecentWarnings` parses each line once through `log.ParseLogLine`; a line qualifies when `ok` is true, `Level` is WARN or ERROR, and its `Time` is not before the cutoff. Unparseable and non-qualifying lines are skipped silently, keeping the swallow-and-skip contract.
why: A 100% mismatch becomes a 0% mismatch while malformed individual lines still skip cleanly.

text: How is `LastWarning` rendered, now that a raw line carries trailing baselines and every attr?
`LastWarning` holds the composed summary `<LEVEL> <component>: <msg>` (e.g. `WARN daemon: tick complete`), timestamp, attrs and baselines omitted, replacing the stored raw line.
why: Readability on the single `(last: …)` status line; a UX call, not correctness.
alternatives: Fork 2A: keep the full raw line; literally matches the prior contract but is noisy with baselines and attrs.

text: With an empty component, `LastWarning` renders `<LEVEL>: <msg>` (e.g. `WARN: tick complete`), with no stray space before the colon.
why: The displayed status line is deterministic for every case.

text: An empty message renders as `<LEVEL> <component>:` or `<LEVEL>:`, with no trailing space.
why: The displayed status line is deterministic for every case.

text: On each qualifying line the reader increments `RecentWarnings` and overwrites `LastWarning`, top to bottom: last-wins is positional, the most recent being the last qualifying line in the file.
why: The writer only ever appends in chronological order, so last in the file equals chronologically most recent.

text: `StatusReport.LastWarning`'s doc comment changes from the full text of the most recent qualifying WARN/ERROR line to the most recent qualifying entry rendered as `<LEVEL> <component>: <msg>`, timestamp prefix and trailing attrs/baselines omitted.
why: The field now holds the trimmed summary.

text: After the change no doc comment or constant in `status.go` references the pipe format: `scanRecentWarnings`'s doc comment drops "wrong field count", and `logEntryQualifies`, folded into the parse-once flow or rewritten over the parsed `LogLine` at the implementer's choice, no longer references `logFieldSeparator` or `expectedLogFieldCount`.
why: The pipe format is gone; the function boundary is left to the implementer.

text: `cmd/state_status.go` is not changed: `warningsLine` renders `LastWarning` directly, so the line reads e.g. `Recent warnings: 1 (last: WARN daemon: tick complete)`, and `isUnhealthy`'s `RecentWarnings > 0` branch fires, exiting non-zero, once real warnings are counted.
why: `LastWarning` arrives pre-trimmed, and the health branch only lacked counted warnings.

text: The recent-warnings window stays the last hour (`recentWarningWindow`): a qualifying-level line older than it is not counted.
why: Behaviour beyond the format is out of scope.

text: The level filter stays WARN/ERROR: INFO and DEBUG lines are not counted.
why: Behaviour beyond the format is out of scope.

text: A missing `portal.log` still gives `RecentWarnings = 0` and an empty `LastWarning`, with no error.
why: Behaviour beyond the format is out of scope.

text: `CollectStatus` keeps its best-effort behaviour, propagating no error; a malformed line is skipped and does not abort the scan of the lines after it.
why: Behaviour beyond the format is out of scope.

text: How is the fix tested so the false green can't recur?

The hand-authored pipe-format fixtures go: `internal/state/status_test.go`'s `writeLogLine` helper is removed, as are the hand-authored pipe-format strings in the two `cmd/state_status_test.go` cases; no test constructs a log line from a format string defined independently of the production writer.
why: The bug survived because the tests validated the parser against input only the parser understood.

text: At least one producer-coupled end-to-end regression test, at the `CollectStatus` (state) layer, drives the real `internal/log` writer to emit a WARN line into the status directory's `portal.log`, runs `CollectStatus`, and asserts `RecentWarnings`, the trimmed `LastWarning` and the `isUnhealthy`/non-zero-exit consequence.
why: It is the guard that would have caught the original mismatch and turns red on any future writer-format drift, its fixtures derived from the single production format source.

text: The producer-coupled test writes its fixtures in append (chronological) order, so last in the file and most recent timestamp coincide.
why: Last-wins is positional.

text: The two `cmd/state_status_test.go` cases are migrated, not deleted: they keep asserting the rendered `Recent warnings: N (last: …)` suffix and the non-zero exit when warnings are present, each sourcing its log line from the real `internal/log` writer, the asserted suffix updated to the trimmed `<LEVEL> <component>: <msg>` form.
why: Their coverage stays while no cmd-layer test constructs a line from an independently defined format.

text: `internal/log` provides a seam that renders one record to its canonical `portal.log` text line through the same rendering path `textHandler.Handle` uses in production (e.g. the line-building factored out of `Handle` into an exported render function, or a `*testing.T`-first test-only helper like `SetTestHandler` that drives the real handler), never a re-implementation of the format; the test writes the rendered lines into a plain file at `PortalLog(dir)` and runs `CollectStatus`. Driving `log.Init` against an isolated dir, restoring the handler on cleanup, is an acceptable alternative, but the render-path seam is preferred.
why: `textHandler` is unexported and `log.Init` mutates the process-wide handler and writes through the rotating sink and symlink; the seam keeps fixtures byte-identical to production output without leaking process-global state, the render path being side-effect-free.
alternatives: Driving `log.Init` against an isolated dir, restoring the handler on cleanup.

text: The existing cases are kept, re-expressed in the slog text format: window cutoff (inside and outside the last hour), level filter (INFO/DEBUG excluded, WARN and ERROR both included), last-wins, missing `portal.log` → zero, and the malformed-line skip case (`status_test.go:368`) as a line not matching the new layout.
why: The coverage stays, translated rather than deleted.

text: `ParseLogLine` gets direct unit tests: a well-formed line gives the right `Time`, `Level`, `Component` and `Message`; the boundary rule strips contextual attrs and the pid/version/process_role baselines; a message with no attrs is kept whole; an empty-component line parses with `Component == ""` and `ok == true`; an unparseable timestamp gives `ok == false`.
why: The helper is the single format definition, so its rules are pinned directly.

text: Done means `portal state status` surfaces the actual recent-warning count with a readable last-warning summary, exits non-zero when warnings are present, and a producer-coupled test fails if the writer's line format changes without a matching parser update.
why: The spec's definition of done.

text: Fix complexity and regression risk are both low: a localised parser change plus a small exported helper, no writer change, a single confined reader with no other consumer of `portal.log`; the main watch-item is parsing robustness for malformed or edge lines, which the swallow-and-skip contract covers.
how: Read in the investigation's risk assessment.

A regular release, not a hotfix.
why: A diagnostic-surface bugfix, not a hotfix-class production outage.

command: tmux list-sessions -F '#{session_name}|#{@portal-dir}' | while IFS='|' read n d; do case "$n" in _portal-*) continue;; esac; [ -n "$d" ] && continue; p=$(tmux display-message -p -t "=$n:" '#{pane_current_path}'); r=$(git -C "$p" rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null || echo "$p"); echo "$n -> $r"; done

text: Keep the live guess for sessions with no record, with the worktree rule applied: a guess resolves the pane's folder to the repository it belongs to (a worktree to the repository it was made from), exactly as creation does. Accepted trade-off: a wrong guess is silent.
why: With filters, being missing is as much a failure as being misplaced: no guess trades 9 misplaced-or-Unknown sessions for 30 missing from every filter until a manual pass; the live guess self-corrects when the pane returns, while a frozen one makes a transient wrong answer permanent (Portal deliberately avoids freezing a drifted cwd today). The worktree rule moves the worktree sessions to their parent project while their worktree exists.
rules_out: Guess once, then keep it: the first guess becomes the session's record.
No guess: sessions without a record sit in Unknown until the user links them.
alternatives: 1. Keep guessing, live (today's behaviour, with the worktree rule applied to the guess).

text: Does Portal save a folder as a project when it finds a session whose project is not a saved project (~/Code/flowx, ~/Code/goosemates, folio/app today)?

Portal never saves a folder as a project on its own when a session's project (its recorded project, or for a session with no record its live guess) is not a saved project. Such a session stays in Unknown until the user saves that folder as a project or links the session to an existing one from the picker.
why: Determined by the live-guess decision's own rationale: for a recorded project a missing project is the user's own deletion, and recreating it would undo them; for a guessed folder, saving it converts a guess chosen because it corrects itself into a durable record that does not. rules_out: Saving the folder as a project automatically.

text: What happens to a project and its tags when its folder is renamed or moved? Housekeeping removes the record silently, and once tags drive filtering a folder rename silently drops sessions out of filters.

Housekeeping removes a saved project whose folder no longer exists, on the daemon's throttled idle tick, when the picker runs it, and under portal doctor --fix, taking the project's tags with it. Its log line is a summary count; the per-project detail is written at DEBUG, below the production level, so neither the project nor its tags can be recovered from the log. From a missing folder alone it cannot tell a rename from a deletion.

At discovery, 34 of the 62 saved projects sat inside another project's folder (folio holds folio/api and folio/sdk; docman holds docman/docman and docman/sdk-php; finder holds finder/finder-api; flowx holds flowx/flowx-api; fabric holds most of the fabric projects), and a project was saved at ~/code, the Code folder itself.
how: Measured read-only against the live projects.json on 2026-10-09; no command given.

text: Excluding the home and Code folder projects, 12 saved projects contain others; only two are git repositories (fabric/folio with api and sdk; fabric/finder with finder-api), the other ten plain folders (acom, acom/mach2, curated, detaillab, dex, evvi, fabric, fabric/docman, fabric/flowv1, fabric/flowx). Under every parent, all nested projects carry the parent's tag but three: acom/mach2 (untagged under acom), fabric/flowx/flowx-api and fabric/packages/laravel-workflow (both personal under fabric).
how: Listed each containing project, whether it is a git repository, and its nested projects' tags.
command: python3 -I -c "import json,os,subprocess as s; ps={p['path']:p for p in json.load(open(os.path.expanduser('~/.config/portal/projects.json')))['projects']}; ex={os.path.expanduser('~'),os.path.expanduser('~/code')}; [print('GIT' if s.run(['git','-C',q,'rev-parse','--show-toplevel'],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout.strip()==q else 'PLAIN', q, ps[q].get('tags'), [(k[len(q)+1:],ps[k].get('tags')) for k in sorted(ps) if k.startswith(q+'/')]) for q in sorted(ps) if q not in ex and any(k.startswith(q+'/') for k in ps)]"

text: Projects stand alone; families are tags. No project takes in the projects nested inside it: a session belongs to the project it was started in, appears under that project's heading in By Project, and matches a project filter for that project only. A group of related projects is expressed by tagging its members. The home folder and Code folder projects are ordinary projects for the sessions started there.
why: The families the user cares about are already expressed as tags at the broad level, and only two of the twelve containing projects are repositories, so a repository-based rollup would serve folio and finder while leaving the plain-folder families flat for reasons the picker cannot show; any containment rule breaks on the home and Code folder projects. Discovery's lean toward rollup was overtaken by the measurement.
rules_out: Repositories take in what's inside them: a project that is a git repository includes the projects inside it.
A per-project switch, 'takes in nested projects', on the project's edit screen.
alternatives: 1. Projects stand alone; tags group them.
2. Repositories take in what's inside them.
3. A per-project switch.

text: What may grouping and tag and project filtering cost? Switching the picker to By Project or By Tag is slow today (about 0.5 s reported) because each unrecorded session's folder is looked up one session at a time, and tag and project filters take the same path.

text: Do tags live on projects only, or can a session carry tags of its own as well?
Tags stay on projects (the directory) only; there are no per-session tags. Every session is tagged indirectly through its project.
why: Sessions are ephemeral — one can last a minute or a month — so tagging them is not useful; a Portal session links to the portal project, which carries the personal tag. Project-only tags also keep the separate reboot bugfix scoped to the project link, with no session-level tags to restore across a reboot.
rules_out: Per-session tags layered on project tags (a session's tags being its project's plus its own), proposed to tag what a session is for and to tag sessions whose folder is not a project — rejected on the ephemerality argument.

Its aim was display casing; case-sensitive matching, dedup and grouping followed from it as a side effect rather than being chosen for itself.

text: On the live install on 2026-10-26 no tag carried a capital letter.
how: Read-only query of the live projects.json.

text: How does tag identity treat case, once suggestions and merging put near-duplicates side by side and a rename can land on a tag that already exists?

Tag identity ignores case everywhere a tag is compared — adding a tag to a project, suggestions, grouping, tag management and tag filters (the tag filter and x --tag inherit it). The user's casing is still shown as written.
why: The deliberate choice behind today's behaviour was display casing, not case-sensitive identity. Once tags are picked from a list, a stray capital is the main way a duplicate gets made, and case-sensitive identity would silently split a tag in two (two headings, a filter that misses half the projects). No real case where API and api should mean different things exists.
rules_out: Case-sensitive identity (today): Work typed where work exists becomes a second tag.
Lower-case everything (the original rule): not reopened; the June fix rejected it for erasing the user's casing.

text: Typing a tag that matches an existing one in another case adds the existing tag, in its existing casing.
why: Follows from case-insensitive identity: two tags differing only in case cannot arise.

text: Changing a tag's casing everywhere (work to Work) is an ordinary rename in tag management, never a merge.
why: Under case-insensitive identity the two casings are one tag; a tag's casing is set by its first use, and changing it is a deliberate rename.

text: A tag's casing is settled once and written, not worked out on every read: whenever Portal writes the projects file (a merge, a rename, a tag added or removed anywhere), any tag carried in more than one casing is rewritten to its winning casing on every project that carries it — the casing carried by more projects, a tie going to the casing that sorts first.
why: A tie-break on a project's last-used time moves every time a session is created in it, and a majority can flip when a tag is removed elsewhere, so the displayed casing could change with no rename. Writing one spelling to disk keeps a tag's heading, chips and suggestions from changing casing on their own, and project-link's merges never leave two casings behind. Accepted cost: Portal rewrites casing a hand edit put on projects the user did not touch — two casings of one tag is never a state the user chose.
rules_out: Showing the casing carried by more projects with a tie kept by the most recently used project, worked out on every read.

text: Between a hand edit of the projects file that introduces a second casing of a tag and Portal's next write, the display shows the tag by the same rule: the casing carried by more projects, a tie going to the casing that sorts first.
why: Keeps what is shown consistent with what the next write will settle on disk.

text: While a tag is being typed in the edit screen's TAGS box, the up and down arrows do nothing today (they move between fields only when no text box is open), so they are free to move through a suggestion list.
how: Counted arrow-key handling in the edit-mode key handler.

text: How do tag suggestions behave while a tag is being typed: what they list, what Enter takes, and how the list fits the screen?

While a tag is being typed — added or edited — a dropdown below the box lists the tags in use on other projects that this project does not carry, each with its project count, most-used first, narrowed as the user types by a case-insensitive match anywhere in the tag.
why: Reusing a tag otherwise depends on remembering its exact spelling, and a misremembered spelling silently makes a new tag; serving chip edits too makes replacing one tag with another a pick, not a retype.

text: Once there is typed text, the best match is highlighted and Enter adds it; up and down move the highlight.
why: Reuse is the common case by a wide margin — five tags on the install after months of use — so the default keystroke belongs to it, and a near-duplicate takes a deliberate move.
rules_out: Enter adds what was typed, nothing highlighted until down: fab + Enter would create fab beside fabric, reopening for prefixes the duplicate trap Tag Case closed for capitals.

text: On a blank box the list shows with nothing highlighted: Enter adds nothing and closes the box, as today, and down steps into the list. Enter on a box the user has not typed into never writes a tag they did not pick.
why: Highlighting the best match on a blank box would put the most-used tag (personal) under a bare Enter, today a no-op that adds nothing (review-001 F1).
rules_out: Keeping the instant pick on a blank box: saves one down when browsing but would need a key other than Enter for closing without adding.

text: Editing an existing chip opens the box with the chip's text, as today, and the chip's own tag heads the list, highlighted and marked as the current value, so Enter with nothing changed leaves the chip as it was; clearing the text and pressing Enter deletes the chip, as today.
why: With the chip's own tag left out, editing api with api-docs on another project would highlight api-docs and Enter with nothing changed would swap the chip (review-001 F1).

text: Any typed text that matches, ignoring case, a tag this project already carries puts that tag at the head of the list in its stored casing, highlighted and marked as already on the project, with other matches below it; Enter on it adds nothing and closes the box. A casing change typed into one chip therefore shows the tag's real casing and changes nothing; changing a tag's casing is a rename in the Tags list.
why: Otherwise the list is blind to carried tags: typing api on a project carrying api would add whatever else contains the text (api-docs) or do nothing unexplained, and a case-only chip edit would silently not take (review-001 F3).
rules_out: Offering a Tags-list rename from a case-only chip edit: a keystroke on one project silently recasing the tag on every project that carries it is the bigger surprise.

text: With typed text, tags that start with it rank above tags that only contain it, most-used first within each group, and the top row is the best match: a highlights acom, per highlights personal, and ail still lists detaillab.
why: People type the start of the word they mean; ranking by use alone turns a short prefix into a guess at the user's favourite tag (a would add personal, with acom fourth) (review-001 F2).

text: When the typed text is not already a tag, a + new tag "…" row closes the list and is the way to create one; when nothing matches, it is the only row and is highlighted, so Enter creates the tag.
why: Creating a new tag is a deliberate move, while the default keystroke reuses an existing tag.

text: The dropdown has a bounded height that fits the space available and scrolls beyond it — it never runs off the screen however many tags exist.
why: The user pushed back on the list showing every tag: with a hundred tags it would run off the bottom of the screen.

text: The + new tag "…" row is pinned at the dropdown's foot, outside the scrolling part, so it is visible whenever it exists; only the matches scroll.
why: A create row placed last would scroll out of sight below many matches (a short new tag like e2e among tags containing e), so creating would look impossible; the way to create a tag is never hidden. Pinning costs one row of list height whenever the create row shows (review-001 F4).

text: The dropdown floats over whatever lies below the box — the modal's footer, the page behind — rather than being fitted inside the modal; when the screen below the box is too short for a few rows plus the create row, it opens above the box instead.
why: TAGS is the edit screen's last field, with only the modal's footer and frame below it, so a dropdown fitted into the remaining space could get a row or none on a short terminal; the dropdown never collapses to nothing (review-001 F4).

text: Where is tag management reached from, and how do rename, delete and per-tag counts behave?
A Tags list, opened by a key on the projects page, manages tags: every tag in use, each with how many projects carry it.
why: Tags have no home of their own (a tag exists only as the union of what projects carry); the projects page is the natural parent, since tags live on projects and the page already owns the edit screen. Management and bulk tagging collapsed into one surface once membership was seen as the thing both act on.

text: The Tags list is reached from the projects page only; the sessions page gains no key for it.
why: Tags live on projects, the sessions page has its own tags editor for a session's project, and x already reaches the projects page in one key (review-001 F10).

text: The Tags list is ordered most-used first, ties alphabetical — the order the suggestions dropdown uses, so a tag sits in the same place on both surfaces.
why: Derived from Tag Suggestions, which orders tags by how many projects carry them.

text: r renames a tag on every project that carries it; renaming into a tag that already exists, ignoring case, merges the two after a confirmation showing the counts involved, and a project carrying both ends up with the one. A rename that changes only the casing is a plain rename.
why: Renaming today means editing every project one by one; Tag Case settled that renaming into an existing tag is a merge and a case-only rename is a rename.

text: d removes a tag from every project after a confirmation showing how many projects carry it.
why: Deleting a tag today means editing every project that carries it one by one.

text: Missing projects (tagged projects whose folder has gone) count toward each tag they carry and appear in its checklist marked missing; the delete confirmation states how many of the projects losing the tag are missing and will be cleared with it.
why: Project-link keeps a tagged project marked missing when its folder disappears and removes untagged ones on every housekeeping path, so removing a missing project's last tag leaves it to housekeeping like any untagged missing project.

text: Every way of removing a missing project's last tag says so first: unticking its last tag in a checklist, or x on its last chip in the edit screen or the sessions-list tag editor, asks in one line before removing that the project's folder is gone and with no tags left Portal will clear the project. Housekeeping still does the clearing at its next pass — no tag surface removes a project itself. Renames and merges never take a tag off a project and ask nothing.
why: A missing project is kept only because it carries a tag — the user's work — and removal is housekeeping's, the same on every path; the loss is shown before it happens (review-001 F7).

text: A + new tag row in the Tags list asks for a name and opens its empty checklist; a name that matches an existing tag, ignoring case, is that tag and opens that tag's checklist instead; a new tag with nothing ticked when the checklist closes leaves nothing behind, since a tag exists only while a project carries it.
why: There is no tag registry: a tag exists only as the union of what projects carry.

text: Where does bulk tagging happen? Marking several items exists only on the sessions list today (m, multi-select), where it opens several sessions at once.

Bulk tagging is the tag's project checklist in the Tags list: Enter on a tag opens a checklist of every saved project, ticked where it carries the tag; Space ticks or unticks the highlighted project, adding or removing the tag on it; typing narrows the list. A new tag opens on an empty checklist.
why: Bulk add and bulk remove sit in one place with the tag's current membership visible while it changes; the mark-first case (these three new projects all get personal) is served tag-first at the same cost, while mark-first cannot show a tag's membership. Families of projects (folio with folio/api and folio/sdk) are the motivating case. Accepted cost: the checklist holds every saved project (66 on the install), so finding rows relies on typing to filter.
rules_out: Mark projects first, then pick a tag: multi-select on the projects page then add-tag or remove-tag on the marked set — needs separate add and remove paths and shows nothing of who already carries the tag.

text: The projects page gains no multi-select.
why: Single-project tagging stays in the edit screen, so a projects-page multi-select would add a mode for nothing the checklist lacks.

text: The sessions list's multi-select keeps its one job, opening several sessions at once; it does not tag. A session's project is tagged from the sessions list one session at a time.
why: Bulk tagging works on one tag at a time in a tag's checklist, so suggestions never span several projects and each row shows that project's current state; the guessed-link rule never meets a set of marked sessions (review-001 F8).

text: A tag's checklist lists the projects in the projects page's order; a tick or untick leaves the row where it is, so the highlight never jumps.
why: Derived from project-link's link chooser, which reuses the projects list exactly as the projects page draws it.

text: Each tick or untick in a tag's checklist is written at once, with no save step; Esc closes the checklist.
why: Derived from the edit screen's existing behaviour: each chip is saved the moment it is added or removed, and closing the screen never discards.

text: Measured 2026-10-26 by nearest enclosing saved project (folders compared without case): 36 projects sit directly under a tagged project and 31 carry exactly its tags. The five that do not are ~/.config/kit and ~/code (untagged under the home-folder project, tagged personal), acom/mach2 (untagged under acom), and fabric/flowx/flowx-api and fabric/packages/laravel-workflow (personal under fabric). Four untagged top-level projects (~/Code/kit, packages, switchboard, terrace) sit directly under the untagged ~/code project, which itself sits under the home folder.

command: python3 -I -c "import json,os; ps={p['path']:p for p in json.load(open(os.path.expanduser('~/.config/portal/projects.json')))['projects']}; enc=lambda q: max((k for k in ps if k!=q and (q.lower()+'/').startswith(k.lower()+'/')), key=len, default=None); r=[(q,e) for q in ps for e in [enc(q)] if e and ps[e].get('tags')]; print(len(r), sum(sorted(ps[q].get('tags') or [])==sorted(ps[e]['tags']) for q,e in r))"

text: Does a newly saved project inherit the tags of the project whose folder encloses it — and if so, from which enclosing project, on which saves, whether later changes reach it, whether the user sees it, and what it does to housekeeping?

When Portal saves a project that did not exist — at session creation, or from the link chooser's "save <folder> as a project" — it gives the new project the tags carried at that moment by the deepest saved project whose folder contains it, folders compared by their on-disk spelling (project-link's Folder Name Case).
why: The folder layout predicts the user's own tagging for 31 of 36 nested projects, and the five misses are cheaper to fix by removing one tag than the hits are to add by hand; acom/mach2 would have been tagged acom with no action. Inheritance runs only on the saves the user's actions make. The log names this the call closest to taste.
rules_out: No inheritance (today): every family member is tagged by hand, and an untagged project silently drops out of the family's tag filter until it is.

text: When the nearest enclosing saved project carries no tags, nothing is inherited; Portal never looks further up.
why: Walking up would make the home folder's personal the default for nearly everything: every new project under the Code folder would take it, though the Code-folder project — the nearest statement — carries nothing.
rules_out: Walk up past an untagged enclosing project to the nearest tagged one.

text: The copy is made once: a later change to the enclosing project's tags never reaches projects already saved, and the inherited tags are the new project's own, edited and removed like any other.
why: Project-link's standing decision that projects stand alone — a tag on a project is the project's, whatever happens to its parent later.
rules_out: Live inheritance: tags would appear and vanish on projects the user never touched, the measured exceptions would need an override mechanism, and it reintroduces folder containment as a grouping rule, which project-link rejected.

text: Re-pointing a missing project at a new folder and merging two projects keep and combine their own tags and inherit nothing; projects that exist when this ships are not touched.
why: Inheritance applies only to a project Portal saves that did not exist.

text: Nothing announces the inheritance; the inherited tags show wherever tags show (By Tag, the Tags list counts, the edit screen).
why: Creation's save is silent today.

text: Inherited tags are tags for housekeeping: a nested project that inherited one is kept, marked missing, when its folder disappears, rather than clearing itself.
why: Weighed and accepted: on the retained logs one traceable deleted folder (dex/business) would have lingered; a lingering missing project is listed on the projects page and by portal doctor, and cleared by deleting it or removing its tag (with Tag Management's confirmation).

text: Does sessions-list tagging treat a session whose project is a guess (or has no saved project at all, such as an Unknown session) the same as one whose project is recorded?

cites.section: Tagging a session's project from the sessions list when its project link is a guess > Context

text: Tagging from the sessions list on a session whose project is a guess opens the link-to-project chooser with the guessed project highlighted; picking a project (the guess or another) records the session's link, and the tag editor then opens on that project. Tagging never writes onto a guessed project.
why: The guess is tolerable because it corrects itself when the pane moves, and a tag does not — so the moment a tag would be written is when a guess has to become a choice (a guessed home-folder project would otherwise take a durable tag, and with it every session filed there). Highlighting the guess makes the right-guess case nearly free and leaves the session with a recorded link.
rules_out: Treat a guess like a recorded link: a wrong guess puts a durable tag on an unrelated project, and through it on every other session filed there, with nothing shown.
Refuse, pointing at the link action: the same chooser behind an extra hop.

text: What is the tag editor opened from the sessions list: what the user lands in, whether it removes as well as adds, where Esc returns, and how the user sees which project they are tagging?

Tagging from the sessions list opens a tags-only editor over the list: the edit screen's TAGS field on its own — the project's chips, + add with the suggestions dropdown, x to remove the highlighted chip.
why: The TAGS field's behaviour exactly, so nothing new to learn; discovery's wording — tagging from the sessions list without the edit screen — rules the full edit screen out here.
rules_out: The full projects edit screen over the sessions list: brings renaming and aliases into a moment that is only about tags.
A single add-a-tag box: cannot remove a tag and shows nothing of what the project already carries.

text: The sessions-list tags editor is titled with the project's name and folder, so the user sees which project they are tagging.
why: The Flat view shows nothing of which project a session belongs to, so the editor's title is where the user sees what they are about to tag.

text: Changes in the sessions-list tags editor save as they are made, as on the edit screen.

text: Esc closes the sessions-list tags editor and returns to the same session row.

why: Stated in the decision; no line shows it decided beyond that.

text: Which keys do tagging a session's project, linking a session to a project and opening the Tags list take, given t opens the theme panel on both pages and new actions compete for footer space?

t opens tagging on both pages: on the sessions page the tags-only editor for the highlighted session's project (through the link chooser first when its project is not a saved project), on the projects page the Tags list. t takes the theme key's place among the footer's core keys on both pages.
why: The key with the strong mnemonic belongs to the action used more often: a theme is set once and rarely revisited, tagging recurs.
rules_out: Theme keeps t and tags take g: a weak mnemonic for the more frequent action.
#, the natural tag symbol: on a UK Mac layout it is Option-3.

text: The theme panel moves to c (colours), opened from help only, out of the footer. This epic's specification carries the move as a change to existing behaviour (the theming-system specification's "Key: t").
why: The theme panel's only cost of moving is the user's own muscle memory, and leaving the footer keeps its width.

text: The NO_COLOR filter that hides the theme key now applies to c; t stays available under NO_COLOR.
why: There is no colour to theme under NO_COLOR, while tagging needs no colour.

text: The link-to-project action takes l on the sessions page, listed in help, not in the footer.
why: The link action is rare; project-link left its key to this topic.

text: README and docs/theming.md, which name t as the theme key, change with the move to c.
why: Both document the theme key today.

text: The sessions-list tags editor uses exactly the TAGS field's keys: left and right move between chips, Enter on + add starts a tag and on a chip edits it, x removes the highlighted chip, Esc closes.
why: The editor is the edit screen's TAGS field on its own.

text: In a tag's checklist typing narrows the list, Space ticks or unticks the highlighted project, up and down move, and Esc clears a typed filter first and otherwise returns to the Tags list.
why: The checklist is a modal list with no letter actions, so typing can narrow it directly as project-link's link chooser is narrowed; Space follows the checkbox convention; Esc behaves as in Portal's filtered lists.

text: In the Tags list up and down move, Enter opens the highlighted tag's checklist (on the + new tag row, starts a new tag), r renames, d deletes, / filters, and Esc returns to the projects page.
why: Matches the pages it sits beside: d deletes on the projects page, r renames on the sessions page, / filters every Portal list, and Esc steps back from the edit screen.

text: How are the new surfaces designed in the current look, including the no-colour mode: the suggestions dropdown, the sessions-list tags editor, the Tags list, a tag's checklist, and the confirmations (merge with counts, delete with its count and missing projects, removing a missing project's last tag)?

Each new surface is designed in Paper, in the existing Portal design file, starting from an existing design. Behaviour — what each surface shows, its markers, its scrolling and placement rules, its keys — is fixed by this discussion; the look is the Paper design's.

text: AcquireDaemonLock (internal/state/daemon_lock.go:55-77) opens whatever inode daemon.lock resolves to and flocks it; flock excludes per inode, not per path, and nothing checks after the open that the locked inode is still the one at the path (no O_EXCL create, no stat cross-check). text: Root cause: the daemon-singleton contract is not enforced end to end. daemon.lock excludes per inode rather than per path, the kill-barrier reaches only daemons bound to the saver pane, and CaptureStructure is not per-session error tolerant; violated together (here, a leaked test daemon on another tmux server holding a stale daemon.lock inode), several daemons write sessions.json and run destructive scrollback GC against one dir. The three symptoms are three downstream effects of that one broken-singleton state.

text: Directly affected: daemon_lock.go, killSaverAndWaitForDaemon, CaptureStructure's per-session loop, the bootstrap orchestrator and the test infrastructure (tmuxtest and state-daemon integration tests). Potentially affected: anything treating sessions.json as authoritative (restore, the TUI list, `portal clean`) and any user upgrading while a prior version's daemon still runs, the inode gap being the upgrade-time landmine.
